q.q: The Father of Mycology is:
q.e: Micheli — Nova Plantarum Genera (1729).

q.q: The word 'virus' (contagium vivum fluidum) was coined by:
q.e: Beijerinck, 1898.

q.q: The first systemic fungicide was:
q.e: Carboxin (oxathiin, 1966).

q.q: Physiologic races of a pathogen were first demonstrated by:
q.e: Stakman — wheat stem rust.

q.q: Mendelian inheritance of disease resistance was shown by:
q.e: Biffen — wheat yellow rust, 1905.

q.q: The Father of Nematology is:
q.e: N. A. Cobb.

q.q: The 'Dictionary of the Fungi' is associated with:
q.e: Ainsworth (Ainsworth & Bisby).

q.q: Woronin bodies are found in the septa of the:
q.e: Ascomycetes — they plug the simple septal pore after injury.

q.q: Basidiospores are borne on the basidium in a manner that is:
q.e: Exogenous — on sterigmata; ascospores are endogenous.

q.q: The zygospore is the sexual spore of the:
q.e: Zygomycetes (e.g. Rhizopus).

q.q: An apothecium is an ascocarp that is:
q.e: Open, cup-shaped (e.g. Sclerotinia); a cleistothecium is closed.

q.q: The powdery mildews bear their asci inside a:
q.e: Cleistothecium — a closed ascocarp with appendages.

q.q: The haustorium of a biotroph functions in:
o: Dispersal of the asexual spore load
Attachment onto the outer leaf surface
q.e: Nutrient absorption inside the living host cell.

q.q: Yeasts characteristically reproduce asexually by:
q.e: Budding — a small daughter cell pinches off.

q.q: The repeating (secondary) spore stage of a cereal rust is the:
q.e: Urediniospore — dikaryotic, re-infects the same host.

q.q: Puccinia graminis tritici is best described as a rust that is:
q.e: Macrocyclic, heteroecious — five spore stages on wheat and barberry.

q.q: A mushroom (toadstool) is technically a:
q.e: Basidiocarp — the basidium-bearing fruiting body.

q.q: The imperfect fungi (Deuteromycetes) are those which:
q.e: Lack (or lost) a known sexual stage — reproduce by conidia.

q.q: Cellulose walls and coenocytic mycelium together indicate the:
q.e: Oomycetes — non-fungal, cellulose walls, no chitin.

q.q: The 'perfect' (sexual) state of a fungus is termed its:
q.e: Teleomorph; anamorph is the asexual state.

q.q: Karyogamy and meiosis in the Basidiomycetes occur in the:
q.e: Young basidium — the only diploid phase; meiosis yields four basidiospores.

q.q: Early blight of potato and tomato is caused by:
q.e: Alternaria solani — concentric 'target-board' lesions.

q.q: Stem (black) rust of wheat is caused by:
q.e: Puccinia graminis tritici.

q.q: Yellow (stripe) rust of wheat is caused by:
q.e: Puccinia striiformis — cool-climate stripe rust.

q.q: Charcoal rot / dry root rot of many crops is caused by:
q.e: Macrophomina phaseolina — microsclerotia in the tissue.

q.q: Panama wilt of banana is caused by:
q.e: Fusarium oxysporum f.sp. cubense — TR4 threatens Grand Naine.

q.q: White mould / stem rot of many vegetables is caused by:
q.e: Sclerotinia sclerotiorum — black sclerotia in white mycelium.

q.q: Black scurf and stem canker of potato are caused by:
q.e: Rhizoctonia solani — sclerotia stuck on the tuber surface.

q.q: Anthracnose diseases are typically caused by species of:
q.e: Colletotrichum — sunken lesions with acervuli.

q.q: Ergot of rye is caused by:
q.e: Claviceps purpurea — sclerotia contain ergot alkaloids.

q.q: Foot rot / gummosis of citrus is caused by:
q.e: Phytophthora (P. parasitica / citrophthora).

q.q: Loose smut of barley is caused by:
q.e: Ustilago nuda — internally seed-borne.

q.q: Powdery mildew of cereals is caused by:
q.e: Blumeria (Erysiphe) graminis.

q.q: Sheath blight of rice is caused by:
q.e: Rhizoctonia solani — banded sheath lesions.

q.q: Downy mildew of grapevine is caused by an oomycete of the genus:
q.e: Plasmopara (P. viticola).

q.q: Damping-off caused by a fungus with brown, right-angled branching hyphae is:
q.e: Rhizoctonia solani — hyphae branch at right angles with a basal constriction.

q.q: Wildfire of tobacco is caused by:
q.e: Pseudomonas syringae pv. tabaci — tabtoxin gives chlorotic haloes.

q.q: Halo blight of bean is caused by:
o: Clavibacter flaccumfaciens causing wilt of bean
Pantoea agglomerans causing a brown seed rot
q.e: P. savastanoi pv. phaseolicola — phaseolotoxin.

q.q: Common scab of potato is caused by:
q.e: Streptomyces scabies — a Gram-positive actinomycete.

q.q: Bacterial canker of tomato is caused by:
q.e: Clavibacter michiganensis subsp. michiganensis — Gram-positive.

q.q: Black rot of crucifers is caused by:
q.e: X. campestris pv. campestris — V-shaped marginal lesions.

q.q: Ratoon stunting of sugarcane is caused by:
q.e: Leifsonia xyli — a fastidious Gram-positive, xylem-limited.

q.q: Olive knot disease is caused by:
q.e: P. savastanoi pv. savastanoi — hyperplastic knots.

q.q: Grassy shoot of sugarcane is caused by a:
q.e: Phytoplasma — leafhopper-transmitted.

q.q: Phytoplasma diseases are typically transmitted by:
q.e: Leafhoppers (and psyllids) — persistent, propagative.

q.q: The majority of plant-pathogenic bacteria are:
q.e: Gram-negative rods — the coryneform group is the Gram-positive exception.

q.q: Cucumber mosaic virus is notable for its:
q.e: Very wide host range — an aphid-borne cucumovirus.

q.q: Potato virus X particles are:
q.e: Flexuous filaments — a potexvirus.

q.q: Bud necrosis of groundnut is caused by a virus transmitted by:
q.e: Thrips — a tospovirus (persistent, propagative).

q.q: Papaya ringspot virus is transmitted by aphids in a manner that is:
q.e: Non-persistent — a potyvirus, stylet-borne.

q.q: Citrus tristeza virus is classified as a:
q.e: Closterovirus — the longest plant-virus particle, aphid-borne.

q.q: Cauliflower mosaic virus is unusual among plant viruses in having:
q.e: dsDNA — a pararetrovirus; source of the 35S promoter.

q.q: An umbravirus, lacking a coat protein, depends for aphid spread on a helper:
q.e: Luteovirus — which encapsidates it (groundnut rosette complex).

q.q: Sugarcane mosaic virus is transmitted by:
q.e: Aphids, non-persistently — a potyvirus.

q.q: The classic local-lesion assay host for TMV is:
q.e: Nicotiana glutinosa — Holmes, 1929.

q.q: A satellite RNA differs from a satellite virus in that it:
o: Is larger than the helper virus
Has no coat protein of its own
q.e: No coat protein — it is encapsidated by the helper virus.

q.q: The reniform (kidney-shaped) nematode is:
q.e: Rotylenchulus reniformis — a semi-endoparasite.

q.q: The burrowing nematode causing toppling of banana is:
q.e: Radopholus similis.

q.q: Lesion nematodes belong to the genus:
q.e: Pratylenchus — migratory endoparasites causing root lesions.

q.q: The rice root nematode is:
q.e: Hirschmanniella oryzae.

q.q: Cyst nematodes are distinguished by the female forming a:
q.e: A cyst — the tanned dead body protecting the eggs.

q.q: Reproduction in most Meloidogyne species is by:
q.e: Parthenogenesis in many species — no male needed.

q.q: A compound-interest (polycyclic) disease is exemplified by:
q.e: Late blight — many cycles per season.

q.q: The Gompertz disease-progress curve reaches maximum rate at about:
q.e: 37% (1/e) — asymmetric, unlike the logistic (50%).

q.q: Apple scab infection periods are predicted by the:
q.e: Mills table — leaf-wetness duration versus temperature.

q.q: The incubation period of a disease ends at:
q.e: First symptoms; the latent period ends at sporulation.

q.q: Disease incidence is expressed as the:
q.e: Proportion of units infected; severity is proportion of tissue affected.

q.q: A sanitation measure such as roguing acts mainly by reducing:
q.e: Reduces x₀ — cutting the starting inoculum.

q.q: The logistic model is linearised by plotting against time the:
q.e: Logit — its slope is the apparent infection rate r.

q.q: A monocyclic (simple-interest) disease typically has:
q.e: One cycle — from a fixed initial inoculum, e.g. smuts and wilts.

q.q: Copper-based fungicides act as:
q.e: Protectant contacts — must be on the surface before infection.

q.q: Azole (triazole) fungicides inhibit the biosynthesis of:
q.e: Ergosterol — via C14-demethylase (DMI).

q.q: Benzimidazoles such as carbendazim act on:
q.e: β-tubulin — a single-site systemic mode.

q.q: Streptocycline / streptomycin is used mainly against:
q.e: Bacterial diseases — an antibiotic bactericide.

q.q: Pseudomonas fluorescens is used in plant protection as a:
q.e: Biocontrol/PGPR — antibiosis, siderophores, induced resistance.

q.q: Neem-based formulations are examples of:
q.e: Botanicals — azadirachtin as the active principle.

q.q: Strobilurin (QoI) fungicides inhibit:
q.e: Complex III (Qo site) — G143A confers resistance.

q.q: Metalaxyl combined with mancozeb is used chiefly against:
q.e: Oomycete diseases — systemic + contact combination.

q.q: Agrobacterium transfers to the plant genome its:
q.e: T-DNA bounded by border repeats.

q.q: Effector-triggered immunity is mediated by:
q.e: NBS-LRR (NLR) proteins recognising effectors.

q.q: The receptor FLS2 recognises the bacterial epitope:
q.e: flg22 — a conserved flagellin peptide (a PAMP).

q.q: Agrobacterium vir genes are switched on by the host phenolic:
q.e: Acetosyringone — sensed by VirA/VirG.

q.q: In the guard hypothesis, R proteins such as RPM1 monitor the host protein:
q.e: RIN4 — its modification by effectors is sensed indirectly.

q.q: The rice bacterial-blight resistance gene Xa21 encodes a:
q.e: Receptor kinase — a surface LRR-kinase.

q.q: The viral silencing suppressor P19 is encoded by a:
q.e: Tombusvirus — P19 sequesters siRNA duplexes.

q.q: The first plant R gene cloned, maize Hm1, encodes a(n):
q.e: HC-toxin reductase — an atypical R gene.

q.q: T-toxin of Bipolaris maydis race T targets the maize protein:
q.e: URF13 — of Texas male-sterile cytoplasm; the 1970 SCLB epidemic.

q.q: Fumonisin, a mycotoxin, is produced by:
q.e: F. verticillioides — inhibits ceramide synthase.

q.q: Cercosporin is unusual as a toxin because it is:
q.e: Light-activated — a photosensitising perylenequinone.

q.q: Fusicoccin causes irreversible stomatal opening by activating the:
q.e: PM H+-ATPase — via 14-3-3 proteins.

q.q: Phaseolotoxin (halo blight of bean) inhibits:
q.e: OCTase — the classic swap-partner of tabtoxin→glutamine synthetase.

q.q: Marsh spot of pea is caused by deficiency of:
q.e: Manganese — brown spot in the cotyledon.

q.q: Internal cork of apple is caused by deficiency of:
q.e: Boron.

q.q: Tipburn of lettuce is caused by deficiency of:
q.e: Calcium — like blossom-end rot, water-relations driven.

q.q: Grey speck of oats is caused by deficiency of:
q.e: Manganese.

q.q: The polymerase chain reaction (PCR) was invented by:
q.e: Kary Mullis (Nobel 1993).

q.q: Bacterial species are commonly identified by sequencing the:
q.e: 16S rRNA; ITS is the fungal barcode.

q.q: Nematodes are extracted from soil/tissue using a:
q.e: Baermann funnel — active nematodes migrate down into water.

q.q: LAMP is valued for field diagnostics because it is:
q.e: Isothermal — ~60–65 °C with Bst polymerase, read by colour/turbidity.

q.q: Sclerotia germinate to produce apothecia in the genus:
q.e: Sclerotinia — carpogenic germination gives stalked apothecia.

q.q: The Father of Plant Bacteriology is:
q.e: Erwin F. Smith established bacterial plant pathology.

q.q: Bordeaux mixture was introduced by:
q.e: Millardet (1885), against grape downy mildew.

q.q: The gene-for-gene hypothesis was proposed by:
q.e: Flor, from flax and flax-rust studies.

q.q: The first viroid discovered was:
q.e: PSTVd — Diener, 1971.

q.q: Tobacco mosaic virus was first crystallised by:
q.e: Stanley, 1935 (Nobel 1946).

q.q: The Father of Indian Plant Pathology is:
q.e: Sir E. J. Butler, first Imperial Mycologist at Pusa.

q.q: Recurrence of wheat rusts in India was traced by:
q.e: K. C. Mehta — annual survival in the Himalayas and Nilgiris.

q.q: The 'one gene–one enzyme' hypothesis came from work on:
q.e: Beadle & Tatum, using Neurospora.

q.q: Coenocytic (aseptate) mycelium is characteristic of the:
q.e: Lower fungi have coenocytic hyphae; higher fungi are septate.

q.q: Clamp connections are a diagnostic feature of the:
q.e: Basidiomycetes — clamps maintain the dikaryon.

q.q: Flagellate zoospores are produced by the:
q.e: Chytrids and Oomycetes; higher fungi lack motile spores.

q.q: Rhizomorphs (root-like hyphal strands) are typical of:
q.e: Armillaria — bootlace fungus.

q.q: The dolipore septum is found in the:
q.e: Basidiomycetes — a barrel-shaped septum flanked by parenthesomes.

q.q: The sexual spore of the Oomycetes is the:
q.e: Oospore — formed after oogonium–antheridium fusion.

q.q: Rust and powdery-mildew fungi are nutritionally:
q.e: Obligate biotrophs — needing living host tissue.

q.q: Aeciospores of a rust are produced within the:
q.e: Aecium; pycnia (spermogonia) bear pycniospores.

q.q: Sclerotia function primarily as:
q.e: Resting structures — melanised, long-lived in soil.

q.q: The teliospores of smut fungi are also known as:
q.e: Chlamydospores — thick-walled resting spores (brand spores).

q.q: Fairy rings on turf are typically caused by:
q.e: Marasmius (and other basidiomycetes) growing outward radially.

q.q: Karyogamy in a rust life cycle occurs in the:
q.e: Teliospore — where the dikaryon fuses before meiosis.

q.q: A pycnidium is a fruiting body that is:
q.e: Flask-shaped, asexual (conidia); a perithecium is its sexual look-alike.

q.q: Vesicular-arbuscular mycorrhiza belong to the:
q.e: Glomeromycota — obligate symbionts forming arbuscules.

q.q: The imperfect (asexual) state of a fungus is called its:
q.e: Anamorph; the sexual state is the teleomorph.

q.q: Late blight of potato is caused by:
q.e: Phytophthora infestans — the Irish famine pathogen.

q.q: Blast of rice is caused by:
q.e: Magnaporthe oryzae (Pyricularia oryzae).

q.q: Tikka disease of groundnut is caused by:
q.e: Cercospora (early and late leaf spot).

q.q: Red rot of sugarcane is caused by:
q.e: Colletotrichum falcatum (Glomerella tucumanensis).

q.q: Karnal bunt of wheat is caused by:
q.e: Tilletia indica (Neovossia indica) — partial bunt, fishy smell.

q.q: Wart disease of potato is caused by:
q.e: Synchytrium endobioticum — an obligate chytrid, quarantine pathogen.

q.q: White rust of crucifers is caused by:
q.e: Albugo candida — an oomycete (white blisters).

q.q: Downy mildew of grapevine is caused by:
q.e: Plasmopara viticola — the disease that prompted Bordeaux mixture.

q.q: Wilt of pigeonpea is caused by:
q.e: Fusarium udum.

q.q: Apple scab is caused by:
q.e: Venturia inaequalis — forecast by Mills periods.

q.q: Ergot of pearl millet (bajra) is caused by:
q.e: Claviceps fusiformis.

q.q: Sigatoka leaf spot of banana is caused by:
q.e: Mycosphaerella (yellow and black Sigatoka).

q.q: Damping-off of seedlings is most commonly caused by:
q.e: Pythium — pre- and post-emergence damping-off.

q.q: Ear cockle and tundu are associated on wheat with the nematode:
q.e: Anguina tritici — which also carries the tundu bacterium.

q.q: Sett rot / pineapple disease of sugarcane is caused by:
q.e: Ceratocystis paradoxa — a pineapple-like smell in rotting setts.

q.q: Citrus canker is caused by:
q.e: Xanthomonas citri subsp. citri — raised corky lesions.

q.q: Bacterial leaf blight of rice is caused by:
q.e: X. oryzae pv. oryzae — kresek and leaf blight phases.

q.q: Crown gall of many hosts is caused by:
q.e: Agrobacterium tumefaciens — T-DNA transfer from the Ti plasmid.

q.q: Fire blight of apple and pear is caused by:
q.e: Erwinia amylovora — shepherd's-crook shoots and ooze.

q.q: Which plant-pathogenic bacterium is Gram-positive?
q.e: Clavibacter — most plant pathogens are Gram-negative.

q.q: Bacterial wilt / brown rot of potato and tomato is caused by:
q.e: Ralstonia solanacearum — bacterial ooze streams from cut stems.

q.q: Angular leaf spot / black arm of cotton is caused by:
q.e: Xanthomonas citri pv. malvacearum.

q.q: Soft rot of vegetables is chiefly caused by:
q.e: Pectobacterium — pectolytic maceration of tissue.

q.q: Phytoplasmas and spiroplasmas are distinctive in being:
q.e: Wall-less Mollicutes — phloem-limited, insect-borne.

q.q: Agrobacterium inserts its T-DNA into the host from the:
q.e: Ti (tumour-inducing) plasmid; Ri plasmid causes hairy root.

q.q: Tobacco mosaic virus particles are:
q.e: Rigid rods, ~300 × 18 nm, helical symmetry.

q.q: Banana bunchy top virus is transmitted by:
q.e: Pentalonia nigronervosa — persistent, circulative.

q.q: Leaf-curl (begomovirus) diseases are transmitted by:
q.e: Whitefly — persistent circulative transmission of ssDNA begomoviruses.

q.q: Rice tungro is transmitted by the:
q.e: Green leafhopper — RTBV needs RTSV as helper.

q.q: Coconut cadang-cadang disease is caused by a:
q.e: Viroid (CCCVd) — naked circular RNA.

q.q: Tomato spotted wilt and bud-necrosis viruses are transmitted by:
q.e: Thrips — persistent, propagative tospoviruses.

q.q: Potato leaf roll virus is transmitted by aphids in a manner that is:
q.e: Persistent circulative, phloem-limited (a luteovirus).

q.q: A viroid differs from a virus in that it:
o: Has RNA but no protein coat
q.e: Naked infectious RNA — no capsid, no coding for protein.

q.q: Vein clearing followed by mosaic is typically an early sign of a:
q.e: Viral — vein clearing is a classic early symptom.

q.q: The begomovirus betasatellite protein βC1 acts as a:
o: Coat protein of the virion shell
q.e: Silencing suppressor (VSR) — helping overcome host defence.

q.q: Root-knot galls are caused by:
q.e: Meloidogyne — inducing giant cells and galls.

q.q: The golden cyst nematode of potato is:
q.e: Globodera rostochiensis.

q.q: Slow decline of citrus is caused by:
q.e: Tylenchulus semipenetrans — the citrus nematode.

q.q: Molya disease of cereals is caused by:
q.e: Heterodera avenae — the cereal cyst nematode.

q.q: The feeding organ that distinguishes plant-parasitic nematodes is the:
q.e: Stylet — a hollow spear to pierce and feed on cells.

q.q: White-tip disease of rice is caused by the nematode:
q.e: Aphelenchoides besseyi — a seed-borne foliar nematode.

q.q: The disease triangle is formed by host, environment and:
q.e: Pathogen — all three must coincide; adding time gives the tetrahedron.

q.q: AUDPC stands for the:
o: Average unit of disease per crop
q.e: Area Under the Disease-Progress Curve — integrates severity over time.

q.q: Horizontal resistance, in Vanderplank's terms, reduces the:
q.e: r — rate-reducing; vertical resistance reduces x₀.

q.q: Late blight of potato is forecast by:
q.e: BLITECAST / Beaumont periods — humidity and temperature based.

q.q: A monocyclic (single-cycle) disease is exemplified by:
q.e: Loose smut — one systemic infection per season.

q.q: The 'inoculum potential' concept was defined by:
q.e: Garrett — energy of growth available for infection.

q.q: The apparent infection rate (r) is a measure of the:
q.e: Speed of the epidemic — the slope of the logit progress line.

q.q: The Vertifolia effect describes the:
o: Gain of durable resistance across generations
Loss of horizontal resistance under a major gene
Toxin-induced collapse of the host tissue
Rapid spread of disease by an insect vector
q.e: Loss of horizontal resistance during breeding under a major gene.

q.q: Which is a systemic fungicide?
q.e: Carbendazim (benzimidazole) — xylem-mobile; the others are contacts.

q.q: Bordeaux mixture is prepared from copper sulphate and:
q.e: Lime (calcium hydroxide) — Burgundy mixture uses washing soda.

q.q: Tricyclazole controls rice blast by inhibiting:
q.e: Melanin biosynthesis — the appressorium cannot generate turgor.

q.q: Mancozeb is best classified as a:
q.e: Multisite contact (dithiocarbamate) — low resistance risk.

q.q: Metalaxyl is specific for controlling:
q.e: Oomycetes — it blocks rRNA synthesis in that group.

q.q: Loose smut of wheat is best managed by:
o: Foliar contact protectant sprays at the booting stage
Deep soil fumigation carried out before the crop is sown
Roguing out every infected plant at the flowering stage
q.e: Systemic (carboxin) or hot-water seed treatment — the fungus is embryo-borne.

q.q: Trichoderma is widely used as a:
q.e: Biocontrol agent — mycoparasitism and antibiosis against soil pathogens.

q.q: Soil solarisation controls soil-borne pathogens mainly by:
o: Adding copper compounds to the soil
q.e: Solar heating under transparent mulch during hot months.

q.q: PAMP-triggered immunity begins with recognition by:
o: Small interfering RNAs produced by the host cell
q.e: PRRs — e.g. FLS2 detecting flagellin (flg22).

q.q: Most plant resistance (R) genes encode proteins of the class:
q.e: NBS-LRR (NLR) — recognising pathogen effectors.

q.q: The hypersensitive response (HR) is characterised by:
q.e: Rapid localised cell death confining a biotroph.

q.q: Systemic acquired resistance is mediated mainly by:
q.e: Salicylic acid → NPR1 → PR proteins.

q.q: RNA silencing degrades target RNA using:
q.e: siRNAs guiding the RISC complex to cleave viral RNA.

q.q: The flagellin epitope recognised by the FLS2 receptor is:
q.e: flg22 — a 22-amino-acid conserved peptide of flagellin.

q.q: In the gene-for-gene relationship, resistance results when:
o: The host lacks any R gene
Avr and R gene products match
q.e: Matching Avr and R triggers recognition and resistance (incompatibility).

q.q: Marker-free transgene-free crop editing is achieved by:
q.e: CRISPR-Cas SDN1/SDN2 — targeted edits with no foreign DNA left behind.

q.q: Victorin, the first host-specific toxin, is produced by a pathogen of:
q.e: Oats — Helminthosporium victoriae (Victoria blight).

q.q: Tabtoxin (wildfire of tobacco) inhibits the enzyme:
q.e: Glutamine synthetase — chlorotic haloes form.

q.q: HC-toxin of Cochliobolus carbonum acts as a(n):
q.e: HDAC inhibitor; the Hm1 reductase detoxifies it.

q.q: Aflatoxin is produced by:
q.e: Aspergillus flavus — carcinogenic (Turkey X disease).

q.q: Ergot alkaloids that cause ergotism are produced by:
q.e: Claviceps purpurea — 'St. Anthony's fire'.

q.q: Whiptail of cauliflower is caused by deficiency of:
q.e: Molybdenum — a physiological disorder, not a pathogen.

q.q: Khaira disease of rice is caused by deficiency of:
q.e: Zinc — bronzing of leaves in nurseries.

q.q: Blossom-end rot of tomato is caused by deficiency of:
q.e: Calcium — often water-stress-induced.

q.q: Phytoalexins are best described as:
q.e: Post-infection antimicrobials — e.g. pisatin, phaseollin.

q.q: ELISA is most widely used in plant pathology to detect:
q.e: Viruses — antibody-based serological detection (DAS-ELISA).

q.q: The universal DNA barcode for fungal identification is the:
q.e: ITS; 16S rRNA is for bacteria.

q.q: Koch's postulates are used to establish:
o: That an organism causes a disease
q.e: Causation — the classic proof that a specific microbe causes a disease.

q.q: The genome of the great majority of plant viruses is:
q.e: ss(+) RNA — the default plant virus; DNA viruses are the exception.

q.q: How many families of plant viruses have a single-stranded DNA genome?
o: None — the plant viruses are RNA
q.e: Two — Geminiviridae and Nanoviridae.

q.q: The only plant viruses with a double-stranded DNA genome belong to:
q.e: Caulimoviridae — and they replicate by reverse transcription (pararetroviruses).

q.q: The largest genus of plant viruses is:
q.e: Potyvirus — flexuous filaments, aphid-borne, pinwheel inclusions.

q.q: The longest plant-virus particle is found in the genus:
q.e: Closterovirus — e.g. Citrus tristeza, aphid-borne.

q.q: The smallest known infectious agents of plants are:
q.e: Viroids — naked circular RNA with no protein coat.

q.q: Tobacco mosaic virus is the type member of which rigid-rod genus?
q.e: Tobamovirus — the classic rigid rod.

q.q: Geminiviruses are named for their particles, which are:
q.e: Twin icosahedra with circular ssDNA.

q.q: Cylindrical 'pinwheel' inclusion bodies are diagnostic of the:
q.e: Potyvirus — the cylindrical inclusion protein forms pinwheels.

q.q: Rhabdoviruses of plants are distinctive in being:
q.e: Bullet-shaped, enveloped, negative-sense RNA.

q.q: Tomato spotted wilt virus (Tospovirus) is transmitted by:
q.e: Thrips — persistent, propagative; ambisense tripartite ssRNA.

q.q: Begomoviruses (leaf curls, ssDNA) are transmitted by:
q.e: Whitefly (Bemisia tabaci) — persistent circulative.

q.q: Luteoviruses (BYDV, PLRV) are transmitted by aphids in a manner that is:
q.e: Persistent circulative, phloem-limited (non-propagative).

q.q: Nepoviruses (e.g. grapevine fanleaf) are transmitted by:
q.e: Nematodes — Xiphinema/Longidorus; 'nepo' = nematode-polyhedral.

q.q: Tobraviruses (tobacco rattle) are transmitted by:
q.e: Nematodes — Trichodorus/Paratrichodorus.

q.q: Furoviruses and Benyviruses are transmitted by:
q.e: Soil fungi (Polymyxa) — 'furo' = fungus-transmitted rod.

q.q: Tenuiviruses (rice stripe) are transmitted by:
q.e: Planthoppers — thin filamentous, ss(−) RNA.

q.q: Cucumber mosaic virus (Cucumovirus) is transmitted by:
q.e: Aphids, non-persistent — with an exceptionally wide host range.

q.q: An umbravirus is unusual because it:
o: Carries a double-stranded DNA genome instead
Replicates only within its aphid vector body
Is by far the largest of all plant viruses
Has no coat protein; needs a luteovirus helper
q.e: No coat protein — encapsidated by a helper luteovirus (groundnut rosette).

q.q: Banana bunchy top virus has a genome that is:
q.e: Multipartite ssDNA (Babuvirus, Nanoviridae) — several small circles.

q.q: Cauliflower mosaic virus replicates its dsDNA genome by:
q.e: Reverse transcription — a pararetrovirus; source of the 35S promoter.

q.q: Rice tungro is a complex in which the bacilliform component (RTBV) needs:
o: RTSV as a helper for transmission
No helper virus of any kind at all
A soil-borne fungal vector to spread
q.e: RTSV (spherical) helper — the leafhopper transmits RTBV only with RTSV.

q.q: The dsRNA plant viruses of family Reoviridae are transmitted by:
q.e: Leaf/planthoppers — Phytoreo-, Fiji-, Oryzavirus; segmented dsRNA.

q.q: Cryptic viruses (Alphacryptovirus, dsRNA) are characterised by:
o: Aphid transmission in a persistent way
Whitefly transmission of a circulative type
q.e: No vector — transmitted only through seed and pollen; symptomless.

spec_detail.title: Specialist Set — Toxins, Teleomorphs, Fungicide MoA

q.q: Victorin (Victoria blight of oats) inhibits:
q.e: Glycine decarboxylase — the first host-specific toxin (H. victoriae).

q.q: T-toxin of Bipolaris maydis race T targets:
q.e: URF13 — Texas male-sterile cytoplasm; the 1970 SCLB epidemic.

q.q: HC-toxin of Cochliobolus carbonum acts as a(n):
q.e: HDAC inhibitor; detoxified by the Hm1 reductase.

q.q: AAL-toxin of Alternaria alternata f.sp. lycopersici inhibits:
q.e: Ceramide synthase — sphingolipid disruption in tomato.

q.q: PC-toxin (peritoxin) of Periconia circinata affects:
q.e: Milo disease of sorghum — a host-specific toxin.

q.q: Tabtoxin (wildfire of tobacco) inhibits:
q.e: Glutamine synthetase — ammonia accumulates, giving chlorotic haloes.

q.q: Phaseolotoxin (halo blight of bean) inhibits:
q.e: OCTase — the swap-partner of tabtoxin→glutamine synthetase.

q.q: Tentoxin causes variegated chlorosis by inhibiting:
q.e: Chloroplast ATP synthase (CF1) — blocking energy transfer.

q.q: Fusicoccin causes irreversible stomatal opening by activating:
q.e: PM H+-ATPase — via 14-3-3 proteins.

q.q: Coronatine, produced by Pseudomonas syringae, functions as a:
q.e: JA-Ile mimic — hijacking jasmonate signalling to reopen stomata.

q.q: Cercosporin is a photosensitising toxin that acts by generating:
q.e: Singlet oxygen — a light-activated perylenequinone.

q.q: Fumonisin (Fusarium verticillioides) inhibits:
q.e: Ceramide synthase — disrupting sphingolipid metabolism.

q.q: HS-toxin (helminthosporoside) is the host-specific toxin of:
q.e: Eyespot of sugarcane — Bipolaris sacchari.

q.q: AK-toxin is the host-specific toxin causing:
q.e: Black spot of Japanese pear — an Alternaria alternata pathotype.

q.q: The teleomorph of Fusarium moniliforme is:
q.e: Gibberella fujikuroi (G. moniliformis) — bakanae.

q.q: The teleomorph of Colletotrichum falcatum is:
q.e: Glomerella tucumanensis — red rot of sugarcane.

q.q: The teleomorph of Botrytis cinerea is:
q.e: Botryotinia fuckeliana — grey mould.

q.q: The teleomorph of Sclerotium rolfsii is:
q.e: Athelia rolfsii (Corticium rolfsii) — a basidiomycete.

q.q: The teleomorph of Rhizoctonia solani is:
q.e: Thanatephorus cucumeris — a basidiomycete.

q.q: The teleomorph of Pyricularia oryzae is:
q.e: Magnaporthe oryzae (M. grisea) — rice blast.

q.q: Cercospora leaf-spot fungi generally have the teleomorph:
q.e: Mycosphaerella.

q.q: The teleomorph of Bipolaris / Helminthosporium species is:
q.e: Cochliobolus (some in Pyrenophora for Drechslera).

q.q: The teleomorph of Fusarium graminearum is:
q.e: Gibberella zeae — head scab of wheat.

q.q: The teleomorph of Colletotrichum gloeosporioides is:
q.e: Glomerella cingulata — anthracnose of many fruits.

q.q: A closed, spherical ascocarp with no opening is a:
q.e: Cleistothecium — powdery mildews.

q.q: A flask-shaped ascocarp with an ostiole (pore) is a:
q.e: Perithecium — e.g. Gibberella, Nectria.

q.q: An open, cup- or saucer-shaped ascocarp is an:
q.e: Apothecium — Sclerotinia, Monilinia.

q.q: Asci borne in locules within a stroma (bitunicate) occur in a:
q.e: Pseudothecium — Loculoascomycetes, e.g. Venturia, Mycosphaerella.

q.q: A flat, saucer-shaped asexual fruiting body (often subcuticular) is an:
q.e: Acervulus — Colletotrichum, Pestalotia (with setae).

q.q: A flask-shaped ASEXUAL fruiting body bearing conidia is a:
q.e: Pycnidium — Phoma, Septoria, Ascochyta.

q.q: A cushion-shaped mass of conidiophores (e.g. Fusarium) is a:
q.e: Sporodochium.

q.q: A compact bundle (column) of conidiophores is a:
q.e: Synnema / coremium — e.g. Graphium, Isariopsis.

q.q: Aeciospores of a rust are produced in the:
q.e: Aecium; pycnia (spermogonia) bear the pycniospores.

q.q: The rust structure producing the overwintering (resting) spores is the:
q.e: Telium — bearing teliospores where karyogamy occurs.

q.q: The principal sterol of the fungal membrane is:
q.e: Ergosterol — the target of azole and polyene fungicides.

q.q: Which group cannot synthesise its own sterols and needs them exogenously?
q.e: Oomycetes — most lack sterol biosynthesis, so azoles are ineffective on them.

q.q: The dominant sterols of higher-plant membranes are:
q.e: Sitosterol/stigmasterol (phytosterols); ergosterol is fungal, cholesterol animal.

q.q: In ergosterol biosynthesis, the enzyme inhibited by azoles is:
q.e: C14-demethylase (CYP51) — the DMI target.

q.q: Polyene antibiotics (e.g. nystatin, amphotericin) act by:
o: Binding ergosterol to form membrane pores
Inhibiting the chitin synthase of the wall
q.e: Binding ergosterol to punch pores in the membrane.

q.q: The committed precursor cyclised toward sterols in the pathway is:
q.e: Squalene → lanosterol → (via C14-demethylation) ergosterol.

q.q: The phytoalexin of pea is:
q.e: Pisatin.

q.q: The phytoalexin of French bean (Phaseolus) is:
q.e: Phaseollin.

q.q: The phytoalexin of soybean is:
q.e: Glyceollin.

q.q: The phytoalexin of potato and tomato is:
q.e: Rishitin — a Solanaceae sesquiterpenoid.

q.q: The phytoalexin of sweet potato is:
q.e: Ipomeamarone.

q.q: The phytoalexin of cotton is:
q.e: Gossypol — a terpenoid aldehyde.

q.q: The stilbene phytoalexin of grapevine is:
q.e: Resveratrol.

q.q: The first phytoalexin ever described (Müller & Börger) was:
q.e: Orchinol — from the orchid-tuber studies of 1940.

q.q: Momilactones and oryzalexins are the phytoalexins of:
q.e: Rice — diterpenoid phytoalexins.

q.q: The classic SAR marker with (unknown-mechanism) antifungal activity is:
q.e: PR-1 — the diagnostic marker of systemic acquired resistance.

q.q: PR-2 proteins have the enzymatic activity of:
q.e: β-1,3-glucanase — degrading fungal wall glucans.

q.q: PR-3 proteins are:
q.e: Chitinases — hydrolysing fungal-wall chitin.

q.q: PR-5 proteins are described as:
q.e: Thaumatin-like — permeabilise fungal membranes (osmotin).

q.q: PR-9 proteins function as:
q.e: Peroxidases — reinforcing cell walls via lignin.

q.q: The PR-12 family comprises:
q.e: Defensins — small cysteine-rich antimicrobial peptides.

q.q: PR-14 proteins are:
q.e: Lipid-transfer proteins (LTPs).

q.q: Azole (DMI) fungicides inhibit:
q.e: C14-demethylase — blocking ergosterol biosynthesis.

q.q: Strobilurin (QoI) fungicides act at the:
q.e: Complex III, Qo site — G143A confers resistance.

q.q: Carboxamides / SDHIs (e.g. carboxin, boscalid) inhibit:
q.e: Complex II (SDH).

q.q: Phenylamides (metalaxyl) inhibit:
q.e: rRNA synthesis (RNA polymerase I) in Oomycetes.

q.q: Benzimidazoles (carbendazim, benomyl) inhibit:
q.e: β-tubulin — a single-site systemic mode.

q.q: Melanin-biosynthesis inhibitors (tricyclazole) block:
q.e: Melanin biosynthesis — the appressorium cannot hold turgor (rice blast).

q.q: Dicarboximides (iprodione) and phenylpyrroles (fludioxonil) act on:
o: Complex III respiration at the Qo site
q.e: Osmotic signal transduction (MAP/histidine kinase).

q.q: Anilinopyrimidines (e.g. cyprodinil) inhibit:
q.e: Methionine biosynthesis (and secreted-enzyme output).

q.q: Carboxylic-acid amides (dimethomorph, mandipropamid) inhibit:
q.e: Cellulose synthase — hitting Oomycete wall synthesis.

q.q: Fosetyl-aluminium and phosphonates are thought to act mainly by:
o: Inhibiting complex III of the respiration
q.e: Inducing host defences plus direct action, against Oomycetes.

q.q: Mancozeb and other dithiocarbamates are classified as:
q.e: Multisite contact protectants — low resistance risk.

q.q: Morpholine (amine) fungicides inhibit ergosterol synthesis at the:
o: Squalene epoxidase early in the pathway
Complex III of the respiratory chain (bc1)
q.e: Δ14-reductase / Δ8-isomerase — a different step from the azoles.

q.q: The logistic (compound-interest) model is linearised by plotting against time:
q.e: ln[x/(1−x)] — the logit; its slope is the apparent infection rate r.

q.q: The monomolecular (simple-interest) model is linearised by plotting against time:
q.e: ln[1/(1−x)] — for monocyclic diseases with a single infection cycle.

q.q: The Gompertz model is linearised by the transformation:
q.e: −ln(−ln x) (the gompit); asymmetric, inflexion near 37%.

q.q: The inflexion point of the logistic curve occurs at a disease level of:
q.e: 50% — the symmetric logistic peaks in rate at x = 0.5.

q.q: The Gompertz curve reaches its maximum rate of increase at about:
q.e: ~37% — its asymmetry distinguishes it from the logistic.

q.q: Very early in a polycyclic epidemic (x small), increase is best approximated by the:
q.e: When x is tiny, (1−x)≈1, so growth is exponential and ln(x) vs t is roughly linear.

q.q: The model with a flexible inflexion point governed by a shape parameter is the:
q.e: Richards model — a generalised growth function that subsumes the others as special cases.

q.q: In a compound-interest disease, the rate of increase dx/dt is proportional to:
q.e: x(1−x) — each lesion begets more, until the (1−x) ceiling slows it.

q.q: In a simple-interest (monocyclic) disease, the rate of increase is:
o: Proportional to the x already present
Independent of x, driven by fixed x₀
Fixed at zero throughout the season
q.e: Independent of x — new infections arise from the fixed initial inoculum; near-linear rise.

q.q: The purpose of a linearising transformation is to:
o: Make the slope a straight-line rate estimate
Convert incidence values into severity ones
Estimate the final disease level directly
q.e: To straighten the S-curve so its slope gives a readable rate (e.g. r for the logistic).

q.q: Disease rises from x₁ = 0.05 to x₂ = 0.95 over 9 days; the logistic r ≈:
Disease rises from x₁ = 0.01 (day 0) to x₂ = 0.50 (day 10); r ≈:
Severity is 0, 10, 30 and 60% on days 0, 7, 14 and 21. By the trapezoidal rule AUDPC (%·days) =:
The logit ln[x/(1−x)] of a disease level of exactly 50% is:
q.e: ln(0.5/0.5)=ln 1=0 — the logistic line crosses zero at 50% disease.

q.q: In the exponential phase with r = 0.2/day, the time for disease to double (ln2/r) is about:
With a 90-day infection window and a 15-day latent period, the number of infection cycles is about:
q.e: 90 ÷ 15 = 6 cycles; a shorter latent period packs in more and speeds the epidemic.

q.q: If disease incidence rises from 4% to 36% over one interval, the increase is best summarised on a:
q.e: A near-nine-fold rise from a small base signals compound-interest growth — best linearised by the logit.

q.q: Horizontal (polygenic) resistance slows an epidemic by reducing the:
q.e: Reduces r — rate-reducing resistance; vertical resistance instead cuts x₀.

q.q: Vertical (race-specific) resistance acts principally by reducing the:
q.e: Reduces x₀ — delaying onset; can fail wholly against a matching virulent race.

q.q: Lengthening the pathogen's latent period during a season will:
o: Raise the initial inoculum level x₀
q.e: Slows it — a longer latent period means fewer generations fit the season.

q.q: The corrected basic infection rate (Rc) differs from the apparent rate by allowing for the:
q.e: Latent + infectious periods — removing not-yet-infectious and no-longer-sporulating tissue.

q.q: A sanitation programme lowers x₀, but in a compound-interest epidemic its benefit over time tends to:
o: Erode as the epidemic catches up
q.e: Erodes — cutting x₀ delays the curve, but multiplication narrows the gap (the sanitation ratio).

q.q: The Vertifolia effect refers to the:
o: Gain of vertical resistance over generations
Loss of horizontal resistance under a major gene
q.e: Loss of horizontal resistance — breeding under a major gene lets background resistance erode.

q.q: Garrett's 'inoculum potential' is best defined as the:
o: Total spore count present in the soil
Energy of growth available for infection
q.e: Energy of growth available for infection — depends on inoculum amount and vigour.

q.q: For most soil-borne monocyclic diseases, the relationship between inoculum density and disease is:
o: Increasing but often reaching a plateau
q.e: Rising to a plateau — beyond a point extra inoculum adds little, as available sites saturate.

q.q: Which is a monocyclic (simple-interest) disease?
q.e: Loose smut — one systemic infection per season, no secondary spread.

q.q: Which is a polycyclic (compound-interest) disease?
q.e: Late blight — many infection cycles per season; wilts and smuts are monocyclic.

q.q: Vanderplank is credited with classifying epidemics into:
q.e: Simple- vs compound-interest — the finance analogy for monocyclic vs polycyclic.

q.q: A disease constantly present at a low level in an area is described as:
q.e: Endemic. Epidemic (epiphytotic) = sudden widespread outbreak; pandemic = across a very wide area.

q.q: A sudden, widespread and destructive increase of a plant disease is an:
q.e: Epiphytotic — the plant-pathology term for an epidemic.

q.q: Infection of a plant by inoculum coming from other, separate plants is called:
q.e: Alloinfection — from external sources; autoinfection is spread within the same plant.

q.q: 'Tardive' epidemics differ from 'explosive' ones in that they:
o: Reach a maximum within a few days
Build up slowly over the season
q.e: Build up slowly — a gradual rise, versus the rapid surge of an explosive epidemic.

q.q: The disease triangle comprises host, pathogen and:
q.e: Environment — all three must coincide for disease; the tetrahedron adds time.

q.q: The disease tetrahedron adds which element to the disease triangle?
q.e: Time — disease develops over a period; some versions add the human/management axis.

q.q: The three components of a disease-progress curve are x₀, r and:
q.e: Time — initial inoculum (x₀), rate (r) and duration together shape the curve.

q.q: 'Predisposition' in epidemiology refers to the effect of:
o: Fungicide acting upon the insect vector
Environment making the host more susceptible
One pathogen acting upon another pathogen
Host age determining the spore dimensions
q.e: Environmental conditioning of the host toward greater susceptibility before infection.

q.q: The incubation period of a disease is the time from:
q.e: Infection to symptoms. The latent period runs from infection to the onset of sporulation.

q.q: The latent period of a pathogen is the interval from infection to:
q.e: Onset of sporulation — when new inoculum becomes available; distinct from incubation period.

q.q: Disease incidence is best defined as the:
o: Proportion of plants or units infected
q.e: Proportion of units infected. Severity is the proportion of tissue area affected.

q.q: Disease severity is best defined as the:
o: Concentration of spores in the air
q.e: Proportion of tissue area affected — distinct from incidence (units infected).

q.q: The Horsfall–Barratt disease-assessment scale is based on the principle that the eye:
o: Registers only necrotic tissue, not chlorosis
Cannot detect disease below the 50% mark
Reads on a strictly linear percent scale
q.e: Logarithmic perception (Weber–Fechner law) — hence its grades are finest near 0% and 100%.

q.q: The Percent Disease Index (PDI) is calculated from the:
o: Value of the rate constant r over time
Number of spores counted per lesion area
Length of the latent period in days
Sum of grades over maximum possible grade
q.e: Sum of numerical grades ÷ (number assessed × maximum grade) × 100 — a weighted severity measure.

q.q: 'Prevalence' of a disease usually refers to its:
o: Rate of increase over the season
q.e: How widespread / commonly it occurs across a region, rather than intensity on a plant.

q.q: AUDPC is most useful for:
o: Comparing whole epidemics or cultivars in one value
Measuring spore germination on the leaf surface
Identifying the causal pathogen from the lesions
Estimating the latent period between two cycles
q.e: Comparing epidemics/cultivars — it integrates severity across the whole season.

q.q: BLITECAST, Beaumont periods and Smith periods all forecast:
q.e: Late blight — based on temperature and humidity favouring Phytophthora sporulation.

q.q: The Mills table (leaf-wetness duration vs temperature) forecasts:
q.e: Apple scab (Venturia inaequalis) — Mills periods predict infection from wetness duration.

q.q: The 'negative prognosis' approach (Schrödter & Ullrich) is used to:
o: Predict when late blight will NOT yet appear
Forecast the maximum severity of a rust epidemic
Determine the optimum harvest and storage time
Estimate the inoculum load present in the soil
q.e: Predict the disease-free period so the first fungicide spray against late blight can be safely delayed.

q.q: EPIDEM, one of the earliest disease simulators (Waggoner & Horsfall), modelled:
q.e: Early blight (Alternaria solani) — a pioneering computer simulation of an epidemic.

q.q: EPIPRE, a supervised-control system developed by Zadoks, was designed for:
q.e: Wheat — integrating disease/pest forecasts to guide need-based spraying.

q.q: A disease-forecasting system is worthwhile mainly because it lets growers:
o: Time controls against predicted infection periods
Eradicate the pathogen permanently from a field
Remove the need for any fungicide use forever
Deliberately raise the inoculum in the crop
q.e: Time interventions — sprays applied ahead of forecast infection cut losses and needless applications.

q.q: The 'apparent infection rate' r is best described as the:
o: Length of the latent period in days
Total amount of inoculum in the soil pool
Slope of the logistic (logit) progress line
Final proportion of the tissue diseased
q.e: Slope of the logit-transformed progress curve — Vanderplank's measure of epidemic speed.

q.q: The first tier of the plant immune system, triggered by conserved microbial molecules, is:
q.e: PTI — surface receptors detect PAMPs/MAMPs (e.g. flagellin, chitin) to mount basal defence.

q.q: The bacterial PAMP flg22 is a 22-amino-acid epitope of:
q.e: Flagellin — flg22 is recognised by the LRR receptor kinase FLS2 at the plant cell surface.

q.q: The plant pattern-recognition receptor FLS2 perceives:
q.e: flg22 — FLS2 partners the co-receptor BAK1 to initiate PTI signalling.

q.q: Fungal chitin as a PAMP is perceived in plants by receptors such as:
q.e: CERK1/CEBiP — LysM-domain receptors that bind chitin oligomers.

q.q: BAK1 functions in PTI as a:
q.e: Co-receptor — BAK1 (SERK3) associates with FLS2, EFR and others to activate downstream signalling.

q.q: The 'zig-zag' model of the plant immune system was articulated by:
q.e: Jones & Dangl (2006) — describing the PTI → ETS → ETI oscillation between host and pathogen.

q.q: When pathogen effectors suppress PTI and permit infection, the state is called:
q.e: ETS — effectors dampen basal immunity; the plant may counter by recognising an effector, giving ETI.

q.q: Effector-triggered immunity is typically mediated by intracellular:
q.e: NBS-LRR / NLR proteins — they recognise specific effectors (directly or indirectly) and often trigger the HR.

q.q: ETI is frequently accompanied by localised:
q.e: Hypersensitive response — rapid cell death that confines biotrophic pathogens at the infection site.

q.q: The reactive-oxygen 'oxidative burst' during defence is generated largely by the plasma-membrane enzyme:
q.e: RBOH (respiratory burst oxidase homolog) — an NADPH oxidase producing superoxide/H₂O₂ for signalling and antimicrobial action.

q.q: The 'guard hypothesis' proposes that an R protein:
o: Monitors (guards) a host target that effectors modify
q.e: Guards a host 'guardee' — e.g. RIN4 is guarded by RPM1/RPS2; effector modification of RIN4 is sensed indirectly.

q.q: Non-host resistance refers to immunity that is:
o: Effective against all pathogens of a whole plant species
Conferred by a single R gene
q.e: Species-wide, durable resistance — an entire plant species resists all isolates of a pathogen; multilayered and rarely broken.

q.q: The conserved host-targeting motif of cytoplasmic oomycete effectors is:
q.e: RxLR (Arg-any-Leu-Arg) — directs translocation into host cells; CRN (crinkler) is a second oomycete effector class.

q.q: Bacterial effectors are delivered into the host cell primarily through the:
q.e: Type III secretion system — the Hrp injectisome translocates effectors that suppress immunity.

q.q: Avr9 and Avr4, classic apoplastic effectors, are produced by:
q.e: Cladosporium fulvum (tomato leaf mould) — recognised by the extracellular Cf-9 and Cf-4 receptor-like proteins.

q.q: The maize gene Hm1, the first plant resistance gene ever cloned (1992), acts by:
o: Encoding a reductase that detoxifies HC-toxin
q.e: HC-toxin reductase — an atypical R gene giving resistance to Cochliobolus carbonum race 1.

q.q: The tomato Pto resistance gene is unusual because it encodes a:
q.e: Protein kinase — Pto recognises AvrPto/AvrPtoB and functions together with the NBS-LRR protein Prf.

q.q: The rice gene Xa21, conferring resistance to bacterial blight, encodes a:
q.e: LRR receptor kinase — a cell-surface receptor recognising a sulfated microbial peptide from Xanthomonas oryzae pv. oryzae.

q.q: The tobacco N gene, conferring resistance to TMV, belongs to which NLR subclass?
q.e: TIR-NBS-LRR — with a Toll/interleukin-1 receptor domain; the flax rust gene L6 is the same type.

q.q: Barley mlo confers durable, broad-spectrum powdery mildew resistance and is unusual because it is:
q.e: Recessive loss-of-function — loss of the MLO protein gives broad, durable resistance, exploited widely in barley breeding.

q.q: RPM1 and RPS2 of Arabidopsis both act by guarding the host protein:
q.e: RIN4 — effector-induced modification of RIN4 is detected by these CC-NBS-LRR proteins (guard hypothesis).

q.q: Quantitative (partial, race-non-specific) resistance is usually controlled by:
q.e: QTLs (polygenic) — the molecular basis of horizontal resistance; more durable but harder to breed for.

q.q: Systemic acquired resistance (SAR) is signalled chiefly through:
q.e: Salicylic acid — accumulation activates PR-gene expression, effective mainly against biotrophs.

q.q: The master regulatory protein of SAR downstream of salicylic acid is:
q.e: NPR1 — the SA receptor/coactivator that switches on PR genes; also required for ISR.

q.q: Induced systemic resistance (ISR) triggered by rhizobacteria depends mainly on:
q.e: JA/ethylene — ISR primes defences without strong PR-1 induction; contrasts with SA-dependent SAR.

q.q: The defence hormone associated with resistance to necrotrophs and chewing insects is:
q.e: Jasmonic acid — the SA and JA pathways are often mutually antagonistic (hormone crosstalk).

q.q: PR-1 protein accumulation is a widely used molecular marker of:
q.e: SAR — PR-1 is the classic salicylate-responsive marker gene.

q.q: The pathogenesis-related protein PR-2 is a:
q.e: β-1,3-glucanase — PR-3 is chitinase; together they degrade fungal cell walls.

q.q: A leading candidate for the mobile signal moving SAR through the plant is:
q.e: Methyl salicylate, with azelaic acid, G3P and pipecolic acid/NHP also implicated in long-distance signalling.

q.q: Phytoalexins in the defence response are:
o: Antimicrobials synthesised de novo after infection
q.e: Induced antimicrobials — e.g. camalexin (Arabidopsis), glyceollin (soybean), rishitin (potato).

q.q: Priming in induced resistance refers to a state in which the plant:
o: Responds faster and stronger upon subsequent attack
q.e: Faster, stronger secondary response — a sensitised state with little fitness cost until challenge.

q.q: RNA silencing (RNAi) as an antiviral defence acts by:
q.e: Sequence-specific RNA degradation — viral dsRNA is diced to siRNAs that guide cleavage of the viral genome.

q.q: The enzyme that cleaves double-stranded RNA into small interfering RNAs is:
q.e: Dicer / DCL — an RNase III enzyme producing 21–24 nt siRNAs from dsRNA precursors.

q.q: The catalytic 'slicer' protein at the core of the RNA-induced silencing complex (RISC) is:
q.e: Argonaute — binds the guide siRNA/miRNA and cleaves complementary target RNA.

q.q: Virus-induced gene silencing (VIGS) is used mainly as a tool for:
o: Transient knock-down of plant genes (functional genomics)
q.e: Transient gene knock-down — a recombinant virus carrying a host-gene fragment triggers silencing of that gene.

q.q: Host-induced gene silencing (HIGS) controls pathogens by:
o: Expressing dsRNA in the plant targeting essential pathogen genes
q.e: Plant-expressed dsRNA silences vital genes in the invading fungus/oomycete/insect (cross-kingdom RNAi).

q.q: Many plant viruses counter RNAi by encoding:
q.e: VSRs — e.g. HC-Pro (potyviruses), P19 (tombusviruses), 2b (CMV) — they disable the silencing machinery.

q.q: The tombusvirus suppressor P19 works by:
q.e: Sequestering siRNAs — P19 measures and binds 21-nt duplexes, preventing their loading into RISC.

q.q: Which molecular marker is dominant (band present/absent) rather than codominant?
q.e: RAPD (also AFLP) — dominant; SSR, RFLP and SNP are codominant, resolving heterozygotes.

q.q: The universal DNA barcode region for fungal identification is:
q.e: ITS — the fungal barcode; 16S rRNA is used for bacteria, COI for animals.

q.q: In real-time (quantitative) PCR, the threshold cycle (Ct) value is:
o: Inversely related to the log of starting template copies
q.e: Inversely related — more starting template crosses threshold in fewer cycles (lower Ct).

q.q: LAMP (loop-mediated isothermal amplification) is valued for field diagnostics because it:
o: Amplifies DNA at a single constant temperature
q.e: Isothermal — ~60–65 °C with Bst polymerase and 4–6 primers; results readable by turbidity or colour change.

q.q: CRISPR-based nucleic-acid diagnostics such as SHERLOCK rely on the collateral activity of:
q.e: Cas13/Cas12 — after target recognition they cleave reporter probes, giving a detectable signal.

q.q: Western blotting detects ____, while Southern blotting detects ____:
q.e: Protein; DNA. Southern = DNA, Northern = RNA, Western = protein.

q.q: To profile an entire microbial community without culturing, one uses:
q.e: Metagenomics — sequencing community DNA (e.g. 16S amplicons) to reveal microbiome composition.

q.q: RNA-seq is used primarily to measure:
q.e: Transcriptome-wide expression — quantifying which genes are up- or down-regulated during infection.

q.q: SCAR and CAPS markers are typically derived to make a marker:
o: Locus-specific and reproducible (often from a RAPD/sequence)
q.e: Locus-specific/reproducible — SCARs convert a RAPD band into a defined primer pair; CAPS add a restriction step.

q.q: Agrobacterium-mediated transformation transfers to the plant genome the:
o: T-DNA region bounded by border repeats
q.e: T-DNA — flanked by 25-bp left/right borders; the vir genes act in trans to mobilise it.

q.q: In a binary vector system, the vir genes and the T-DNA are:
o: On separate replicons (T-DNA on a small binary vector, vir on a helper)
q.e: On separate plasmids — simplifying cloning; the disarmed helper supplies Vir functions.

q.q: The reporter gene uidA (GUS) encodes:
q.e: β-glucuronidase — cleaves X-Gluc to a blue product marking transformed tissue.

q.q: The bar (pat) selectable/marker gene confers tolerance to:
q.e: Glufosinate — bar encodes phosphinothricin acetyltransferase; nptII = kanamycin, hpt = hygromycin.

q.q: The most widely used constitutive promoter in dicot plant transformation is:
q.e: CaMV 35S — from cauliflower mosaic virus; drives strong constitutive expression in most tissues.

q.q: Biolistic ('gene gun') transformation delivers DNA by:
q.e: Micro-projectile bombardment — the method of choice for cereals and organelle transformation.

q.q: Coat-protein-mediated resistance is an example of:
q.e: Pathogen-derived resistance — expressing a viral gene (e.g. TMV coat protein) in the host confers resistance.

q.q: Bt crops resist insects because the cry transgene encodes a protein that:
o: Forms pores in the insect midgut epithelium
q.e: Midgut pore formation — the activated δ-endotoxin binds receptors and lyses gut cells.

q.q: In Magnaporthe oryzae, appressorium formation is controlled by the MAP kinase:
q.e: Pmk1 — a MAP kinase essential for appressorium development and penetration; loss abolishes pathogenicity.

q.q: Appressorial melanin in Magnaporthe is DHN-type; tricyclazole blocks its synthesis by inhibiting:
q.e: A DHN-melanin pathway enzyme (scytalone dehydratase/reductase) — without melanin the appressorium cannot hold penetration turgor.

q.q: Quorum sensing that coordinates bacterial virulence at high cell density is mediated in Gram-negatives by:
q.e: AHLs — diffusible autoinducers synthesised by LuxI-type enzymes and sensed by LuxR-type regulators.

q.q: The Woronin body of ascomycetes is derived from a:
q.e: Peroxisome — Woronin bodies carry the Hex1 protein and plug the septal pore after injury.

q.q: The Spitzenkörper at a growing hyphal apex functions as a:
o: Vesicle supply centre for tip growth
Septal plug sealing a damaged hypha
q.e: Vesicle supply centre — it organises secretory vesicle delivery to the extending tip.

q.q: Forcible basidiospore discharge is powered by the:
o: Active ciliary beating of the spore
q.e: Buller's drop — a condensing droplet coalesces with the spore film and flings it off the sterigma.

q.q: The secondary (reniform) zoospore of an Oomycete bears:
o: An anterior tinsel and posterior whiplash
q.e: Tinsel + whiplash, laterally inserted — biflagellate; contrast the chytrid's single posterior whiplash.

q.q: Two distinct motile zoospore phases (diplanetism) are shown by:
q.e: Saprolegnia — primary pyriform and secondary reniform zoospores separated by an encysted stage.

q.q: Croziers (hook cells) in ascomycetes function to:
o: Partition compatible nuclei into the ascus
Anchor the fruiting body onto host tissue
Release the ascospores by explosive turgor
q.e: Ensure correct dikaryotic nuclear distribution into the ascus mother cell.

q.q: The membranous caps flanking the dolipore septum are called:
q.e: Parenthesomes — the perforated caps of the Basidiomycota dolipore apparatus.

q.q: Chitin in the true fungal wall is polymerised through:
q.e: β-1,4 — N-acetylglucosamine chains laid down by chitin synthase.

q.q: The Oomycete cell wall is composed principally of:
q.e: Cellulose/glucans, essentially without chitin — reflecting their non-fungal lineage.

q.q: The predominant sterol of the true fungal membrane is:
q.e: Ergosterol — the target of azole and polyene fungicides.

q.q: The teleomorph of Colletotrichum falcatum (red rot of cane) is:
q.e: Glomerella tucumanensis (= Physalospora tucumanensis).

q.q: The teleomorph of Botrytis cinerea is:
q.e: Botryotinia fuckeliana — grey mould, a broad-host-range necrotroph.

q.q: The teleomorph of Sclerotium rolfsii is:
q.e: Athelia rolfsii (= Corticium rolfsii) — a basidiomycete.

q.q: Cercospora leaf-spot fungi most commonly have the teleomorph:
q.e: Mycosphaerella — many Cercospora/Pseudocercospora fungi have Mycosphaerella sexual states.

q.q: The zoospore of a chytrid is characterised by:
q.e: Single posterior whiplash — the defining chytrid feature.

q.q: In Ascomycetes, karyogamy and meiosis occur within the:
q.e: Young ascus — the only diploid stage; meiosis yields (usually eight) ascospores.

q.q: A demicyclic rust is one that lacks the:
q.e: Lacks the urediniospore stage (e.g. Gymnosporangium) — so no repeating cycle in a season.

q.q: A heteroecious macrocyclic rust is best described as producing:
o: Uredia and telia without a sexual stage
All spore stages on a single host
Five spore stages across two unlike hosts
Only telia and basidia on one host
q.e: Five spore stages on two hosts — e.g. Puccinia graminis on wheat and barberry.

q.q: Brown spot of rice, implicated in the 1943 Bengal famine, is caused by:
q.e: Bipolaris oryzae (Cochliobolus miyabeanus).

q.q: Bakanae of rice, from which gibberellins were discovered, is caused by:
q.e: Fusarium moniliforme (Gibberella fujikuroi).

q.q: Downy mildew (green ear) of pearl millet is caused by:
q.e: Sclerospora graminicola.

q.q: The aecial (alternate) host of wheat leaf rust is:
q.e: Thalictrum — stem rust uses Berberis; a classic swap-trap.

q.q: Take-all disease of wheat is caused by:
q.e: Gaeumannomyces graminis var. tritici — a root/crown pathogen.

q.q: Coffee rust, historically devastating in Ceylon, is caused by:
q.e: Hemileia vastatrix.

q.q: Ring rot of potato, a quarantine disease, is caused by:
q.e: Clavibacter michiganensis subsp. sepedonicus — a Gram-positive vascular pathogen.

q.q: Little leaf of brinjal is caused by a:
q.e: Phytoplasma — a leafhopper-transmitted, phloem-limited mollicute.

q.q: Sterility mosaic of pigeonpea is transmitted by an:
q.e: Eriophyid mite (Aceria cajani) — the 'green plague' emaravirus.

q.q: Gram-negative plant pathogens inject effectors into host cells via the:
q.e: Type III secretion (Hrp injectisome) — delivering immunity-suppressing effectors.

q.q: Harpin (HrpN) is a bacterial protein that characteristically:
o: Nucleates ice crystals on the leaf
q.e: Elicits the HR — a heat-stable, glycine-rich elicitor secreted via the T3SS.

q.q: Quorum sensing in Gram-negative plant pathogens is mediated by:
q.e: AHLs — LuxI/LuxR-type systems coordinating virulence at high cell density.

q.q: Agrobacterium vir genes are induced by the wound phenolic:
q.e: Acetosyringone — sensed by the VirA/VirG two-component system.

q.q: Ice-nucleation frost injury by Pseudomonas syringae involves the protein:
q.e: InaZ — templates ice at warm sub-zero temperatures; the target of 'ice-minus' strains.

q.q: Which pathogen is phloem-limited and still unculturable on standard media?
q.e: Ca. Liberibacter asiaticus — the citrus greening agent.

q.q: Citrus stubborn disease is caused by a helical, wall-less but culturable:
q.e: Spiroplasma citri — a Mollicute, but (unlike phytoplasmas) culturable.

q.q: In the LOPAT scheme, the letter 'A' denotes the test for:
q.e: Arginine dihydrolase — with Levan, Oxidase, Pectinolysis and Tobacco-HR.

q.q: The Gram-positive wall differs from the Gram-negative by having:
o: No wall at all, being a wall-less form
A waxy mycolic-acid outer capsule layer
q.e: Thick peptidoglycan + teichoic acids, no outer membrane — hence crystal violet is retained.

q.q: Soft-rot bacteria macerate host tissue chiefly by secreting:
q.e: Pectinolytic enzymes — degrading the pectin-rich middle lamella.

q.q: The genome of the majority of plant viruses is:
q.e: (+)ssRNA — able to act directly as messenger RNA.

q.q: Tomato spotted wilt virus has a genome that is:
q.e: Ambisense tripartite ssRNA, enveloped; propagative in thrips.

q.q: Luteoviruses (BYDV, PLRV) are transmitted by aphids in a manner that is:
q.e: Circulative non-propagative — gut to salivary glands without replicating; phloem-limited.

q.q: Cylindrical 'pinwheel' inclusion bodies are diagnostic of the genus:
q.e: Potyvirus — the CI protein forms pinwheels seen by electron microscopy.

q.q: Geminiviruses are distinctive for possessing:
o: Rigid rods with linear plus-sense RNA
q.e: Twin icosahedra, circular ssDNA — includes the whitefly-borne begomoviruses.

q.q: Banana bunchy top virus belongs to a group with a genome that is:
q.e: Multipartite circular ssDNA (Babuvirus/Nanoviridae) — at least six components.

q.q: Cauliflower mosaic virus is unusual in replicating its genome by:
q.e: Reverse transcription of a dsDNA genome — source of the 35S promoter.

q.q: Members of family Avsunviroidae replicate in the:
q.e: Chloroplast with hammerhead ribozymes; Pospiviroidae replicate in the nucleus.

q.q: The first viroid to be discovered (1971) was:
q.e: PSTVd (Diener) — the type species of Pospiviroidae.

q.q: An umbravirus lacks a coat protein and for aphid transmission depends on a helper:
q.e: Luteovirus — which encapsidates it (e.g. the groundnut rosette complex).

q.q: The classical local-lesion assay for TMV quantification uses:
q.e: Nicotiana glutinosa — Holmes (1929) showed countable necrotic lesions.

q.q: Rice tungro, a two-virus complex, is transmitted by the:
q.e: Green leafhopper (Nephotettix) — carrying RTBV with RTSV as helper.

q.q: Multinucleate giant cells (not a syncytium) are induced by:
q.e: Meloidogyne → giant cells; cyst nematodes form a syncytium.

q.q: Molya disease of cereals is caused by:
q.e: Heterodera avenae — the cereal cyst nematode.

q.q: The burrowing nematode Radopholus similis is the agent of:
q.e: Radopholus similis — banana toppling and citrus spreading decline.

q.q: Females of Meloidogyne are identified to species mainly by the:
q.e: Perineal pattern — the cuticular striae around the vulva and anus.

q.q: Rotylenchulus reniformis feeds as a:
q.e: Sedentary semi-endoparasite — anterior embedded, kidney-shaped body outside.

q.q: The logistic (compound-interest) model is linearised by plotting:
q.e: ln[x/(1−x)] — the logit; its slope is the apparent infection rate r.

q.q: The monomolecular (simple-interest) model is linearised by plotting:
q.e: ln[1/(1−x)] — for monocyclic diseases with one infection cycle.

q.q: The Gompertz disease-progress curve has its inflexion at about:
q.e: ~37% — asymmetric, unlike the symmetric logistic at 50%.

q.q: Horizontal (polygenic) resistance slows an epidemic by reducing the:
q.e: Reduces r — rate-reducing resistance; vertical resistance instead cuts x0.

q.q: Vertical (race-specific) resistance acts principally by reducing the:
q.e: Reduces x0 — delaying onset; it can fail wholly against a virulent race.

q.q: The Vertifolia effect refers to the:
o: Gain of vertical resistance over generations
Loss of horizontal resistance under a major gene
q.e: Loss of horizontal resistance — breeding under a major gene lets background resistance erode.

q.q: Garrett's 'inoculum potential' is best defined as the:
o: Energy of growth available for infection
Total spore count present in the soil
q.e: Energy of growth available for infection — a function of inoculum amount and vigour.

q.q: Disease amount rises from x₁ = 0.02 to x₂ = 0.98 over 8 days; the logistic r ≈:
Azole (DMI) fungicides inhibit the enzyme:
q.e: C14-demethylase (FRAC 3) — blocking ergosterol biosynthesis.

q.q: Strobilurin (QoI) fungicides act at the:
o: Succinate site of respiratory complex II
Qo site of respiratory complex III
Rotenone site of respiratory complex I
F1 catalytic head of the ATP synthase
q.e: Complex III, Qo site (FRAC 11) — resistance via the G143A mutation.

q.q: Carboxin, a classic smut/rust seed dressing, inhibits:
o: Cytochrome bc1 oxidase at the Qo site
q.e: Succinate dehydrogenase (SDHI, FRAC 7) — the original oxathiin.

q.q: Metalaxyl is specific to Oomycetes because it inhibits:
q.e: rRNA synthesis (FRAC 4) — single-site, so resistance appears readily.

q.q: Benzimidazoles (carbendazim, benomyl) inhibit:
q.e: β-tubulin (FRAC 1) — a single mutation confers resistance.

q.q: Tricyclazole controls rice blast by blocking:
q.e: Melanin biosynthesis (MBI) — the appressorium then cannot hold penetration turgor.

q.q: Mancozeb and other dithiocarbamates are classified as:
q.e: Multisite contact protectants (FRAC M) — low resistance risk.

q.q: The G143A target-site mutation confers resistance to:
q.e: QoI (strobilurins) — a cytochrome b substitution that abolishes binding at the Qo site.

q.q: PAMP-triggered immunity is initiated by:
q.e: Surface PRRs detecting PAMPs — e.g. FLS2 recognising flg22.

q.q: Effector-triggered immunity is usually mediated by:
q.e: NBS-LRR / NLR proteins — recognising specific effectors, often with HR.

q.q: In the guard hypothesis, RPM1 and RPS2 of Arabidopsis monitor the host protein:
q.e: RIN4 — effector-induced modification of RIN4 is sensed indirectly.

q.q: The first plant R gene cloned, maize Hm1, acts by:
o: Encoding a surface LRR receptor kinase
q.e: HC-toxin reductase — an atypical R gene against Cochliobolus carbonum.

q.q: The tomato Pto resistance gene is unusual in encoding a:
q.e: Protein kinase — Pto works with the NBS-LRR protein Prf, recognising AvrPto.

q.q: The tobacco N gene conferring TMV resistance belongs to the subclass:
q.e: TIR-NBS-LRR — like the flax rust gene L6.

q.q: Barley mlo gives durable powdery-mildew resistance and is unusual in being:
q.e: Recessive loss-of-function — broad, durable resistance widely used in barley.

q.q: Systemic acquired resistance is signalled chiefly through:
q.e: SA → NPR1 → PR genes — effective mainly against biotrophs.

q.q: The enzyme dicing double-stranded RNA into small interfering RNAs is:
q.e: Dicer/DCL — an RNase III enzyme producing 21–24 nt siRNAs.

q.q: The conserved host-targeting motif of cytoplasmic oomycete effectors is:
q.e: RxLR — directs translocation into host cells; CRN is a second class.

q.q: Agrobacterium transfers to the plant genome the:
o: Entire Ti plasmid with vir genes
vir operon on a helper plasmid
q.e: T-DNA — flanked by 25-bp borders; vir genes act in trans.

q.q: Tabtoxin (wildfire of tobacco) inhibits the enzyme:
q.e: Glutamine synthetase — ammonia accumulates, giving chlorotic halos.

q.q: Phaseolotoxin (halo blight of bean) inhibits:
q.e: OCTase — the classic swap-partner of tabtoxin→GS.

q.q: Tentoxin causes seedling chlorosis by inhibiting:
q.e: Chloroplast ATP synthase (CF1) — blocking energy transfer.

q.q: HC-toxin of Cochliobolus carbonum race 1 acts as a(n):
q.e: HDAC inhibitor — the Hm1 reductase detoxifies it (first R gene cloned).

q.q: Fusicoccin causes irreversible stomatal opening by activating:
q.e: Plasma-membrane H+-ATPase — locking guard cells open via 14-3-3 proteins.

q.q: The 'Father of Plant Pathology' is:
q.e: Anton de Bary — proved late blight was fungal.

q.q: The gene-for-gene hypothesis was proposed by:
q.e: H. H. Flor — from flax and flax-rust studies.

q.q: Bordeaux mixture, the first successful fungicide, was introduced by:
q.e: Millardet (1885) — copper sulphate plus lime for grape downy mildew.

q.q: The 'Father of Indian Plant Pathology' is:
q.e: Sir E. J. Butler — first Imperial Mycologist at Pusa.

q.q: Tobacco mosaic virus was first crystallised (1935) by:
q.e: Wendell Stanley (Nobel 1946).

q.q: The universal DNA barcode region for fungal identification is the:
q.e: ITS — 16S rRNA is used for bacteria, COI for animals.

q.q: In real-time qPCR, the Ct (threshold cycle) value is:
o: Equal to the primer melting temperature
Inversely related to log starting copies
q.e: Inversely related — more template crosses threshold in fewer cycles.

q.q: LAMP is valued for field diagnostics because it:
o: Depends on a bench-top DNA sequencer
Detects only proteins, not nucleic acids
Amplifies DNA at one constant temperature
q.e: Isothermal — ~60–65 °C with Bst polymerase; read by turbidity or colour.

q.q: AUDPC is used primarily to:
o: Identify the causal pathogen from lesions
Summarise an epidemic as one comparable value
Measure the latent period between cycles
Estimate spore germination on the host
q.e: Area Under the Disease Progress Curve — integrates severity over time for ranking.

q.q: Loose smut of wheat survives internally as dormant mycelium in the:
q.e: Embryo — Ustilago tritici; needs systemic or hot-water seed treatment.

q.q: In common bunt, reticulate (net-patterned) teliospores indicate:
q.e: T. caries = reticulate; T. laevis (foetida) = smooth.

q.q: Which cereal smut is externally (seed-surface) borne rather than embryo-borne?
q.e: U. hordei (covered smut) — surface-borne, so seed treatment works easily.

q.q: Phytoalexins are correctly defined as:
o: Structural lignin polymers of the wall
q.e: Induced after infection — e.g. pisatin, phaseollin, rishitin.

q.q: 'Tolerance' in host–pathogen interaction describes a plant that:
o: Prevents the pathogen from ever entering
Kills the pathogen at the penetration site
Escapes contact with the inoculum source
Endures infection with little yield loss
q.e: Endures infection — distinct from resistance and escape.

organisms_mcq_p1.title: Causal Organisms — MCQ Drill · Part 1 of 2

q.q: The causal organism of Blast of Rice is:
q.e: Pyricularia oryzae (Magnaporthe oryzae) — Blast of Rice.

q.q: The causal organism of Brown spot of Rice is:
q.e: Bipolaris oryzae (Cochliobolus miyabeanus) — Brown spot of Rice.

q.q: The causal organism of Sheath blight of Rice is:
q.e: Rhizoctonia solani (Thanatephorus cucumeris) — Sheath blight of Rice.

q.q: The causal organism of Sheath rot of Rice is:
q.e: Sarocladium oryzae — Sheath rot of Rice.

q.q: The causal organism of False smut of Rice is:
q.e: Ustilaginoidea virens — False smut of Rice.

q.q: The causal organism of Bakanae / foot rot of Rice is:
q.e: Fusarium moniliforme (Gibberella fujikuroi) — Bakanae / foot rot of Rice.

q.q: The causal organism of Stem rot of Rice is:
o: Fusarium oxysporum f.sp. psidii / Nalanthamala psidii
q.e: Sclerotium oryzae (Magnaporthe salvinii) — Stem rot of Rice.

q.q: The causal organism of Bacterial leaf blight of Rice is:
q.e: Xanthomonas oryzae pv. oryzae — Bacterial leaf blight of Rice.

q.q: The causal organism of Bacterial leaf streak of Rice is:
q.e: Xanthomonas oryzae pv. oryzicola — Bacterial leaf streak of Rice.

q.q: The causal organism of Tungro disease of Rice is:
q.e: Rice tungro viruses RTBV + RTSV (green leafhopper) — Tungro of Rice.

q.q: The causal organism of Grassy stunt of Rice is:
q.e: Rice grassy stunt virus (brown planthopper) — Grassy stunt of Rice.

q.q: The causal organism of Ragged stunt of Rice is:
q.e: Rice ragged stunt virus (brown planthopper) — Ragged stunt of Rice.

q.q: The causal organism of Ufra of Rice is:
q.e: Ditylenchus angustus — Ufra of Rice.

q.q: The causal organism of White tip disease of Rice is:
q.e: Aphelenchoides besseyi — White tip of Rice.

q.q: The causal organism of Root knot disease of Rice is:
q.e: Meloidogyne graminicola — Root knot of Rice.

q.q: The causal organism of Black / stem rust of Wheat is:
q.e: Puccinia graminis f.sp. tritici — Black / stem rust of Wheat.

q.q: The causal organism of Brown / leaf rust of Wheat is:
q.e: Puccinia triticina (P. recondita) — Brown / leaf rust of Wheat.

q.q: The causal organism of Yellow / stripe rust of Wheat is:
q.e: Puccinia striiformis — Yellow / stripe rust of Wheat.

q.q: The causal organism of Loose smut of Wheat is:
q.e: Ustilago tritici (U. segetum var. tritici) — Loose smut of Wheat.

q.q: The causal organism of Karnal bunt disease of Wheat is:
q.e: Tilletia indica (Neovossia indica) — Karnal bunt of Wheat.

q.q: The causal organism of Common / hill bunt disease of Wheat is:
q.e: Tilletia caries and T. laevis — Common / hill bunt of Wheat.

q.q: The causal organism of Flag smut of Wheat is:
q.e: Urocystis agropyri — Flag smut of Wheat.

q.q: The causal organism of Powdery mildew of Wheat is:
q.e: Blumeria graminis f.sp. tritici — Powdery mildew of Wheat.

q.q: The causal organism of Head scab of Wheat is:
q.e: Fusarium graminearum (Gibberella zeae) — Head scab of Wheat.

q.q: The causal organism of Spot blotch / foliar blight of Wheat is:
q.e: Bipolaris sorokiniana — Spot blotch / foliar blight of Wheat.

q.q: The causal organism of Tundu / yellow ear rot of Wheat is:
q.e: Rathayibacter tritici (with Anguina tritici) — Tundu / yellow ear rot of Wheat.

q.q: The causal organism of Ear cockle of Wheat is:
q.e: Anguina tritici — Ear cockle of Wheat.

q.q: The causal organism of Turcicum leaf blight of Maize is:
q.e: Exserohilum turcicum — Turcicum leaf blight of Maize.

q.q: The causal organism of Maydis leaf blight of Maize is:
q.e: Bipolaris maydis (Cochliobolus heterostrophus) — Maydis leaf blight of Maize.

q.q: The causal organism of Common rust of Maize is:
q.e: Puccinia sorghi — Common rust of Maize.

q.q: The causal organism of Polysora rust of Maize is:
q.e: Puccinia polysora — Polysora rust of Maize.

q.q: The causal organism of Common smut of Maize is:
q.e: Ustilago maydis — Common smut of Maize.

q.q: The causal organism of Head smut of Maize is:
q.e: Sporisorium reilianum (Sphacelotheca reiliana) — Head smut of Maize.

q.q: The causal organism of Banded leaf & sheath blight of Maize is:
q.e: Rhizoctonia solani f.sp. sasakii — Banded leaf & sheath blight of Maize.

q.q: The causal organism of Post-flowering stalk rot of Maize is:
q.e: Macrophomina phaseolina / Fusarium spp. — Post-flowering stalk rot of Maize.

q.q: The causal organism of Downy mildew of Maize is:
q.e: Peronosclerospora sorghi / P. heteropogoni — Downy mildew of Maize.

q.q: The causal organism of Grain (covered) smut of Sorghum is:
q.e: Sporisorium sorghi — Grain (covered) smut of Sorghum.

q.q: The causal organism of Loose smut of Sorghum is:

q.e: Colletotrichum capsici / Taphrina maculans — Leaf spot of Turmeric / ginger.

q.q: The causal organism of Bacterial wilt (ginger) of Turmeric / ginger is:
q.e: Ralstonia solanacearum — Bacterial wilt (ginger) of Turmeric / ginger.

q.q: The causal organism of Black shank disease of Tobacco is:
q.e: Phytophthora nicotianae — Black shank of Tobacco.

q.q: The causal organism of Damping off disease of Tobacco is:
q.e: Pythium spp. — Damping off of Tobacco.

q.q: The causal organism of Wildfire disease of Tobacco is:
q.e: Pseudomonas syringae pv. tabaci — Wildfire of Tobacco.

q.q: The causal organism of Mosaic of Tobacco is:
q.e: Tobacco mosaic virus — Mosaic of Tobacco.

q.q: The causal organism of Leaf curl of Tobacco is:
q.e: Tobacco leaf curl virus (whitefly) — Leaf curl of Tobacco.

q.q: Late blight of potato is caused by:
q.e: Phytophthora infestans — the Oomycete of the Irish famine; sporangia and zoospores in cool, wet weather.

q.q: Downy mildew of grapevine is caused by:
q.e: Plasmopara viticola — the disease that prompted the discovery of Bordeaux mixture.

q.q: Powdery mildew appendages with swollen bulbous bases belong to:
q.e: Phyllactinia — needle appendages with bulb bases; Podosphaera forks at the tips, Uncinula curls.

q.q: Ergot of pearl millet (bajra) is caused by:
q.e: Claviceps fusiformis — honeydew and sclerotia in the ear; C. purpurea is the rye ergot.

q.q: The anamorph Pyricularia oryzae has the teleomorph:
q.e: Magnaporthe oryzae — rice blast; the fungus penetrates via a melanised appressorium.

q.q: On barberry, aecia of Puccinia graminis form on the:
q.e: Lower (abaxial) surface; pycnia (spermogonia) form on the upper surface.

q.q: The perfect state of Rhizoctonia solani is:
q.e: Thanatephorus cucumeris — a basidiomycete; the anamorph shows right-angle branching.

q.q: In Puccinia graminis, nuclear fusion (karyogamy) occurs in the:
q.e: Teliospore — meiosis follows in the basidium on germination.

q.q: The sexual resting spore of the Zygomycota is the:
q.e: Zygospore — formed by fusion of two equal gametangia (gametangial conjugation).

q.q: Coenocytic (aseptate) mycelium is characteristic of:
q.e: Oomycota and Zygomycota — long multinucleate hyphae with few cross-walls.

q.q: The chitin of the true fungal wall is polymerised through:
q.e: β-1,4 — chains of N-acetylglucosamine laid down by chitin synthase.

q.q: The principal sterol of the fungal plasma membrane is:
q.e: Ergosterol — the target of azole and polyene fungicides.

q.q: The cell wall of the Oomycetes is composed mainly of:
q.e: Cellulose/glucans, essentially without chitin — reflecting their non-fungal lineage.

q.q: The dolipore septum is a diagnostic feature of the:
q.e: Basidiomycota — a barrel-shaped pore flanked by parenthesomes.

q.q: The Woronin body is associated with the septal pore of the:
q.e: Ascomycota — it plugs the pore after hyphal injury; derived from peroxisomes.

q.q: The zoospore of a chytrid characteristically bears:
q.e: Single posterior whiplash — contrast the biflagellate Oomycete zoospore (tinsel + whiplash).

q.q: False smut of rice is caused by:
q.e: Ustilaginoidea virens — greenish spore balls replace the grains.

q.q: Karnal bunt of wheat is caused by:
q.e: Tilletia indica — a partial bunt with a fishy trimethylamine odour; a quarantine pathogen.

q.q: Loose smut of wheat survives internally as dormant mycelium in the:
q.e: Embryo — Ustilago tritici; needs systemic or hot-water seed treatment.

q.q: Rhizomorphs (dark shoestring strands) are typical of:
q.e: Armillaria mellea — the honey fungus spreads through soil by rhizomorphs.

q.q: Coffee rust is caused by:
q.e: Hemileia vastatrix — the rust that ended coffee growing in colonial Ceylon.

q.q: The hypersensitive response is best described as:
q.e: Localised programmed cell death — it confines biotrophs at the infection site.

q.q: Phytoalexins are compounds that are:
q.e: Induced after infection — e.g. pisatin (pea), phaseollin (bean), rishitin (potato).

q.q: The rishitin phytoalexin is produced by:
q.e: Potato. Pisatin = pea, phaseollin = bean, glyceollin = soybean.

q.q: During tissue maceration the enzymes acting first are usually the:
q.e: Pectinases — they dissolve the pectin-rich middle lamella, loosening cells.

q.q: Wilt caused by vascular occlusion is typical of:
q.e: Fusarium and Verticillium — they colonise the xylem, causing vascular wilt.

q.q: The disease tetrahedron adds which factor to the disease triangle?
q.e: Time — host, pathogen and environment plus time; the human axis is sometimes added.

q.q: Most plant-pathogenic bacteria are:
q.e: Gram-negative rods; the main exceptions are Clavibacter and Streptomyces.

q.q: Fire blight of apple and pear is caused by:
q.e: Erwinia amylovora — the first disease proven to be bacterial (Burrill).

q.q: Bacterial wilt of solanaceous crops is caused by:
q.e: Ralstonia solanacearum — classified by race, biovar and phylotype.

q.q: Crown gall of many plants is caused by:
q.e: A. tumefaciens — T-DNA from the Ti plasmid drives tumour formation.

q.q: Bacterial blight of rice (kresek) is caused by:
q.e: X. oryzae pv. oryzae — vascular; pv. oryzicola gives (parenchymatous) leaf streak.

q.q: Common scab of potato is caused by:
q.e: Streptomyces scabies — a Gram-positive actinobacterium favoured by dry alkaline soil.
