q.q: Citrus greening (HLB) is associated with the phloem-limited:
q.e: Ca. Liberibacter asiaticus — vectored by the psyllid Diaphorina citri; unculturable.

q.q: Pierce's disease of grape is caused by the xylem-limited:
q.e: Xylella fastidiosa — sharpshooter-transmitted; fastidious but culturable.

q.q: Phytoplasmas differ fundamentally from true bacteria in:
q.e: Lacking a cell wall — wall-less, phloem-limited, tetracycline-sensitive mollicutes.

q.q: Soft rot of vegetables is caused chiefly by pectolytic:
q.e: Pectobacterium/Dickeya — pectate lyases macerate tissue into a slimy rot.

q.q: The genome of most plant viruses is:
q.e: (+)ssRNA — it can act directly as messenger RNA.

q.q: Tobacco mosaic virus particles show which symmetry?
q.e: Helical rod ~300 × 18 nm with ~2130 coat-protein subunits.

q.q: Geminiviruses are distinctive for having:
q.e: Twinned icosahedra, circular ssDNA — includes the whitefly-borne begomoviruses.

q.q: Tomato spotted wilt virus is transmitted by thrips in a manner that is:
q.e: Persistent-propagative — acquired by larvae; the virus multiplies in the vector.

q.q: Leaf curl diseases of cotton and tomato are transmitted by:
q.e: Bemisia tabaci — persistently circulative transmission of begomoviruses.

q.q: Luteoviruses (BYDV, PLRV) are transmitted by aphids as:
q.e: Circulative non-propagative — gut to salivary glands without replicating; phloem-limited.

q.q: Rice tungro is transmitted by:
q.e: Green leafhopper (Nephotettix) — carrying RTBV with RTSV as helper.

q.q: Bunchy top of banana is caused by a virus spread by the aphid:
q.e: Pentalonia nigronervosa — persistently transmitting the Babuvirus (BBTV).

q.q: A viroid is best described as:
o: A defective virus with a coat
q.e: Naked circular ssRNA — the smallest infectious agent, encoding no protein.

q.q: The first viroid to be discovered was:
q.e: PSTVd (Diener, 1971) — the type species of Pospiviroidae, replicating in the nucleus.

q.q: Root-knot nematodes induce which feeding site?
q.e: Giant cells — induced by Meloidogyne; cyst nematodes form syncytia.

q.q: Molya disease of cereals is caused by:
q.e: Heterodera avenae — the cereal cyst nematode, serious on wheat in Rajasthan.

q.q: Ufra disease of rice is caused by:
q.e: Ditylenchus angustus — the rice stem nematode.

q.q: The burrowing nematode Radopholus similis causes:
q.e: Radopholus similis — banana toppling and citrus spreading decline.

q.q: The logistic (compound-interest) model is linearised by plotting:
q.e: ln[x/(1−x)] — the logit; its slope is the apparent infection rate r.

q.q: The monomolecular (simple-interest) model is linearised by plotting:
q.e: ln[1/(1−x)] — suited to monocyclic diseases with one infection cycle.

q.q: The Gompertz model has its inflexion point at a disease level of about:
q.e: ~37% — asymmetric, unlike the logistic which peaks in rate at 50%.

q.q: Horizontal resistance slows an epidemic mainly by reducing the:
q.e: Reduces r — rate-reducing, polygenic resistance; vertical resistance instead cuts x0.

q.q: Vertical (race-specific) resistance acts principally by reducing the:
q.e: Reduces x0 — delaying onset; it can fail completely when matched by a virulent race.

q.q: AUDPC is used mainly to:
o: Estimate spore germination on the host surface
Summarise an epidemic as one comparable value
Identify the causal pathogen from lesion shape
Measure the latent period between successive cycles
q.e: Area Under the Disease Progress Curve — integrates severity over time for ranking.

q.q: Garrett's 'inoculum potential' is defined as the:
o: Total number of spores present in the soil
Length of the latent period between two cycles
Severity of disease recorded at final harvest
Energy of growth available for infection
q.e: Energy of growth available for infection — depends on inoculum amount and vigour.

q.q: Wilt of sugarcane and most vascular wilts follow a pattern that is:
q.e: Monocyclic — one infection cycle per season, no secondary spread; fits the monomolecular model.

q.q: Azole (triazole) fungicides act by inhibiting:
q.e: C14-demethylase (DMI) — blocking ergosterol biosynthesis.

q.q: Strobilurin (QoI) fungicides act at:
o: Complex I of the respiratory chain
The Qo site of complex III
q.e: Complex III, Qo site — blocking mitochondrial electron transport; resistance-prone (G143A).

q.q: Carboxin, a classic smut/rust seed treatment, inhibits:
q.e: Succinate dehydrogenase (SDHI) — the original oxathiin.

q.q: Metalaxyl controls Oomycetes by inhibiting:
q.e: rRNA synthesis — highly specific to Oomycetes; single-site and resistance-prone.

q.q: Benzimidazoles (carbendazim, benomyl) act by inhibiting:
q.e: β-tubulin — blocking mitosis; a single mutation confers resistance.

q.q: Tricyclazole controls rice blast by inhibiting:
q.e: Melanin biosynthesis — without it the appressorium cannot generate penetration turgor.

q.q: Mancozeb and other dithiocarbamates are best described as:
q.e: Multisite contact protectants — low resistance risk, applied preventively.

q.q: Bordeaux mixture, the first successful fungicide, was introduced by:
q.e: Millardet (1885) — copper sulphate plus lime for grape downy mildew.

q.q: PAMP-triggered immunity is initiated by:
q.e: Surface PRRs detecting PAMPs — e.g. FLS2 recognising flagellin (flg22).

q.q: Effector-triggered immunity is usually mediated by:
q.e: NBS-LRR / NLR proteins — recognising specific effectors and often triggering HR.

q.q: The maize gene Hm1, the first R gene cloned, acts by:
o: Silencing the invading pathogen's genomic RNA
Encoding a reductase that detoxifies HC-toxin
Producing a phytoalexin at the infection court
Encoding a surface LRR receptor kinase protein
q.e: HC-toxin reductase — an atypical R gene against Cochliobolus carbonum.

q.q: The rice gene Xa21 encodes a:
q.e: LRR receptor kinase — recognising a sulfated peptide from Xanthomonas oryzae.

q.q: Systemic acquired resistance is signalled chiefly through:
q.e: Salicylic acid → NPR1 → PR genes — effective mainly against biotrophs.

q.q: Induced systemic resistance triggered by rhizobacteria depends mainly on:
q.e: JA/ethylene — a primed defence state; contrasts with SA-dependent SAR.

q.q: The enzyme that dices double-stranded RNA into small interfering RNAs is:
q.e: Dicer/DCL — an RNase III enzyme producing 21–24 nt siRNAs.

q.q: Agrobacterium-mediated transformation transfers to the plant genome the:
o: Entire Ti plasmid with vir region
vir gene operon on a helper plasmid
q.e: T-DNA — flanked by 25-bp borders; the vir genes act in trans.

q.q: The reporter gene uidA (GUS) encodes:
q.e: β-glucuronidase — cleaves X-Gluc to a blue product in transformed tissue.

q.q: Which molecular marker is dominant rather than codominant?
q.e: RAPD (also AFLP) — band present/absent, so heterozygotes are not distinguished.

q.q: The universal DNA barcode for fungal identification is the:
q.e: ITS — 16S rRNA is used for bacteria, COI for animals.

q.q: Tabtoxin (wildfire of tobacco) inhibits the enzyme:
q.e: Glutamine synthetase — ammonia accumulates, giving chlorotic halos.

q.q: Phaseolotoxin (halo blight of bean) inhibits:
q.e: OCTase — the classic swap-partner of tabtoxin→GS.

q.q: Victorin, the first host-specific toxin isolated pure, affects:
q.e: Oat — from Helminthosporium victoriae (Victoria blight).

q.q: T-toxin of Cochliobolus heterostrophus race T is toxic to maize carrying:
q.e: T-cytoplasm — via the URF13 protein; cause of the 1970 corn leaf blight epidemic.

q.q: The 'Father of Plant Pathology' is:
q.e: Anton de Bary — proved late blight was fungal, disproving spontaneous generation.

q.q: The gene-for-gene hypothesis was proposed by:
q.e: H. H. Flor — from flax and flax rust studies.

q.q: The 'Father of Indian Plant Pathology' is:
q.e: Sir E. J. Butler — first Imperial Mycologist at Pusa; wrote 'Fungi and Disease in Plants'.

q.q: K. C. Mehta is renowned for tracing the annual recurrence of wheat rusts from the:
q.e: Nilgiri and Himalayan hills — the off-season reservoir that reseeds the north Indian plains.

q.q: Tobacco mosaic virus was first crystallised in 1935 by:
q.e: Wendell Stanley (Nobel 1946); Bawden & Pirie then showed it was nucleoprotein.

q.q: The bacterium first proven to cause a plant disease (fire blight) was studied by:
q.e: T. J. Burrill — around 1878–82; E. F. Smith later established the discipline.

q.q: The classical local-lesion assay for TMV uses:
q.e: Nicotiana glutinosa — Holmes (1929) showed countable necrotic lesions for quantification.

q.q: DAS-ELISA is most widely used to detect:
q.e: Plant viruses — the virus is trapped between coating and enzyme-linked antibodies.

q.q: LAMP is valued for field diagnostics because it:
o: Requires precise repeated thermal cycling steps
Depends on a bench-top DNA sequencer machine
Detects only proteins and never nucleic acids
Amplifies DNA at one constant temperature
q.e: Isothermal — ~60–65 °C with Bst polymerase; results readable by turbidity or colour.

q.q: To detect an RNA virus by PCR, the essential first step is:
o: Restriction digestion of the sample DNA
Gram staining of the plant sample
q.e: Reverse transcription (RT-PCR) — the RNA is copied to cDNA before amplification.

q.q: Downy mildew of pearl millet is caused by:
q.e: Sclerospora graminicola — green ear / crazy top of bajra.

q.q: Wart disease of potato is caused by:
q.e: Synchytrium endobioticum — a chytrid causing cauliflower-like warts; a quarantine pathogen.

q.q: Ergot alkaloids ('St. Anthony's fire') are produced in the sclerotia of:
q.e: Claviceps purpurea — ergotism from contaminated rye.

q.q: Turkey X disease, which launched mycotoxin research, was caused by:
q.e: Aflatoxin (Aspergillus flavus) — a 1960 UK poultry outbreak.

q.q: The determinative scheme LOPAT is used to identify:
q.e: Fluorescent pseudomonads — Levan, Oxidase, Pectinolysis, Arginine dihydrolase, Tobacco HR.

q.q: Coat-protein-mediated virus resistance is an example of:
q.e: Pathogen-derived resistance — expressing a viral gene (e.g. TMV CP) confers resistance.

q.q: Cauliflower mosaic virus is unusual among plant viruses in having:
q.e: dsDNA replicated via reverse transcription — source of the 35S promoter.

q.q: Cyst nematodes (Heterodera, Globodera) induce which feeding site?
q.e: Syncytium — formed by cell-wall dissolution and fusion; root-knot nematodes form giant cells.

q.q: The genome of the majority of plant viruses is:
q.e: (+)ssRNA — it can act directly as mRNA. dsRNA, ssDNA and dsDNA plant viruses exist but are the minority.

q.q: Tobacco mosaic virus particles have which symmetry?
q.e: Helical — a rigid rod ~300 × 18 nm with ~2130 coat-protein subunits spiralling around the RNA.

q.q: The protein shell enclosing a virus genome is the:
q.e: Capsid, built of repeating subunits called capsomeres; genome + capsid together form the nucleocapsid.

q.q: Flexuous filamentous particles ~750 nm long are typical of the genus:
q.e: Potyvirus — long flexuous rods; the largest plant-virus genus, translated as a single polyprotein.

q.q: Enveloped, bacilliform (bullet-shaped) particles characterise the family:
q.e: Rhabdoviridae — (−)ssRNA, replicating (propagatively) in both plant and insect-vector cells.

q.q: Geminiviruses are distinctive for their:
q.e: Twin icosahedra, circular ssDNA — includes the whitefly-borne begomoviruses causing leaf curls.

q.q: Cytoplasmic 'pinwheel' cylindrical inclusion bodies are diagnostic of:
q.e: Potyvirus — the CI (cylindrical inclusion) protein forms pinwheels seen by electron microscopy.

q.q: A tripartite (three-component) RNA genome is found in:
q.e: Cucumber mosaic virus — RNAs 1, 2 and 3 packaged separately; a very broad-host-range Cucumovirus.

q.q: RNA plant viruses replicate their genomes using a virus-encoded:
q.e: RdRp — the replicase; the notable exception is Caulimovirus, which reverse-transcribes.

q.q: The term 'virus' as a contagium vivum fluidum was introduced by:
q.e: Beijerinck (1898) — building on Mayer's sap transmission and Ivanowski's filterability work on TMV.

q.q: Tobacco mosaic virus was first crystallised (1935) by:
q.e: Wendell Stanley (Nobel 1946); Bawden & Pirie soon showed the crystals were nucleoprotein (RNA + protein).

q.q: The demonstration that TMV is a nucleoprotein (contains RNA) is credited to:
q.e: Bawden and Pirie — establishing that the infectious principle carries nucleic acid, not just protein.

q.q: In the Baltimore system, positive-sense ssRNA viruses fall in:
q.e: Class IV. Class V = (−)ssRNA, Class III = dsRNA, Class VI = ssRNA reverse-transcribing, Class VII = dsDNA-RT.

q.q: The official body responsible for virus taxonomy is the:
q.e: ICTV — the International Committee on Taxonomy of Viruses, which sanctions family/genus/species names.

q.q: Which family reproduces its dsDNA genome through reverse transcription (a pararetrovirus)?
q.e: Caulimoviridae (e.g. CaMV) — dsDNA replicated via an RNA intermediate; source of the 35S promoter.

q.q: Banana bunchy top virus belongs to a family whose genome is:
q.e: Multipartite circular ssDNA (Babuvirus, Nanoviridae) — at least six ~1 kb components.

q.q: Tomato spotted wilt virus (Tospovirus) has a genome that is:
q.e: Ambisense tripartite ssRNA, enveloped — in the order Bunyavirales; propagative in thrips.

q.q: Plant reoviruses (rice dwarf, rice ragged stunt) have a genome of:
q.e: Segmented dsRNA (10–12 segments) — propagative in leaf/planthopper vectors.

q.q: The genus containing the largest number of known plant viruses is:
q.e: Potyvirus — roughly a quarter to a third of characterised plant viruses; hence its economic weight.

q.q: Citrus tristeza virus, with the longest flexuous plant-virus particle, belongs to genus:
q.e: Closterovirus — particles up to ~2000 nm; semi-persistently aphid-transmitted (Toxoptera citricida).

q.q: Maize streak virus is a geminivirus of the genus, transmitted by leafhoppers:
q.e: Mastrevirus — monopartite, leafhopper-borne; begomoviruses instead are whitefly-borne.

q.q: Which virus is readily transmitted mechanically by sap?
q.e: TMV — extremely stable and sap-transmissible; the phloem-limited luteoviruses and DNA viruses generally are not.

q.q: Non-persistent, stylet-borne transmission is typical of aphid-vectored:
o: Cucumber mosaic virus / Potato virus Y
q.e: CMV and PVY — acquired and inoculated within seconds/minutes; retained only briefly on the stylet.

q.q: Luteoviruses such as BYDV and PLRV are transmitted by aphids in a manner that is:
q.e: Circulative non-propagative — the virus traverses gut to salivary glands without replicating; also phloem-limited.

q.q: Begomoviruses (leaf curls of cotton, tomato, chilli) are transmitted by:
q.e: Bemisia tabaci, persistently and circulatively — the basis of the leaf-curl epidemics across India.

q.q: Tospoviruses (e.g. groundnut bud necrosis) are transmitted by thrips in a way that is:
o: Persistent and propagative (virus multiplies in the thrips)
q.e: Persistent-propagative — acquired only by larvae; the virus replicates in the vector before transmission.

q.q: Nepoviruses are transmitted by which soil organisms?
q.e: Xiphinema/Longidorus (dagger/needle nematodes). Tobraviruses instead go with trichodorids; both also seed/pollen-borne.

q.q: Beet necrotic yellow vein virus (rhizomania) is vectored by the plasmodiophorid:
q.e: Polymyxa betae — a soil-borne protist vector; Olpidium vectors TNV and lettuce big-vein agent.

q.q: Rice tungro is transmitted by the green leafhopper and involves:
o: RTBV (dsDNA) plus RTSV (ssRNA), with RTSV as helper
q.e: RTBV + RTSV — the spherical RTSV enables semi-persistent transmission of the bacilliform RTBV by Nephotettix.

q.q: Pigeonpea sterility mosaic ('green plague') is transmitted by:
q.e: Eriophyid mite Aceria cajani — spreading the emaravirus that causes bushy, sterile plants.

q.q: Which is a recognised route of plant-virus spread in addition to vectors?
q.e: Seed, pollen, vegetative grafting and dodder — plus mechanical sap; many potyviruses/tobamoviruses are seed-borne.

q.q: Bunchy top of banana is caused by a virus of genus, spread by the aphid Pentalonia:
q.e: Babuvirus (BBTV) — dwarfed 'bunched' crown; persistently transmitted by Pentalonia nigronervosa.

q.q: Papaya ringspot disease is caused by a:
q.e: PRSV (Potyvirus) — aphid-borne, non-persistent; managed historically with coat-protein transgenic papaya in Hawaii.

q.q: Among potato viruses, which is a Potyvirus?
q.e: PVY is a Potyvirus (aphid, non-persistent). PVX = Potexvirus (mechanical), PLRV = Polerovirus (persistent aphid).

q.q: Leaf curl diseases of cotton, tomato and chilli in India are predominantly caused by:
q.e: Begomoviruses — whitefly-transmitted ssDNA geminiviruses, often with associated betasatellites.

q.q: Citrus tristeza (quick decline) is caused by a:
q.e: Closterovirus (CTV) — aphid-transmitted; devastating on sour-orange rootstock.

q.q: Cadang-cadang, a lethal disease of coconut, is caused by a:
q.e: Viroid (CCCVd) — the coconut cadang-cadang viroid, one of the few viroids lethal to its host.

q.q: Groundnut bud necrosis is caused by a:
q.e: Tospovirus (GBNV) — thrips-transmitted; ring/necrotic patterns and bud death.

q.q: The X-body (amorphous inclusion) in TMV-infected cells is composed largely of:
q.e: Virus and replication-associated material — one of several inclusion types used diagnostically in light microscopy.

q.q: A satellite virus is characterised by:
o: Dependence on an unrelated helper virus for replication
q.e: Dependence on a helper — e.g. Satellite tobacco necrosis virus needs TNV; it encodes only its own coat protein.

q.q: Satellite RNAs differ from satellite viruses in that they:
o: Depend on the helper virus's coat protein for encapsidation
q.e: Use the helper's coat protein — they can modulate (intensify or attenuate) helper-virus symptoms.

q.q: A viroid is best described as:
o: A small naked circular ssRNA with no protein coat
A defective virus with a coat
q.e: Naked circular ssRNA of a few hundred nucleotides — the smallest known infectious agent, non-coding.

q.q: The first viroid to be discovered (Diener, 1971) was:
q.e: PSTVd — the type species of family Pospiviroidae; replicates in the nucleus.

q.q: Members of family Avsunviroidae (e.g. avocado sunblotch) are unusual in that they:
o: Replicate in the chloroplast using hammerhead ribozymes
q.e: Chloroplastic replication with hammerhead ribozymes — Pospiviroidae, by contrast, replicate in the nucleus via RNA Pol II.

q.q: Viroids cause disease despite:
q.e: Encoding no protein — pathogenesis is thought to involve RNA-based interference with host gene regulation/silencing.

q.q: Citrus exocortis is caused by a:
q.e: Viroid (CEVd) — bark scaling and stunting; spread on contaminated tools.

q.q: Replication of viroids proceeds by a:
q.e: Rolling-circle — host RNA polymerases copy the circular RNA; no viroid-encoded polymerase exists.

q.q: The classical local-lesion assay for quantifying TMV uses:
q.e: Nicotiana glutinosa — Holmes (1929) showed countable necrotic local lesions, enabling virus quantification.

q.q: For routine serological detection of plant viruses, the most widely used format is:
q.e: DAS-ELISA — double-antibody sandwich ELISA traps the virus between coating and enzyme-linked antibodies.

q.q: To detect an RNA virus by PCR, the essential first step is:
q.e: Reverse transcription (RT-PCR) — the RNA is copied to cDNA before amplification.

q.q: Immunosorbent electron microscopy (ISEM) aids virus detection by:
o: Using antibodies to trap and decorate virions on the grid
q.e: Antibody trapping/decoration — concentrates virions and confirms identity on the EM grid.

q.q: Two plant genera widely used as diagnostic assay/indicator hosts are:
q.e: Chenopodium and Datura — reliable local-lesion or systemic reactions for many sap-transmissible viruses.

q.q: The standard technique to obtain virus-free planting material is:
q.e: Meristem-tip culture ± thermotherapy — the apical dome is often virus-free; heat further reduces titre.

q.q: Cross-protection as a control strategy relies on:
o: A mild strain pre-occupying the host and excluding a severe related strain
q.e: Mild-strain interference — used for citrus tristeza and papaya ringspot, though risky if the mild strain mutates.

q.q: Coat-protein-mediated resistance, the first engineered virus resistance in plants, was demonstrated against:
q.e: TMV — Beachy and colleagues (1986) expressed the TMV coat-protein gene in tobacco, conferring resistance (pathogen-derived resistance).

q.q: RNA silencing (RNAi) contributes to virus resistance by:
o: Degrading viral RNA in a sequence-specific manner
q.e: Sequence-specific degradation of viral RNA — the natural antiviral defence exploited in transgenic and now spray-based approaches.

q.q: A key cultural measure against persistently transmitted phloem-limited viruses is:
o: Vector (aphid/whitefly) control plus rogueing of infected plants
q.e: Vector management + rogueing — removing inoculum sources and controlling the insect that circulates the virus.

q.q: Which statement about phytoplasmas vs viruses is correct?
o: Phytoplasmas are wall-less bacteria (prokaryotes); viruses are not cellular
q.e: Phytoplasmas are prokaryotes (wall-less Mollicutes); viruses are acellular nucleoprotein particles — a common exam contrast.

q.q: Cassava mosaic disease, a major constraint in Africa and India, is caused by:
q.e: Begomoviruses (e.g. Indian/Sri Lankan cassava mosaic virus) — whitefly-transmitted ssDNA geminiviruses.

q.q: Most plant-pathogenic bacteria are:
q.e: Gram-negative rods. The main Gram-positive exceptions are Clavibacter, Streptomyces, Rhodococcus, Curtobacterium and Rathayibacter.

q.q: Rigidity of the bacterial cell wall is due to:
q.e: Peptidoglycan — NAG–NAM chains cross-linked by peptides; the target of penicillin (ineffective against wall-less mollicutes).

q.q: Lipopolysaccharide (LPS), the endotoxin of Gram-negative bacteria, is located in the:
q.e: Outer membrane — a defining feature of the Gram-negative envelope, absent in Gram-positives.

q.q: Teichoic acids are characteristic of the wall of:
q.e: Gram-positive bacteria — anchored in the thick peptidoglycan; Gram-negatives have an outer membrane with LPS instead.

q.q: A bacterium with a single polar flagellum is termed:
q.e: Monotrichous. Lophotrichous = tuft at one pole, amphitrichous = at both poles, peritrichous = all over.

q.q: The yellow pigment of Xanthomonas colonies is:
q.e: Xanthomonadin — a membrane-bound brominated aryl-polyene unique to Xanthomonas.

q.q: Under UV light, fluorescent pseudomonads produce the diffusible pigment:
q.e: Pyoverdine — a yellow-green fluorescent siderophore; the basis of the 'fluorescent' group of Pseudomonas.

q.q: The industrially valuable exopolysaccharide 'xanthan gum' is produced by:
q.e: Xanthomonas campestris — the EPS also aids attachment and vascular plugging in disease.

q.q: Bacteria multiply chiefly by:
q.e: Binary fission — one cell divides into two; conjugation transfers DNA but is not reproduction.

q.q: Ti and Ri plasmids are examples of:
o: Extrachromosomal circular DNA carrying pathogenicity genes
q.e: Extrachromosomal plasmids — the tumour-inducing (Ti) and root-inducing (Ri) plasmids of Agrobacterium.

q.q: Bacteriophages were independently discovered by:
q.e: Twort (1915) and d'Herelle (1917) — viruses that infect bacteria; used in phage typing.

q.q: The predatory bacterium that invades and multiplies within other Gram-negative bacteria is:
q.e: Bdellovibrio — enters the periplasm of its prey; of interest as a biocontrol agent.

q.q: Fire blight of apple and pear, the first disease proven to be caused by a bacterium, is caused by:
q.e: Erwinia amylovora — T. J. Burrill established its bacterial cause around 1878–82.

q.q: The scientist who first demonstrated that a bacterium can cause plant disease (fire blight) was:
q.e: T. J. Burrill. Erwin F. Smith later established bacterial plant pathology as a discipline against Alfred Fischer's scepticism.

q.q: Bacterial soft rot of vegetables is caused chiefly by pectolytic:
q.e: Pectobacterium carotovorum / Dickeya — pectate lyases macerate the middle lamella, giving a slimy, foul-smelling rot.

q.q: Bacterial wilt of solanaceous crops (potato brown rot) is caused by:
q.e: Ralstonia solanacearum — a soil-borne, xylem-invading pathogen classified by race, biovar and phylotype.

q.q: Ring rot of potato is caused by the Gram-positive bacterium:
q.e: Clavibacter michiganensis subsp. sepedonicus — a vascular pathogen of major quarantine importance.

q.q: Bacterial canker of tomato is caused by:
q.e: Clavibacter michiganensis subsp. michiganensis — 'bird's-eye' fruit spots and vascular wilting.

q.q: Common scab of potato is caused by the filamentous, Gram-positive:
q.e: Streptomyces scabies — an actinobacterium favoured by dry, alkaline soils; produces the toxin thaxtomin.

q.q: Crown gall is caused by:
q.e: A. tumefaciens — T-DNA from the Ti plasmid integrates and drives tumorous growth. A. rhizogenes (Ri) causes hairy root.

q.q: Citrus canker is caused by:
q.e: Xanthomonas citri subsp. citri — raised corky lesions with a water-soaked yellow halo.

q.q: Bacterial blight of rice (with its 'kresek' wilting phase) is caused by:
q.e: X. oryzae pv. oryzae — vascular. The parenchymatous pv. oryzicola instead causes bacterial leaf streak.

q.q: Black rot of crucifers, with characteristic V-shaped marginal lesions and blackened veins, is caused by:
q.e: Xanthomonas campestris pv. campestris — a vascular pathogen entering through hydathodes.

q.q: Bacterial blight ('black arm') of cotton is caused by:
q.e: Xanthomonas citri pv. malvacearum (older X. campestris pv. malvacearum) — angular leaf spots and blackened stems.

q.q: Halo blight of bean, whose toxin produces a chlorotic halo, is caused by:
q.e: P. syringae pv. phaseolicola — phaseolotoxin inhibits ornithine carbamoyltransferase, causing the halo.

q.q: Wildfire of tobacco is caused by:
q.e: P. syringae pv. tabaci — tabtoxin (a glutamine-synthetase inhibitor) yields spreading chlorotic halos.

q.q: Tundu / yellow ear rot (spike blight) of wheat is a complex of Rathayibacter tritici with the nematode:
q.e: Anguina tritici — the seed-gall nematode carries the bacterium into the ear, producing a yellow bacterial ooze.

q.q: Ratoon stunting disease of sugarcane is caused by:
q.e: Leifsonia xyli subsp. xyli (formerly Clavibacter xyli) — a fastidious xylem-limited Gram-positive.

q.q: Red stripe and top rot of sugarcane is caused by:
q.e: Acidovorax avenae subsp. avenae (old Pseudomonas rubrilineans) — a bacterial, not fungal, disease.

q.q: Leaf scald of sugarcane is caused by:
q.e: Xanthomonas albilineans — produces the toxin albicidin, causing white 'pencil-line' streaks.

q.q: Bacterial blight ('oily spot' / telya) of pomegranate, a serious problem in India, is caused by:
q.e: Xanthomonas axonopodis pv. punicae — oily, water-soaked spots and stem cracking, causing heavy losses in Maharashtra/Karnataka.

q.q: Angular leaf spot of cucumber is caused by:
q.e: P. syringae pv. lachrymans — angular water-soaked lesions bounded by veins, with milky exudate.

q.q: Olive knot / oleander gall is caused by:
q.e: Pseudomonas savastanoi — produces IAA and cytokinins that induce galls (hyperplasia).

q.q: Basal rot / bacterial wilt of banana known as Moko disease is caused by:
q.e: Ralstonia solanacearum race 2. (Xanthomonas musacearum causes the separate banana Xanthomonas wilt in East Africa.)

q.q: Phytoplasmas differ from true bacteria most fundamentally in:
q.e: Lacking a cell wall — pleomorphic, phloem-limited mollicutes; sensitive to tetracycline but not penicillin.

q.q: Which of these is a phytoplasma disease?
q.e: Little leaf of brinjal — like sesame phyllody, sandal spike and sugarcane grassy shoot, it is leafhopper-transmitted phytoplasma.

q.q: Citrus stubborn disease is caused by the helical, wall-less, but culturable:
q.e: Spiroplasma citri — a Mollicute like phytoplasma, but it is helical and can be grown in culture.

q.q: Pierce's disease of grapevine and citrus variegated chlorosis are caused by the xylem-limited:
q.e: Xylella fastidiosa — sharpshooter-transmitted; fastidious but culturable on special media.

q.q: Citrus greening (Huanglongbing) is associated with the phloem-limited, still-unculturable:
q.e: Ca. Liberibacter asiaticus — vectored by the psyllid Diaphorina citri; diagnosed by PCR.

q.q: Phytoplasmas (then called MLOs) were first observed in 1967 by:
q.e: Doi et al. (1967) — electron microscopy of yellows-diseased plants revealed mycoplasma-like bodies in the phloem.

q.q: Gram-negative plant pathogens inject effector proteins into host cells through the:
q.e: Type III secretion system — encoded by hrp/hrc genes; a syringe-like apparatus delivering effectors.

q.q: The abbreviation 'hrp' stands for:
q.e: Hypersensitive Response and Pathogenicity — hrp mutants lose both the ability to cause disease and to elicit HR.

q.q: Harpin (HrpN) is best described as a bacterial protein that:
q.e: Elicits the HR — a heat-stable, glycine-rich elicitor secreted through the T3SS.

q.q: In the gene-for-gene interaction, the bacterial avr gene product is:
o: Recognised by a matching host R protein, triggering resistance
q.e: Recognised by a matching R protein — recognition triggers HR/resistance; without the match, disease results.

q.q: Induction of Agrobacterium vir genes for T-DNA transfer is triggered by the wound phenolic:
q.e: Acetosyringone — sensed by the VirA/VirG two-component system, switching on the transfer machinery.

q.q: Opines produced by crown-gall tissue serve the bacterium as a:
o: Carbon and nitrogen source usable mainly by the inciting Agrobacterium
q.e: C/N source — the T-DNA reprograms the plant to make opines (octopine, nopaline) that the pathogen can catabolise.

q.q: Quorum sensing in most Gram-negative plant pathogens is mediated by:
q.e: AHLs — LuxI-type synthases and LuxR-type receptors coordinate virulence and EPS at high cell density.

q.q: Frost injury is enhanced by ice-nucleation-active bacteria such as Pseudomonas syringae via the protein:
q.e: InaZ — templates ice formation at warm sub-zero temperatures; 'ice-minus' strains were an early biotech application.

q.q: The exopolysaccharide implicated in the systemic ooze and wilt of fire blight is:
q.e: Amylovoran — the EPS of Erwinia amylovora that plugs vessels and forms the characteristic bacterial ooze.

q.q: The principal virulence enzymes of soft-rot bacteria are:
q.e: Pectinolytic enzymes — degrading the pectin-rich middle lamella, causing tissue maceration.

q.q: Coronatine, a virulence factor of some P. syringae pathovars, mimics:
q.e: JA-Ile — hijacking jasmonate signalling to reopen stomata and suppress salicylate-based defence.

q.q: The LOPAT scheme is used to sort which group of bacteria?
q.e: Fluorescent pseudomonads. LOPAT = Levan, Oxidase, Pectinolysis, Arginine dihydrolase, Tobacco hypersensitivity.

q.q: The rapid 3% KOH string test determines a bacterium's:
q.e: Gram reaction — Gram-negative cells lyse in dilute KOH and release DNA, forming a viscous string; Gram-positives do not.

q.q: For confirming bacterial wilt in the field, the simple 'ooze / streaming' test involves:
o: Suspending a cut stem in water to observe milky bacterial streaming
q.e: Bacterial streaming — turbid threads flow from a cut infected stem, indicating Ralstonia (fungal wilts do not stream).

q.q: The most widely used gene for molecular identification and phylogeny of bacteria is:
q.e: 16S rRNA — conserved with variable regions; ITS is used for fungi, COI for animals.

q.q: FAME/MIDI profiling identifies bacteria on the basis of their:
q.e: Fatty-acid methyl esters — the cellular fatty-acid fingerprint is matched against a database.

q.q: Koch's postulates are hardest to satisfy for phytoplasmas and Liberibacter because they:
o: Cannot be grown in pure culture
q.e: Cannot be cultured axenically — so molecular Koch's postulates and graft/vector transmission are used instead.

q.q: The antibiotic combination marketed in India as 'Streptocycline' consists of:
q.e: Streptomycin + tetracycline (9:1) — used against several bacterial blights, though resistance is a growing concern.

q.q: Below-species groupings of plant-pathogenic bacteria based mainly on host range are called:
q.e: Pathovars — e.g. Pseudomonas syringae pv. tabaci; distinguished chiefly by the hosts they attack.

q.q: The standard reference for bacterial classification and identification is:
q.e: Bergey's Manual of Systematic Bacteriology — the authoritative taxonomy of prokaryotes.

q.q: Hot-water seed/sett treatment is a classic control for which bacterial disease?
o: Black rot of crucifers (and ratoon stunt of cane)
q.e: Seed-borne vascular pathogens — hot water eradicates Xanthomonas campestris in crucifer seed and Leifsonia in cane setts.

q.q: The transformation that linearises the logistic (compound-interest) model against time is:
q.e: ln[x/(1−x)] — the logit. Its slope is the apparent infection rate r.

q.q: The monomolecular (simple-interest) model is linearised by plotting against time:
q.e: ln[1/(1−x)] — appropriate for monocyclic diseases with a single infection cycle.

q.q: The Gompertz model is linearised by the transformation:
q.e: −ln(−ln x) (the 'gompit'). Gompertz is asymmetric with its inflexion near 37% disease.

q.q: Very early in a polycyclic epidemic, while x is small, disease increase is best approximated by the:
q.e: When x is tiny the (1−x) term ≈ 1, so growth is exponential and ln(x) vs t is roughly linear.

q.q: The inflexion point (maximum rate of increase) of the logistic curve occurs at a disease level of:
q.e: 50% — the symmetric logistic peaks in rate at x = 0.5; contrast Gompertz at ~37%.

q.q: The inflexion point of the Gompertz curve occurs at a disease level of about:
q.e: ~37% (1/e ≈ 0.368) — the asymmetry that distinguishes it from the logistic.

q.q: In a simple-interest (monocyclic) disease, the rate of increase dx/dt is:
o: Proportional to x (the amount already present)
Independent of x — driven by the fixed initial inoculum
q.e: Independent of x — new infections come from the fixed initial inoculum (x₀), giving a near-linear rise, e.g. soil-borne wilts.

q.q: In a compound-interest (polycyclic) disease, dx/dt is proportional to:
q.e: x(1−x) — each lesion begets more (like compound interest), until the (1−x) ceiling slows it. E.g. late blight, rusts.

q.q: Which is a monocyclic (simple-interest) disease?
q.e: Loose smut — one systemic infection per season, no secondary spread. The others cycle repeatedly (polycyclic).

q.q: Horizontal (polygenic) resistance slows an epidemic mainly by lowering:
o: The final disease level to zero
q.e: Reduces r — it flattens the progress curve rather than eliminating infection (rate-reducing resistance).

q.q: Vertical (race-specific) resistance acts principally by reducing:
q.e: Reduces x₀ — it delays epidemic onset; when matched by a virulent race it can fail completely (boom-and-bust).

q.q: Lengthening a pathogen's latent period (p) during a season will:
q.e: Slows it — a longer p means fewer generations fit into the season, lowering the effective rate.

q.q: The corrected basic infection rate (Rc) improves on the apparent rate by accounting for the:
q.e: Latent + infectious periods — Rc removes tissue that is infected-but-not-yet-infectious and lesions that have ceased sporulating.

q.q: A sanitation (roguing) programme lowers x₀, but in a compound-interest epidemic its benefit over the season tends to:
q.e: Erodes — reducing x₀ delays the curve, but exponential multiplication narrows the gap over time (Vanderplank's sanitation ratio).

q.q: Vanderplank is credited with classifying plant diseases into:
q.e: Simple- vs compound-interest — borrowing the finance analogy to model monocyclic vs polycyclic epidemics.

q.q: Garrett's 'inoculum potential' is the:
o: Energy of growth of a pathogen available for infection at the host surface
q.e: Energy of growth available for infection — a function of inoculum amount and vigour, modified by environment and antagonists.

q.q: The disease tetrahedron adds which element to the host–pathogen–environment triangle?
q.e: Time — recognising that disease develops over a period; the human/management axis is sometimes added too.

q.q: AUDPC is most useful for:
o: Comparing the overall severity of epidemics or cultivars in one number
q.e: Comparing epidemics/cultivars — it integrates severity across the whole season into a single index.

q.q: BLITECAST and the earlier Beaumont/Smith period systems forecast:
q.e: Late blight — based on humidity and temperature thresholds favouring Phytophthora infestans sporulation.

q.q: The Mills table (leaf-wetness duration versus temperature) is the basis for forecasting:
q.e: Apple scab (Venturia inaequalis) — Mills periods predict infection from wetness duration at a given temperature.

q.q: A disease forecasting/warning system is worthwhile chiefly when it lets growers:
o: Time control measures against predicted infection periods
q.e: Time interventions — sprays applied ahead of forecast infection periods cut both losses and unnecessary applications.

q.q: Disease rises from x₁ = 0.02 to x₂ = 0.98 over 8 days. Using the logistic rate r = (1/Δt)·[logit(x₂) − logit(x₁)], r ≈:
q.e: logit(0.98)=ln(49)=+3.89; logit(0.02)=−3.89; difference = 7.78; ÷8 = 0.97 per unit per day. The logit is ln[x/(1−x)].

q.q: The logit ln[x/(1−x)] of a disease level of exactly 50% (x = 0.5) equals:
q.e: ln(0.5/0.5)=ln(1)=0. The logistic curve's inflexion sits here, so the logit line crosses zero at 50% disease.

q.q: In the exponential (early) phase with r = 0.1 /day, the time for the disease amount to double (ln2 / r) is about:
q.e: Doubling time = ln2 / r = 0.693 / 0.1 = 6.9 ≈ 7 days. Early on, growth is effectively exponential (x = x₀e^{rt}).

q.q: A field record gives severity 0, 10, 40 and 70% on days 0, 10, 20 and 30. By the trapezoidal rule the AUDPC (%·days) is:
If the season allows infection for 60 days and the pathogen's latent period is 12 days, the approximate number of infection cycles is:
q.e: 60 ÷ 12 = 5 cycles. A shorter latent period packs in more generations and a faster epidemic.

repair_weak.title: Hard Set B — Traps and Swaps

q.q: The disease-progress model whose curve is asymmetric with its inflexion point at ~37% (1/e) disease is the:
q.e: Gompertz — inflexion at 1/e ≈ 0.37, unlike the logistic which is symmetric about 50%. Often fits polycyclic epidemics better.

q.q: The monomolecular ('simple-interest') model is linearised by plotting against time:
q.e: ln[1/(1−x)] vs t gives a straight line for monocyclic diseases (one infection cycle, e.g. soil-borne wilts).

q.q: In Vanderplank's scheme, vertical resistance acts mainly by reducing:
q.e: Initial inoculum x0 — it delays epidemic onset (a race-specific, all-or-nothing effect). Horizontal resistance instead lowers r.

q.q: The corrected basic infection rate (Rc) differs from the apparent rate by accounting for the:
q.e: Latent period (p) and infectious period (i) — Rc corrects for tissue that is infected-but-not-yet-infectious and lesions that have stopped sporulating.

q.q: AUDPC is used primarily to:
o: Summarise a whole epidemic as one value for comparison
q.e: Area Under the Disease Progress Curve — integrates severity over time so cultivars/treatments can be ranked.

q.q: Garrett's 'inoculum potential' is best defined as:
o: The energy of growth of a pathogen available for infection at the host surface
q.e: Energy of growth available for infection — depends on inoculum quantity and vigour, modified by environment and antagonists.

q.q: A sanitation or roguing programme mainly reduces which term of the epidemic?
q.e: x0 — removing initial inoculum lowers the epidemic's starting point (the 'sanitation ratio').

q.q: Wilt of sugarcane and most vascular wilts are cited as examples of:
q.e: Simple-interest — one infection cycle per season with no secondary plant-to-plant spread; fits the monomolecular model.

q.q: The 'disease tetrahedron' extends the disease triangle by adding:
q.e: Time — host, pathogen and environment plus time; the human/management axis is sometimes added as a further dimension.

q.q: Reticulate (net-patterned) teliospores distinguish which common bunt pathogen?
q.e: T. caries = reticulate wall; T. laevis (foetida) = smooth wall. 'Laevis' literally means smooth.

q.q: Which barley smut is externally (seed-surface) borne rather than embryo-borne?
q.e: U. hordei (covered smut) is seed-surface borne, so simple seed treatment works. U. nuda and U. tritici are internal/embryo-borne and need systemic or hot-water treatment.

q.q: Multinucleate 'giant cells' (as opposed to a syncytium) are induced by:
q.e: Meloidogyne → giant cells; cyst nematodes (Heterodera/Globodera) → syncytium formed by cell-wall dissolution and fusion.

q.q: A single posterior whiplash flagellum belongs to the zoospore of a:
q.e: Chytrid — single posterior whiplash. The Oomycete zoospore is biflagellate: one anterior tinsel + one posterior whiplash.

q.q: In Puccinia graminis, karyogamy (nuclear fusion) occurs in the:
q.e: Teliospore — the dikaryon fuses here; meiosis then follows in the basidium (promycelium) that emerges on germination.

q.q: On the barberry host, aecia of Puccinia graminis form on the leaf's:
q.e: Lower (abaxial) surface; pycnia (spermogonia) form on the upper surface — a frequently swapped pair.

q.q: Northern blotting detects ____, whereas Western blotting detects ____:
q.e: RNA; protein. Southern = DNA, Northern = RNA, Western = protein, Southwestern = DNA–protein interactions.

q.q: Which marker pair is correctly described (dominant vs codominant)?
q.e: RAPD dominant, SSR codominant — RAPD scores band presence/absence only; SSR resolves both alleles, so heterozygotes are visible.

q.q: Which anamorph → teleomorph link is correct?
q.e: Pyricularia oryzae → Magnaporthe oryzae. (Rhizoctonia → Thanatephorus; F. graminearum → Gibberella zeae; Botrytis → Botryotinia.)

q.q: Correct downy-mildew-to-host assignment is:
o: Sclerospora graminicola – pearl millet; Peronosclerospora sorghi – sorghum
Sclerospora graminicola – sorghum; Peronosclerospora sorghi – pearl millet
q.e: Sclerospora graminicola = pearl millet (green ear); Peronosclerospora sorghi = sorghum.

q.q: Tabtoxin (wildfire of tobacco) inhibits the enzyme:
q.e: Glutamine synthetase — ammonia accumulates, causing chlorotic halos.

q.q: Phaseolotoxin (halo blight of bean) inhibits:
q.e: OCTase — the classic swap-trap partner of tabtoxin→GS.

q.q: Tentoxin produces chlorosis by inhibiting:
q.e: Chloroplast ATP synthase (CF1) — energy-transfer failure blocks normal chloroplast development.

q.q: HC-toxin (Cochliobolus carbonum race 1) acts as a(n):
q.e: HDAC inhibitor — the resistance gene Hm1 encodes a reductase that detoxifies it (first plant R-gene cloned).

q.q: Victorin (Victoria blight of oats) targets the mitochondrial enzyme:
q.e: Glycine decarboxylase complex — Victorin was the first host-specific toxin isolated in pure form.

q.q: The T-toxin of Cochliobolus heterostrophus race T is toxic specifically to maize carrying:
q.e: T-cytoplasm — the toxin binds the URF13 mitochondrial protein, cause of the 1970 southern corn leaf blight epidemic.

q.q: Cercosporin causes damage only in the presence of:
q.e: Light-activated — generates singlet oxygen that peroxidises host membranes.

q.q: Azole (triazole) fungicides such as tebuconazole inhibit:
q.e: C14-demethylase (DMI, FRAC 3) — blocking ergosterol biosynthesis in the membrane.

q.q: Strobilurin (QoI) fungicides such as azoxystrobin act at:
o: The Qo site of complex III (cytochrome bc1)
q.e: Complex III, Qo site (FRAC 11) — blocking mitochondrial electron transport; single-site, so resistance-prone (G143A).

q.q: Carboxin, used especially as a seed treatment for smuts and rusts, inhibits:
q.e: Succinate dehydrogenase (complex II, SDHI, FRAC 7) — the original oxathiin SDHI.

q.q: Metalaxyl (a phenylamide) is effective against Oomycetes because it inhibits:
q.e: rRNA synthesis (FRAC 4) — highly specific to Oomycetes; single-site, so resistance appears readily.

q.q: Benzimidazoles (carbendazim, benomyl) inhibit:
q.e: β-tubulin (FRAC 1) — blocking mitosis; a single point mutation confers resistance.

q.q: Tricyclazole controls rice blast by inhibiting:
q.e: Melanin biosynthesis (MBI, FRAC 16.1) — without melanin the appressorium cannot generate turgor to penetrate.

q.q: Mancozeb and other dithiocarbamates are best described as:
q.e: Multisite contact protectants (FRAC M) — low resistance risk, used preventively on the plant surface.

q.q: Copper-based fungicides (e.g. Bordeaux mixture) act by:
o: Multisite denaturation of proteins/enzymes on the surface
q.e: Multisite protectant — copper ions inactivate many enzymes/proteins; must be applied before infection.

q.q: Ergot of rye (and wheat) is caused by:
q.e: Claviceps purpurea — sclerotia contain the alkaloids causing ergotism ('St. Anthony's fire').

q.q: Ergot of pearl millet (bajra) is caused by:
q.e: Claviceps fusiformis — the pearl-millet ergot pathogen in India.

q.q: Sugary disease (ergot) of sorghum is caused by:
q.e: Claviceps sorghi / C. africana — honeydew exudation followed by sclerotia in the panicle.

q.q: The sticky 'honeydew' stage of ergot corresponds to the anamorph:
q.e: Sphacelia — the conidial (honeydew) phase precedes hardening into the dark sclerotium.

q.q: Phytoalexins are correctly defined as:
o: Low-molecular-weight antimicrobials synthesised de novo after infection
q.e: Induced (post-infection) antimicrobials — e.g. pisatin (pea), phaseollin (bean), glyceollin (soybean), rishitin (potato).

q.q: Match the phytoalexin to its plant: rishitin is produced by:
q.e: Potato. Pisatin = pea, phaseollin = bean, glyceollin = soybean — a standard matching set.

q.q: In the two-tier plant immunity model, ETI is triggered by:
o: Recognition of pathogen effectors, usually by intracellular R proteins
q.e: Effector recognition by R proteins (ETI) — stronger, often with HR; PTI is the first tier, triggered by PAMPs at the cell surface.

q.q: During tissue maceration, the cell-wall-degrading enzymes usually acting first are:
q.e: Pectinases — pectate lyases/polygalacturonases dissolve the pectin-rich middle lamella, loosening cells first.

q.q: The sexual resting spore of the Zygomycota is the:
q.e: Zygospore — a thick-walled spore formed by fusion of two equal gametangia (gametangial conjugation).

q.q: Which genus possesses rhizoids and stolons, distinguishing it from a closely related mould that lacks them?
q.e: Rhizopus has rhizoids and stolons; Mucor lacks rhizoids — a classic Zygomycete identification point.

q.q: In a Rhizopus sporangium, the sterile dome-shaped structure projecting into it is the:
q.e: Columella — the swollen sterile tip of the sporangiophore inside the sporangium.

q.q: The teleomorph (perfect state) of Colletotrichum falcatum, cause of red rot of sugarcane, is:
q.e: Glomerella tucumanensis (= Physalospora tucumanensis) is the ascigerous state of C. falcatum.

q.q: The perfect state of Rhizoctonia solani is:
q.e: Thanatephorus cucumeris — a basidiomycete; Rhizoctonia is the sterile anamorph identified by right-angle branching and a basal septum.

q.q: Gibberella zeae is the teleomorph of:
q.e: Fusarium graminearum — cause of head scab of wheat; produces the mycotoxin deoxynivalenol (DON).

q.q: Bakanae ('foolish seedling') of rice, from which gibberellins were first discovered, is caused by:
q.e: Fusarium moniliforme (G. fujikuroi). Kurosawa showed the fungal filtrate caused elongation; Yabuta & Sumiki isolated gibberellin.

q.q: The Woronin body of ascomycetes is derived from:
q.e: Peroxisomes — Woronin bodies contain the Hex1 protein and plug the septal pore after hyphal damage.

q.q: The Spitzenkörper in a growing hypha functions as:
o: A vesicle supply centre for apical growth
q.e: Vesicle supply centre — it organises secretory vesicle delivery to the extending hyphal tip.

q.q: The cell wall of Oomycetes is composed mainly of:
q.e: Cellulose/β-glucans, not chitin — one reason Oomycetes are placed with Straminipila, away from true fungi.

q.q: The predominant sterol of the true fungal membrane, and the target of azole and polyene fungicides, is:
q.e: Ergosterol — azoles block its synthesis (C14-demethylase); polyenes bind it directly.

q.q: Forcible discharge of a basidiospore is driven by:
q.e: Buller's drop — a water droplet condenses at the hilum and coalesces with the spore surface film, catapulting it off the sterigma.

q.q: The secondary (reniform) zoospore of an Oomycete bears:
o: One anterior tinsel and one posterior whiplash flagellum
q.e: Tinsel (anterior) + whiplash (posterior) — biflagellate and laterally inserted. Contrast the chytrid's single posterior whiplash.

q.q: Diplanetism, two distinct motile zoospore phases, is shown by:
q.e: Saprolegnia — a primary (pyriform) and a secondary (reniform) zoospore stage, separated by an encysted phase.

q.q: Downy mildew of pearl millet is caused by:
q.e: Sclerospora graminicola — causes green ear / crazy top of bajra.

q.q: False smut of rice is caused by:
q.e: Ustilaginoidea virens — greenish velvety spore balls replace grains; produces ustiloxins.

q.q: Brown spot of rice, implicated in the 1943 Bengal famine, is caused by:
q.e: Bipolaris oryzae (Cochliobolus miyabeanus, old Helminthosporium oryzae) — sesame-seed spots that devastated the Bengal crop.

q.q: The alternate (aecial) host of wheat leaf rust, Puccinia triticina, is:
q.e: Thalictrum (and Isopyrum). Stem rust uses Berberis; do not confuse the two aecial hosts.

q.q: The biochemical target of tabtoxin (wildfire of tobacco) is:
q.e: Glutamine synthetase — inhibition raises ammonia to toxic levels, causing chlorotic halos.

q.q: Phaseolotoxin, in halo blight of bean, inhibits:
q.e: Ornithine carbamoyltransferase — blocking the urea/arginine pathway. The classic swap-trap with tabtoxin→GS.

q.q: Tentoxin causes chlorosis by inhibiting:
q.e: Chloroplast ATP synthase (CF1) — blocks energy transfer and pigment accumulation in sensitive seedlings.

q.q: Fusicoccin (from Fusicoccum amygdali) causes irreversible stomatal opening by activating:
q.e: Plasma-membrane H+-ATPase — locking guard cells open via 14-3-3 protein stabilisation, causing wilt.

q.q: Coronatine, a virulence factor of Pseudomonas syringae, is a structural mimic of:
q.e: JA-Ile — it hijacks jasmonate signalling to reopen stomata and suppress salicylate defence.

q.q: AAL-toxin and fumonisin share the same target enzyme:
q.e: Ceramide synthase — disrupting sphingolipid metabolism and triggering apoptosis-like cell death.

q.q: The primary role of oxalic acid in Sclerotinia pathogenesis is to:
o: Directly kill cells like an antibiotic
Chelate Ca2+, acidify tissue and suppress the host oxidative burst
q.e: Ca2+ chelation + acidification + suppression of the ROS burst — priming tissue for the pectinolytic enzymes.

q.q: The genome of Tomato spotted wilt virus (Tospovirus) is:
q.e: Ambisense tripartite ssRNA — and it is propagative in its thrips vector (multiplies in the insect).

q.q: Luteoviruses (e.g. BYDV, PLRV) are transmitted by aphids in a manner that is:
q.e: Circulative non-propagative — the virus passes through the gut to the salivary glands but does not replicate in the aphid; also phloem-limited.

q.q: Cylindrical (pinwheel) cytoplasmic inclusion bodies are diagnostic of the genus:
q.e: Potyvirus — the CI protein forms characteristic pinwheels visible by electron microscopy.

q.q: The first viroid to be discovered (Diener, 1971) was:
q.e: Potato spindle tuber viroid (PSTVd) — the type member of family Pospiviroidae, replicating in the nucleus.

q.q: Members of family Avsunviroidae (e.g. avocado sunblotch) replicate in the:
q.e: Chloroplast — via a symmetric rolling-circle route using hammerhead ribozymes; Pospiviroidae instead replicate in the nucleus.

q.q: Cauliflower mosaic virus and hepatitis B share the unusual replication feature of being:
q.e: Pararetroviruses — dsDNA genomes replicated through an RNA intermediate by reverse transcriptase.

q.q: Banana bunchy top virus belongs to a group with a genome that is:
q.e: Multipartite circular ssDNA (Babuvirus/Nanoviridae) — at least six ~1 kb components, aphid-transmitted persistently.

q.q: An umbravirus lacks a conventional coat protein and depends for aphid transmission on a helper:
q.e: Luteovirus — the umbravirus is encapsidated by the luteovirus CP to be transmitted (e.g. groundnut rosette complex).

q.q: Gram-negative plant pathogenic bacteria deliver effector proteins into host cells via the:
q.e: Type III secretion system encoded by hrp genes — a molecular syringe injecting effectors that suppress immunity or trigger HR.

q.q: Harpin (HrpN) is a bacterial protein that characteristically:
q.e: Elicits the HR — a heat-stable, glycine-rich protein secreted via the T3SS.

q.q: Quorum sensing in most Gram-negative plant pathogens is mediated by:
q.e: N-acyl homoserine lactones (AHLs) — diffusible autoinducers that coordinate virulence and biofilm at high cell density.

q.q: Induction of Agrobacterium vir genes for T-DNA transfer requires the plant phenolic:
q.e: Acetosyringone — a wound-released phenolic sensed by the VirA/VirG two-component system.

q.q: Ice-nucleation activity that worsens frost injury is conferred in Pseudomonas syringae by the protein:
q.e: InaZ — a membrane protein that templates ice formation at warm sub-zero temperatures.

q.q: Citrus stubborn disease is caused by the helical, wall-less mollicute:
q.e: Spiroplasma citri — leafhopper-transmitted, phloem-inhabiting, and (unlike phytoplasmas) culturable.

q.q: Which of these pathogens is unculturable on standard media and phloem-limited?
q.e: Ca. Liberibacter asiaticus — the citrus greening (HLB) agent, still not routinely culturable.

q.q: AFLP markers are best described as:
o: Dominant, based on restriction digestion plus selective PCR
q.e: Dominant — combine restriction fragments with adaptor-primed selective amplification; high multiplex ratio.

q.q: In real-time qPCR, the Ct (threshold cycle) value is:
o: Directly proportional to starting template amount
Inversely related to the log of starting template copies
q.e: Inversely related — more starting template crosses threshold in fewer cycles, giving a lower Ct.

q.q: The universal DNA barcode region for fungal identification is:
q.e: ITS — the internal transcribed spacer; 16S rRNA is used for bacteria, COI for animals.

q.q: The restriction enzyme EcoRI recognises the sequence:
q.e: GAATTC — cut between G and A to leave 5′ AATT overhangs (sticky ends).

q.q: A TaqMan probe reports amplification through:
o: Fluorescence resonance energy transfer (FRET) on probe cleavage
q.e: FRET — Taq's 5′ exonuclease cleaves the probe, separating reporter from quencher and releasing fluorescence.

q.q: The nptII selectable marker gene confers resistance to:
q.e: Kanamycin — neomycin phosphotransferase II; a classic marker in plant transformation vectors.

q.q: Green fluorescent protein was originally isolated from:
q.e: Aequorea victoria, a jellyfish — the reporter needs no substrate, only UV/blue excitation.

q.q: The septal pore of Basidiomycota is flanked by membranous caps called:
q.e: Parenthesomes — the perforated caps of the dolipore septum apparatus.

q.q: Croziers (hook cells) in ascomycetes ensure that:
o: Two compatible nuclei are correctly partitioned into the ascus mother cell
q.e: Correct dikaryotic nuclear distribution — the hook mechanism keeps one nucleus of each mating type in the penultimate ascus-forming cell.

q.q: K. C. Mehta is renowned for establishing that wheat rusts in India survive the off-season and re-infect the plains from the:
q.e: Nilgiri and Himalayan hills — his classic work traced the annual recurrence of rust inoculum into the north Indian plains.

q.q: The 'Father of Indian Plant Pathology / Mycology', who wrote 'Fungi and Disease in Plants' (1918), is:
q.e: Sir Edwin John Butler — first Imperial Mycologist at Pusa and founder of organised plant pathology in India.

q.q: The teleomorph of Botrytis cinerea is:
q.e: Botryotinia fuckeliana — grey mould; a broad-host-range necrotroph.

q.q: Ergot alkaloids responsible for 'St. Anthony's fire' are produced in the sclerotia of:
q.e: Claviceps purpurea — ergotism from contaminated rye; alkaloids cause vasoconstriction and gangrene/convulsions.

q.q: The species-diagnostic feature used to identify Meloidogyne females is the:
q.e: Perineal pattern — the cuticular striae around the vulva/anus of the mature female.

q.q: The burrowing nematode Radopholus similis is the cause of:
o: Toppling disease of banana / spreading decline of citrus
q.e: Radopholus similis — a migratory endoparasite; 'toppling' in banana and 'spreading decline' in citrus.

q.q: Reniform nematode (Rotylenchulus reniformis) feeds as a:
q.e: Sedentary semi-endoparasite — the female's anterior embeds in the root while the swollen kidney-shaped body remains outside.

q.q: Vanderplank's monomolecular model best fits a disease that is:
q.e: Monocyclic / simple-interest — one infection cycle per season (e.g. soil-borne wilts), no secondary spread.

q.q: Compared with the logistic curve, the Gompertz model of disease progress is:
o: Asymmetric, with the inflexion below 50% disease
q.e: Asymmetric — inflexion near 37%; often fits polycyclic epidemics better than the symmetric logistic.

q.q: Systemic acquired resistance (SAR) is signalled primarily through:
q.e: Salicylic acid → PR proteins, NPR1-dependent, effective against biotrophs. ISR uses JA/ethylene via rhizobacteria.

q.q: Induced systemic resistance (ISR) triggered by PGPR is typically dependent on:
q.e: Jasmonate/ethylene — priming rather than direct PR-gene activation; contrasts with SA-dependent SAR.

q.q: The main structural polysaccharide of the true fungal cell wall is:
q.e: Chitin — β-1,4-linked N-acetylglucosamine; Oomycetes are the notable cellulose-walled exception.

q.q: Sclerotium rolfsii (southern blight) has the teleomorph:
q.e: Athelia rolfsii (= Corticium rolfsii) — a basidiomycete; the anamorph forms mustard-seed sclerotia.

q.q: Reoviruses infecting plants (e.g. rice dwarf, wound tumour) have a genome of:
q.e: Segmented dsRNA — and they are propagative in their leafhopper vectors.

q.q: A monopartite begomovirus often requires which associated molecule for full symptom expression?
q.e: Betasatellite (DNA-β) — its βC1 protein is a symptom determinant and RNA-silencing suppressor.

q.q: The Gram-positive bacterial wall differs from the Gram-negative by having:
o: Thick peptidoglycan with teichoic acids and no outer membrane
q.e: Thick peptidoglycan + teichoic acids, no outer membrane — hence crystal violet is retained during Gram staining.

q.q: To distinguish two closely related fungal species by DNA, the region most routinely sequenced is:
q.e: ITS, supplemented by protein-coding loci like TEF-1α and β-tubulin for fine resolution (relevant to isolate-variability studies).

q.q: In Ascomycetes, karyogamy and meiosis occur in the:
q.e: Young ascus — the only diploid stage; meiosis (usually + one mitosis) yields eight ascospores.

q.q: 'Damping-off' seedling collapse is most classically caused by:
q.e: Pythium (pre-emergence) and Rhizoctonia (post-emergence) — favoured by high moisture and dense sowing.

q.q: The dikaryotic condition is maintained during mitosis in Basidiomycota with the help of:
q.e: Clamp connections — a bridge that ensures each daughter cell receives one nucleus of each mating type.

q.q: The hypersensitive response (HR) is a form of:
o: Localised programmed cell death at the infection site
q.e: Localised programmed cell death — confines biotrophs by killing host cells around the invasion point.

q.q: In the gene-for-gene interaction, incompatibility (resistance) results when:
o: Neither R nor Avr is present
A dominant R gene matches a dominant Avr gene
Only the R gene is present
Only the Avr gene is present
q.e: Matching R and Avr — recognition triggers defence. Any other combination is compatible (disease).

q.q: Appressorium melanisation in Magnaporthe is essential because melanin:
o: Makes the appressorial wall impermeable so turgor can build to puncture the cuticle
q.e: Seals the wall — retaining glycerol-driven turgor (up to ~8 MPa) to force the penetration peg through the cuticle.

q.q: Soft rot Pectobacterium/Dickeya macerate tissue chiefly by secreting:
q.e: Pectinolytic enzymes — degrading the middle lamella; secreted mainly via the Type II system.

q.q: Cross-protection is exploited in management because a mild strain:
o: Occupies the host and blocks a severe related strain
q.e: Pre-occupies the host — related-strain interference (e.g. mild PRSV, mild CTV) reduces severe-strain damage.

q.q: Sori of Tilletia indica (Karnal bunt) characteristically emit the odour of:
q.e: Trimethylamine (fishy) — only part of the grain is bunted, unlike the fully replaced grain of common bunt.

q.q: The J2 (second-stage juvenile) is the infective stage in:
q.e: Meloidogyne and Heterodera — the J2 hatches, migrates and invades roots; the first moult occurs within the egg.

q.q: Sudden death and 'red rot'-like internal reddening aside, the anamorph genus producing setae in acervuli is:
q.e: Colletotrichum — acervuli with dark setae and falcate/oval conidia; anthracnose pathogens.

q.q: Marker-assisted backcrossing accelerates breeding mainly by allowing:
o: Selection of the target gene plus recovery of recurrent-parent genome
q.e: Foreground + background selection — markers track the target allele and speed recovery of the recurrent parent.

q.q: Phytoalexins are best defined as:
o: Low-molecular-weight antimicrobials synthesised de novo after infection
q.e: Induced (post-infection) antimicrobials — e.g. pisatin in pea, phaseollin in bean, glyceollin in soybean.

q.q: Pisatin is a phytoalexin of:
q.e: Pea (Pisum). Phaseollin = bean, glyceollin = soybean, rishitin = potato — a common matching set.

q.q: Which structure represents a compact, dark, resting mass that germinates to produce fruiting bodies?
q.e: Sclerotium — survives adversity, then germinates myceliogenically or to bear apothecia/pycnidia.

q.q: The satellite tobacco necrosis virus (STNV) is unusual because it:
o: Depends on tobacco necrosis virus for replication
q.e: Depends on TNV (helper) for replication; STNV encodes only its own coat protein.

q.q: The determinative test that detects the enzyme splitting arginine in the LOPAT scheme is:
q.e: Arginine dihydrolase (the 'A') — with Levan, Oxidase, Pectinolysis and Tobacco-HR it sorts fluorescent pseudomonads into groups.

q.q: In r = (1/Δt) · ln[x2(1−x1)/x1(1−x2)], the parameter r is the:
q.e: Apparent infection rate — Vanderplank's slope of the logistic model between two assessment dates.

q.q: The disease tetrahedron adds which factor to the classic disease triangle?
q.e: Time (host, pathogen, environment + time); some versions add the human/management dimension.

q.q: Puccinia graminis is macrocyclic and heteroecious, meaning it:
o: Has all spore stages on one host
Produces all five spore stages across two unlike hosts
q.e: Five spore stages on two hosts — wheat (uredinial/telial) and barberry (pycnial/aecial).

q.q: A demicyclic rust is one that:
q.e: Lacks the urediniospore stage (e.g. Gymnosporangium) — so no repeating cycle within a season.

q.q: Bt δ-endotoxins (Cry proteins) act by:
o: Forming pores in insect midgut epithelial membranes
q.e: Midgut pore formation — after alkaline solubilisation and protease activation, the toxin binds receptors and lyses gut cells.

q.q: Which pairing of downy mildew and host is correct?
q.e: Peronospora tabacina – tobacco (blue mould). Bremia = lettuce, Plasmopara viticola = grape, Pseudoperonospora cubensis = cucurbits.

q.q: 'Tolerance' in host–pathogen interaction refers to a plant that:
o: Supports the pathogen yet suffers little yield loss
q.e: Endures infection with minimal damage — distinct from resistance (limits the pathogen) and escape (avoids contact).

q.q: Ophiobolin, a non-host-specific toxin, is produced by species of:
q.e: Cochliobolus/Bipolaris — a membrane-active sesterterpenoid affecting Ca2+/calmodulin signalling.

q.q: Potyviruses are among the largest plant-virus genera; their genome is:
q.e: Monopartite (+)ssRNA polyprotein — cleaved by viral proteases; VPg is linked at the 5′ end.

q.q: Streptomycin acts on bacteria by:
o: Binding the 30S ribosomal subunit and blocking translation
q.e: 30S ribosome inhibition — misreading/blocked initiation; resistance can arise rapidly (e.g. in Erwinia amylovora).

q.q: The anamorph–teleomorph link Cercospora → is:
q.e: Mycosphaerella — many Cercospora leaf-spot fungi have Mycosphaerella (or Pseudocercospora) sexual states.

q.q: 'Inoculum potential' as defined by Garrett is:
o: The energy of growth of a pathogen available for infection at the host surface
q.e: Energy of growth available for infection — a function of inoculum quantity and vigour, modified by the environment and antagonists.

q.q: Papilla and callose deposition at penetration sites represent:
o: A structural/pre-formed-like induced defence reinforcing the wall
q.e: Induced wall apposition — callose-rich papillae attempt to block the penetration peg.

q.q: Koch's postulates are difficult to fulfil for obligate parasites and phytoplasmas mainly because they:
o: Cannot be grown in pure culture
q.e: Cannot be cultured axenically — so molecular Koch's postulates or graft/vector transmission are used instead.

q.q: Which statement about Deuteromycetes (Fungi Imperfecti) is correct?
o: They are an artificial grouping lacking a known sexual stage
q.e: Artificial (form-)taxon — anamorphs whose teleomorphs are unknown or lost; most belong with Ascomycota.

q.q: The vector relationship in which a virus multiplies inside the insect is termed:
q.e: Persistent propagative — e.g. tospoviruses in thrips, reoviruses and rhabdoviruses in hoppers; often trans-ovarially passed.

q.q: HC-toxin (Cochliobolus carbonum race 1) exerts its effect by inhibiting:
q.e: Histone deacetylase — altering host gene expression; resistance gene Hm1 (a reductase) detoxifies it.

q.q: Which cereal smut is 'internally seed-borne as dormant mycelium in the embryo'?
q.e: Ustilago tritici — embryo-borne, so hot-water/solar or systemic seed treatment is required, unlike surface-borne bunts.

q.q: Ralstonia solanacearum causes bacterial wilt and is classified below species by:
q.e: Race + biovar (and now phylotype/sequevar) — the broad-host-range agent of wilt in solanaceous and many other crops.

q.q: Detoxification of the host defence compound and suppression of RNA silencing are both examples of:
q.e: Counter-defence — e.g. pisatin demethylase in Nectria, and viral silencing suppressors such as potyviral HC-Pro.

q.q: Coffee rust, one of the most historically destructive plant diseases, is caused by:
q.e: Hemileia vastatrix — the rust that destroyed Sri Lanka's coffee industry in the 1870s and turned it into a tea producer.

q.q: Whip smut of sugarcane is caused by:
q.e: Sporisorium scitamineum (old name Ustilago scitaminea) — produces the characteristic black whip from the shoot apex.

q.q: Take-all disease of wheat is caused by:
q.e: Gaeumannomyces graminis var. tritici — a soil-borne root/crown pathogen giving blackened roots.

q.q: The bacterium that parasitises other bacteria is:
q.e: Bdellovibrio — a predatory bacterium that invades the periplasm of Gram-negative bacteria.

q.q: Northern blotting is used to detect:
q.e: RNA. Southern = DNA, Northern = RNA, Western = protein, Eastern = post-translational modifications.

q.q: Western blotting detects:
q.e: Protein, separated by SDS-PAGE then probed with antibodies.

q.q: The model organism of fungal genetics is:
q.e: Neurospora crassa — Beadle & Tatum's 'one gene–one enzyme' work; ordered tetrads make it ideal for genetics.

q.q: Reverse transcriptase catalyses synthesis of:
q.e: DNA from RNA — used to make cDNA. Found in retroviruses and used in RT-PCR.

q.q: Which is NOT a PCR-based molecular marker?
q.e: RFLP is hybridisation-based (restriction digestion + Southern blot), not PCR-based. The others amplify DNA.

q.q: Rice blast is caused by:
q.e: Magnaporthe grisea (anamorph Pyricularia oryzae) — forms melanised appressoria that generate huge turgor to punch the cuticle.

q.q: Onion smut is caused by:
q.e: Urocystis cepulae — attacks seedlings, forming dark streaks on leaves and bulbs.

q.q: Thermus aquaticus is the source of:
q.e: Taq polymerase — a thermostable enzyme from a hot-spring bacterium, enabling PCR without re-adding enzyme each cycle.

q.q: Citrus exocortis is caused by a:
q.e: Viroid — a small naked circular ssRNA, the smallest known infectious agent.

q.q: Ufra disease of rice is caused by:
q.e: Ditylenchus angustus — the rice stem nematode causing twisted, chlorotic 'swollen' upper leaves.

q.q: Appendages with bulbous swollen bases are characteristic of the powdery mildew genus:
q.e: Phyllactinia — needle-like appendages with bulb-shaped bases. Podosphaera = dichotomous tips; Uncinula = curled tips.

q.q: A spore formed by fragmentation of a hypha into cells is a(n):
q.e: Arthrospore (arthroconidium) — hyphae break up at the septa into spore-like segments.

q.q: Grassy shoot disease of sugarcane is caused by:
q.e: Phytoplasma — a wall-less prokaryote, transmitted by leafhoppers, giving proliferation of thin white shoots.

q.q: Hm1, the first resistance gene ever cloned in plants, gives resistance against:
q.e: Cochliobolus carbonum race 1. Hm1 encodes a reductase that detoxifies HC-toxin — cloned in 1992.

q.q: The Central wheat rust research/quarantine station in India is located at:
q.e: Mahabaleshwar — historically key for off-season rust survival studies; Flowerdale (Shimla) is also a wheat rust centre.

q.q: The LOPAT test scheme is used to identify:
q.e: Fluorescent Pseudomonas. LOPAT = Levan, Oxidase, Pectinolysis, Arginine dihydrolase, Tobacco hypersensitivity.

q.q: The repeating (recurrent) spore stage of the rust cycle is the:
q.e: Urediospore — dikaryotic, reinfects the same host repeatedly, driving the epidemic ('repeating stage').

q.q: In Puccinia graminis, aecia are typically borne on the:
q.e: On barberry, aecia form on the lower (abaxial) surface, while pycnia form on the upper surface.

q.q: The hybridoma technique is used to produce:
q.e: Monoclonal antibodies — B-cell fused with myeloma cell (Köhler & Milstein).

q.q: The Vertifolia effect refers to:
q.e: Loss of horizontal resistance — breeding under protection of a major gene lets background polygenic resistance erode (Vanderplank).

q.q: Clamp connections are a diagnostic feature of:
q.e: Basidiomycota — clamp connections maintain the dikaryon during cell division.

q.q: Loss of virulence in a pathogen is termed:
q.e: Attenuation — reduction/loss of virulence, e.g. on repeated subculture.

q.q: Which is a Gram-positive plant pathogenic bacterium?
q.e: Clavibacter (Corynebacterium) and Streptomyces are the main Gram-positive plant pathogens; the rest listed are Gram-negative.

q.q: Dichotomously branched appendage tips characterise the powdery mildew genus:
q.e: Podosphaera (and Microsphaera) — appendages fork repeatedly at the tips.

q.q: An alcoholic/fermented smell in split canes is diagnostic of:
q.e: Red rot (Colletotrichum falcatum) — reddened internodes with white cross-patches and a sour/alcoholic smell.

q.q: Which of the following is NOT a true rust?
q.e: White rust (Albugo) is an Oomycete, not a Basidiomycete rust — it just resembles one.

q.q: Citrus canker, a major quarantine disease, is caused by:
q.e: Xanthomonas citri subsp. citri (formerly X. axonopodis pv. citri) — corky, water-soaked lesions with yellow halo.

q.q: Banana bunchy top disease was first reported from:
q.e: First recorded from Sri Lanka (Ceylon) in 1889; caused by Banana bunchy top virus, a Babuvirus, aphid-transmitted.

q.q: The glycosidic bond is found in the bacterial cell-wall layer:
q.e: Peptidoglycan — NAG–NAM backbone linked by β-1,4 glycosidic bonds, cross-linked by peptides.

q.q: Which is NOT typically seed-borne?
q.e: Soybean yellow mosaic (a Begomovirus) is whitefly-transmitted, not seed-borne. The others are classic seed-transmitted viruses.

q.q: Rhizoids are a characteristic structure of:
q.e: Rhizopus — root-like rhizoids anchor the thallus; Mucor lacks them, a key distinguishing feature.

q.q: Olpidium belongs to the division:
q.e: Chytridiomycota — a holocarpic root parasite and a vector of some plant viruses; produces zoospores with a single posterior flagellum.

q.q: The zoospore of a chytrid bears:
q.e: Single posterior whiplash flagellum — the defining chytrid feature. Oomycetes instead have one tinsel + one whiplash (biflagellate).

q.q: The taxonomic rank whose name ends in '-ales' is the:
q.e: Order = -ales (e.g. Peronosporales). Class = -mycetes, family = -aceae, division = -mycota.

q.q: Citrus greening (Huanglongbing) is transmitted by:
q.e: Diaphorina citri — the Asian citrus psyllid, vector of Candidatus Liberibacter.

q.q: Pea early browning virus is transmitted by the nematode:
q.e: Trichodorus (and Paratrichodorus) — trichodorid nematodes transmit tobraviruses like PEBV and TRV.

q.q: Mycorrhiza is an association between:
q.e: Fungus + higher-plant root — a mutualistic symbiosis improving phosphorus uptake.

q.q: Victorin (HV-toxin) affects which host?
q.e: Oat — Helminthosporium victoriae, Victoria blight; the first host-specific toxin isolated in pure form.

q.q: An obligate biotroph among the following is:
q.e: Erysiphe (powdery mildew) — cannot be cultured on media; it feeds only on living tissue via haustoria.

q.q: In PCR, the primer binds to the template during the:
q.e: Annealing — temperature drops (~50–60°C) so primers hybridise to complementary sequences before extension.

q.q: The lag phase of a bacterial growth curve is best described as the:
q.e: Adaptation phase — cells adjust to the medium and synthesise enzymes; no net increase in number yet.

q.q: Uranyl acetate is used in electron microscopy as a:
q.e: Negative stain (also phosphotungstic acid) — heavy metals scatter electrons around the specimen, outlining virus particles.

q.q: Spectrophotometry is governed by:
q.e: Beer–Lambert law — absorbance is proportional to concentration and path length.

q.q: Ashby's mannitol agar is a selective medium for:

q.q: The headquarters of the Indian Society of Mycology and Plant Pathology is at:

q.q: Wilt of sugarcane is an example of a disease following:

q.q: Turkey X disease was caused by:

q.q: CRISPR-Cas9 technology is used for:

q.q: The knapsack sprayer typically has a tank capacity of about:

q.q: The dolipore septum is characteristic of:

q.q: DAS-ELISA is most widely used for detecting:

q.q: The smallest known infectious pathogen is a:
q.e: Viroid — a naked circular ssRNA of a few hundred nucleotides, with no protein coat.

q.q: Geminiviruses have a genome of:
q.e: ssDNA, in twinned (geminate) particles; includes the whitefly-borne begomoviruses (leaf curls).

q.q: Cauliflower mosaic virus has a genome of:

q.q: Phytoplasmas differ from true bacteria in that they:

q.q: Local lesion assay of TMV classically uses:

q.q: The gene-for-gene hypothesis was proposed by:
q.e: H. H. Flor — from flax–flax rust studies: for each resistance gene there is a matching avirulence gene.

q.q: The 'Father of Plant Pathology' is:
q.e: Anton de Bary — proved late blight of potato was caused by a fungus, disproving spontaneous generation.

q.q: Bordeaux mixture was introduced by:
q.e: P. M. A. Millardet (1885) — the first successful fungicide, copper sulphate + lime, for grape downy mildew.

q.q: The Irish potato famine (late blight epidemic) occurred in:
q.e: 1845 — Phytophthora infestans devastated the Irish potato crop, causing mass famine and emigration.

q.q: Late blight of potato is caused by:
q.e: Phytophthora infestans — an Oomycete; sporangia germinate directly or release zoospores in cool wet weather.

q.q: Wart disease of potato is caused by:
q.e: Synchytrium endobioticum — a chytrid causing cauliflower-like warts; a strict quarantine pathogen.

q.q: Common scab of potato is caused by:
q.e: Streptomyces scabies — a Gram-positive filamentous actinobacterium; favoured by dry alkaline soils.

q.e: Heterodera avenae — the cereal cyst nematode, a major problem in wheat/barley in Rajasthan.

q.e: Tilletia indica (= Neovossia indica) — partial bunt with a fishy smell; a key quarantine pathogen.

q.e: Embryo — Ustilago tritici mycelium sits dormant in the embryo, so systemic fungicide or hot-water treatment is needed.

q.e: T. caries = reticulate; T. laevis (foetida) = smooth. 'Laevis' literally means smooth.

q.q: Metalaxyl is a systemic fungicide especially effective against:
q.e: Oomycetes (downy mildews, Phytophthora, Pythium) — a phenylamide that inhibits rRNA synthesis.

q.q: Triazole fungicides (e.g. tebuconazole) inhibit:

o: Absolute Unit of Disease per Cycle
Area of Uredial Disease Pattern Curve
q.e: Area Under the Disease Progress Curve — a single value summarising an epidemic's severity over time.

q.e: ln[x/(1−x)] vs time — gives a straight line whose slope is r for a compound-interest (polycyclic) epidemic.

q.q: The Ti plasmid is found in:

q.q: RAPD markers are:

q.q: Oil immersion is used with the objective of magnification:

q.e: Zygospore — a thick-walled resting spore formed by fusion of two gametangia (e.g. Rhizopus).

q.q: Coenocytic (aseptate) mycelium is typical of:
q.e: Oomycota and Zygomycota — long multinucleate hyphae with few or no cross-walls.

q.q: Crown gall of many plants is caused by:
q.e: Agrobacterium tumefaciens — T-DNA transfer causes tumorous galls at the crown.

q.q: Xylella fastidiosa is best described as a:
q.e: Xylem-limited fastidious bacterium — sharpshooter-borne; causes Pierce's disease of grape and citrus variegated chlorosis.

q.q: Fire blight of apple and pear is caused by:
q.e: Erwinia amylovora — blackened 'shepherd's crook' shoots and bacterial ooze.

q.q: Ring rot of potato is caused by:
q.e: Clavibacter michiganensis subsp. sepedonicus — a Gram-positive vascular pathogen; strict quarantine importance.

q.e: Dependence on a helper virus for replication (e.g. Satellite tobacco necrosis virus needs TNV).

q.q: Cross-protection in plant virology means:
o: A mild strain protects against a severe strain
q.e: A mild strain protects the plant from a related severe strain — the basis of some early virus management.

q.e: Stylet — a hollow spear used to puncture plant cells and withdraw contents.
