q.e: Neurospora crassa — Beadle & Tatum's one-gene-one-enzyme.

q.q: Clamp connections occur in
q.e: Basidiomycota. Also seen in Sclerotium rolfsii (= Athelia).

q.q: Sclerotinia produces which ascocarp?
q.e: Apothecium — the open cup on a stalk from the sclerotium.

q.q: Muriform, beaked conidia borne in chains
q.e: Alternaria — cross AND longitudinal septa = muriform.

q.q: Rhizoids are present in
q.e: Rhizopus has rhizoids and stolons; Mucor has neither.

q.q: The parasexual cycle was discovered by Pontecorvo & Roper in
q.e: A. nidulans, 1952.

q.q: The 25-volume Sylloge Fungorum was compiled by
q.e: Saccardo — who also created the Fungi Imperfecti group.

q.q: A taxonomic order name ends with the suffix
q.e: Order = -ales, family = -aceae, class = -mycetes, division = -mycota.

q.q: Northern blotting detects
q.e: Northern = RNA. Southern = DNA, Western = protein.

q.q: Thermus aquaticus is the source of
q.e: A thermophile from hot springs — hence heat-stable Taq.

q.q: Reverse transcriptase catalyses
q.e: RNA → cDNA. The basis of RT-PCR for RNA viruses.

q.q: In PCR, the primer binds to the template during
q.e: Annealing, roughly 50–60 °C.

q.q: Which is a non-PCR based marker?
q.e: RFLP is hybridisation-based. The rest need amplification.

q.q: CRISPR-Cas9 is used for
q.e: Targeted gene editing.

q.q: The stain commonly used in electron microscopy
q.e: Uranyl acetate — heavy metal, scatters electrons.

q.q: Spectrophotometry works on
q.e: Absorbance is proportional to concentration and path length.

q.q: Micrometry is the technique for
q.e: Ocular + stage micrometer to measure spores and hyphae.

q.q: The hybridoma technique produces
q.e: Myeloma cell fused with a B lymphocyte — Köhler & Milstein.

q.q: Viroids are best detected by
q.e: No coat protein means no serology works. PAGE (or RT-PCR).

q.q: DAS-ELISA stands for
q.e: Antibody coats the plate, antigen is trapped, enzyme-linked antibody detects. Standard for viruses.

q.q: Ashby's mannitol agar is selective for
q.e: Nitrogen-free medium — only free-living N-fixers grow.

q.q: The LOPAT test scheme is used for
q.e: Levan, Oxidase, Pectolytic, Arginine, Tobacco hypersensitivity.

q.q: TZC agar gives red-centred colonies for
q.e: Tetrazolium chloride — virulent colonies are fluidal with pink centres.

q.q: In the bacterial growth curve, the adaptable phase is
q.e: Lag — cells adjust to the medium, no division yet.

q.q: The refractive index of air is approximately
q.e: Air ≈ 1.0, water ≈ 1.33, glass and immersion oil ≈ 1.5.

q.q: Native PAGE separates molecules on the basis of
q.e: Native PAGE keeps protein folded; SDS-PAGE denatures and sorts by size.

q.q: Take-all of wheat is caused by
q.e: Gaeumannomyces graminis var. tritici — black rotted roots.

q.q: Whip smut of sugarcane (current name)
q.e: Sporisorium scitamineum, formerly Ustilago scitaminea. Know both.

q.q: Onion smut is caused by
q.e: Urocystis cepulae (= U. colchici).

q.q: Red rot of sugarcane is recognised in the field by its
q.e: Alcoholic smell, with red internodes crossed by white patches.

q.q: Grassy shoot of sugarcane is caused by
q.e: Phytoplasma. Contrast ratoon stunting — a bacterium.

q.q: Ratoon stunting of sugarcane is caused by
q.e: Leifsonia xyli subsp. xyli — a Gram-positive xylem-limited bacterium.

q.q: Melanised appressoria are the hallmark of
q.e: Melanin builds turgor to punch through the cuticle. Tricyclazole blocks melanin.

q.q: The Cavendish banana is threatened worldwide by Fusarium
q.e: Tropical Race 4. Race 1 destroyed Gros Michel earlier.

q.q: Ergot of pearl millet (bajra)
q.e: C. fusiformis. Rye = C. purpurea; sorghum = C. sorghi.

q.q: Black scurf of potato
q.e: Black sclerotia stuck to the tuber. Scab = Streptomyces, corky.

q.q: Common scab of potato
q.e: An actinomycete. Favoured by alkaline soil and dry conditions.

q.q: Loose smut of wheat is
q.e: Dormant mycelium inside the embryo — hence hot water or carboxin.

q.q: Karnal bunt of wheat
q.e: Tilletia indica (= Neovossia indica). Major quarantine disease.

q.q: Panama wilt of banana
q.e: Soil-borne, chlamydospores persist for decades.

q.q: Citrus greening (HLB) is vectored by
q.e: The citrus psylla. Pathogen: Candidatus Liberibacter.

q.q: Bakanae of rice, from which gibberellin was first isolated
q.e: = Gibberella fujikuroi. The 'foolish seedling' elongation.

q.q: Turkey X disease was traced to
q.e: Aspergillus flavus in groundnut meal, UK 1960.

q.q: Victorin (HV toxin) is toxic to
q.e: Cochliobolus victoriae on oats — first host-specific toxin purified.

q.q: Rice tungro is caused by a complex whose genomes are
q.e: RTBV is a dsDNA badnavirus; RTSV is a ssRNA waikavirus.

q.q: Citrus exocortis is caused by a
q.e: CEVd — naked circular ssRNA.

q.q: Most plant viruses have a genome of
q.e: Positive-sense ssRNA is the default. Gemini = ssDNA, Caulimo = dsDNA.

q.q: Geminiviruses (leaf curls, YVMV) have
q.e: Twin particles, ssDNA, whitefly-transmitted.

q.q: Which is an example of a begomovirus?
q.e: Begomovirus = geminivirus genus, whitefly-borne: ToLCV, CLCuV, YVMV, MYMV.

q.q: Pea early browning virus is transmitted by
q.e: A tobravirus — stubby-root nematode. Nepoviruses go with Xiphinema.

q.q: Banana bunchy top virus is transmitted by
q.e: The banana aphid, persistently.

q.q: A circulative, non-propagative virus is exemplified by
q.e: PLRV circulates through the aphid but does not multiply in it. TSWV and rice dwarf DO multiply — propagative.

q.q: The term 'viroid' was coined by
q.e: Diener, 1971, working on potato spindle tuber.

q.q: Which is not readily seed-transmitted?
q.e: Yellow mosaic of soybean is whitefly-borne, not seed-borne.

q.q: A bacterium that parasitises other bacteria
q.e: Bdellovibrio bacteriovorus — the predatory bacterium.

q.q: Which is Gram-positive?
q.e: Gram-positive plant pathogens: Corynebacterium, Clavibacter, Streptomyces, Leifsonia. The rest are mostly Gram-negative rods.

q.q: In peptidoglycan, the sugar backbone (NAG–NAM) is joined by
q.e: β-1,4 glycosidic bonds; peptide cross-links join the chains.

q.q: The first plant disease proven to be bacterial (Burrill)
q.e: Erwinia amylovora, 1878–82.

q.q: Crown gall is caused by Agrobacterium using its
q.e: Ti = tumour-inducing. Ri = root-inducing, hairy root.

q.q: Citrus canker is historically associated with which US state?
q.e: Florida — repeated eradication campaigns.

q.q: Phytoplasmas are sensitive to
q.e: No cell wall, so penicillin fails. Tetracycline hits the ribosome.

q.q: The repeating spore stage of a rust
q.e: Dikaryotic, re-infects the same host, drives the epidemic.

q.q: In wheat stem rust on barberry, aecia are formed on the
q.e: Pycnia on the upper surface, aecia on the lower.

q.q: Which spore infects the barberry?
q.e: Basidiospores from germinating telia infect barberry; aeciospores go back to wheat.

q.q: Which is not a true rust?
q.e: White rust is Albugo — an oomycete, not a Basidiomycete rust.

q.q: The wheat rust research station in India is at
q.e: Mahabaleshwar, Maharashtra.

q.q: The Vertifolia effect is
o: Loss of horizontal resistance while breeding for vertical
q.e: Vanderplank — selecting under vertical-resistance cover lets background resistance erode.

q.q: The first plant disease resistance gene cloned
q.e: Hm1 from maize, 1992, against Cochliobolus carbonum race 1.

q.q: Horizontal resistance is
q.e: Partial but durable; slows the epidemic rather than blocking infection.

q.q: A simple-interest disease is exemplified by
q.e: Soil-borne, monocyclic — inoculum does not multiply within the season.

q.q: In Vanderplank's model, r denotes
q.e: r = rate; x = amount of disease. Do not cross them.

q.q: Disease severity refers to
q.e: Severity = tissue area. Incidence = number of plants.

q.q: SAR is mediated chiefly by
q.e: SA and PR proteins. ISR runs on JA and ethylene.

q.q: PR proteins are
o: Host proteins induced by infection, e.g. chitinases and glucanases
q.e: Pathogenesis-related — induced, SA-dependent, markers of SAR.

q.q: Loss of virulence by a pathogen is called
q.e: Attenuation — the basis of mild-strain cross protection.

q.q: An obligate biotroph among these
q.e: Powdery mildews cannot be cultured on media.

q.q: Primary inoculum most typically arises from
q.e: Oospores, ascospores, sclerotia, chlamydospores — the overwintering stage.

q.q: Benzimidazoles (carbendazim, benomyl) act on
q.e: They bind β-tubulin and block spindle formation.

q.q: Triazoles act by inhibiting
q.e: DMI/SBI group — the fungal membrane sterol.

q.q: Carboxin acts on
q.e: SDHI — and it was the first true systemic fungicide, 1966.

q.q: Strobilurins (azoxystrobin) act at
o: The Qo site of cytochrome bc1
q.e: QoI — respiration, complex III.

q.q: Metalaxyl is effective specifically against
q.e: Phenylamide — targets rRNA polymerase in Oomycetes only.

q.q: Mancozeb is a
q.e: Multisite contact protectant.

q.q: Validamycin is used mainly against
q.e: Rhizoctonia solani.

q.q: The golden cyst nematode of potato
q.e: Restricted to the Nilgiris in India. Tomato is used as an indicator host.

q.q: Ufra disease of rice
q.e: Stem nematode. White-tip is Aphelenchoides besseyi.

q.q: Headquarters of the Indian Society of Mycology and Plant Pathology
q.e: Udaipur. The journal Indian Phytopathology comes from New Delhi.

q.q: Mycorrhiza is an association between
q.e: Ecto- and endo- (VAM/arbuscular) types.

q.q: Koch's postulates cannot be applied to
o: Obligate parasites such as rusts and viruses
q.e: They need pure culture, which obligates refuse.

q.q: The typical tank capacity of a knapsack sprayer
q.e: Most Indian texts give 9–22 L, with 16 L the standard. Worth confirming against your local extension notes — sources vary.

q.q: The word smut derives from a term meaning
q.e: From the German Schmutz — the sori look like soot smeared on the ear.

q.q: An abnormal increase in organ size caused by an increase in cell size is
q.e: Hypertrophy = bigger cells. Hyperplasia = more cells.

q.q: An abnormal increase caused by an increase in cell number is
q.e: Galls and clubroot involve both, but hyperplasia is division.

q.q: Under-development of an organ, as in little leaf, is
q.e: Hypoplastic symptoms: stunting, rosetting, little leaf, chlorosis.

q.q: A translucent, wet, water-soaked appearance of tissue is termed
q.e: Typical early sign of bacterial infection.

q.q: Pale, elongated, spindly growth in the absence of light is
q.e: Etiolation — distinct from chlorosis, which is loss of chlorophyll.

q.q: Progressive death of a shoot from the tip downwards is
q.e: Blight is rapid and general; dieback moves tip to base.

q.q: A localised, sunken, corky lesion on a woody stem is a
q.e: Canker. Spot = discrete leaf lesion; blotch = large diffuse discolouration.

q.q: A fruit that shrivels, dries and remains attached to the tree shows
q.e: Mummification — as in brown rot of stone fruit.

q.q: Anthracnose lesions characteristically bear
q.e: Sunken lesion with acervuli — Colletotrichum.

q.q: A sign of disease, as opposed to a symptom, is
o: The pathogen or its parts made visible
The host's reaction such as wilting
q.e: Mycelium, ooze, pustules, sclerotia are signs. Wilt and chlorosis are symptoms.

q.q: Death of plant cells and tissues is described as
q.e: The necrotic group covers spots, blights, cankers, rots and damping-off.

q.q: The arrival of inoculum on the infection court is called
q.e: Inoculation comes first; infection is establishment and nutrient withdrawal.

q.q: The period between inoculation and the appearance of symptoms is the
q.e: The latent period ends when the pathogen becomes infectious, not when symptoms show.

q.q: Primary inoculum typically arises from
q.e: Oospores, sclerotia, chlamydospores, dormant mycelium.

q.q: Inoculum potential refers to
o: The energy of the inoculum available for infection
q.e: Garrett's concept — quantity and vigour together.

q.q: The infection court is
o: The site where infection is initiated
q.e: Leaf surface, wound, root tip — wherever the pathogen establishes.

q.q: The structure that generates turgor pressure to force entry through the cuticle is the
q.e: Appressorium plus penetration peg. Melanin in the wall lets it hold the pressure.

q.q: A haustorium functions in
o: Nutrient absorption inside a host cell
q.e: Typical of biotrophs: rusts, powdery and downy mildews.

q.q: Entry through hydathodes is characteristic of
q.e: Xanthomonas campestris enters leaf margins through hydathodes, giving V-shaped lesions.

q.q: Which pathogen enters exclusively through stomata?
q.e: Rust germ tubes locate stomata and form appressoria over them.

q.q: A collateral host is
o: A wild host of the same family that carries the pathogen between seasons
A second host required to complete the life cycle
q.e: The alternate host is the one required for the sexual cycle — that is the distinction.

q.q: The most important agent of long-distance dispersal of fungal spores is
q.e: Rust uredospores travel hundreds of kilometres on wind.

q.q: Conidia of Colletotrichum are dispersed mainly by
q.e: They sit in a sticky mucilaginous matrix in the acervulus — splash-dispersed, not wind.

q.q: Macrophomina phaseolina survives in soil chiefly as
q.e: Tiny black microsclerotia — they persist for years.

q.q: Phytophthora and Pythium survive adverse periods as
q.e: The oospore is the thick-walled sexual survival structure.

q.q: Loose smut of wheat survives as
o: Dormant mycelium inside the seed embryo
q.e: Which is why surface disinfection fails and a systemic or hot water is needed.

q.q: Ergot survives between seasons as
o: Sclerotia (ergots) in soil or seed lot
q.e: The sclerotium germinates to give stromata with perithecia.

q.q: An alternate host differs from a collateral host in that it
o: Is required to complete the pathogen's life cycle
q.e: Barberry for wheat stem rust — the sexual stage happens there.

q.q: Which is a classic example of a seed-borne bacterium?
q.e: Black rot of crucifers moves on seed — hence hot water treatment of seed.

q.q: A simple-interest disease is
q.e: Vanderplank's term — inoculum does not multiply within the season.

q.q: A compound-interest disease is
o: Polycyclic, with repeated cycles in one season
q.e: Late blight, rusts — the epidemic compounds on itself.

q.q: A polycyclic disease typically gives a disease progress curve that is
q.e: S-shaped — slow start, rapid rise, plateau as tissue runs out.

q.q: A monocyclic disease typically follows which model?
q.e: A saturating curve with no self-multiplication term.

q.q: In Vanderplank's equation, r stands for
q.e: r is the rate, x is the amount. Crossing these is the single commonest slip.

q.q: Disease incidence means
q.e: Incidence counts plants; severity measures tissue.

q.q: AUDPC stands for a measure of
o: Disease accumulated over the whole epidemic
q.e: Area under the disease progress curve.

q.q: The disease tetrahedron adds which factor to the triangle?
q.e: Host, pathogen, environment, plus time. Adding man gives the disease pyramid.

q.q: Slow rusting is an expression of
q.e: Longer latent period, fewer and smaller pustules — the epidemic runs slower.

q.q: An epiphytotic is the plant equivalent of
q.e: Sudden, severe, widespread outbreak.

q.q: A disease regularly present in a locality at moderate levels is
q.e: Endemic — established and persistent.

q.q: Mills periods are used to forecast
q.e: Leaf wetness duration against temperature.

q.q: Beaumont periods and Blitecast are used to forecast
q.e: Temperature and humidity thresholds for Phytophthora infestans.

q.q: The first enzyme to act when a pathogen breaches the leaf surface is
q.e: The cuticle is the first barrier, so cutin is the first substrate.

q.q: Tissue maceration and soft rot are caused chiefly by
q.e: They dissolve the pectin of the middle lamella, so cells fall apart.

q.q: Ligninases are produced mainly by
q.e: Lignin is the hardest wall polymer to degrade.

q.q: According to Horsfall and Dimond, high-sugar diseases are favoured in
o: Juvenile tissue with high sugar content
q.e: Typically caused by obligate parasites such as rusts and powdery mildews.

q.q: Low-sugar pathogens attack more severely in
o: Mature or senescing tissue with low sugar
q.e: Alternaria and Botrytis are typical — facultative parasites of ageing tissue.

q.q: Vascular wilting is caused mainly by
o: Occlusion of xylem by tyloses, gums and mycelium
q.e: Physical blockage of water transport, often with toxins contributing.

q.q: Fusaric acid is
q.e: It damages many species, so it is non-specific.

q.q: Victorin is toxic only to
q.e: A host-specific toxin — the first isolated in pure form.

q.q: T-toxin from Bipolaris maydis race T acts specifically on
q.e: It targets a mitochondrial protein encoded by the T cytoplasm.

q.q: Tabtoxin causes wildfire of tobacco and is
q.e: It harms many species — non-specific.

q.q: Excessive elongation in bakanae of rice is caused by pathogen-produced
q.e: Gibberellin was first isolated from this fungus.

q.q: Gall formation in crown gall involves bacterial genes directing production of
q.e: T-DNA carries the hormone biosynthesis genes — hence uncontrolled growth.

q.q: Vertical resistance is
o: Race-specific and governed by major genes
q.e: Strong, but breaks down when a matching virulent race appears.

q.q: Horizontal resistance is
q.e: Partial but durable — it slows the epidemic rather than blocking it.

q.q: Tolerance means the plant
o: Becomes infected but still yields acceptably
q.e: Not true resistance — the pathogen multiplies normally.

q.q: The N gene of tobacco confers resistance to
q.e: A classic TIR-NBS-LRR gene giving a hypersensitive response to TMV.

q.q: The hypersensitive response is
o: Localised programmed cell death at the infection site
q.e: It starves the biotroph by killing the cells around it.

q.q: Phytoalexins are
o: Low molecular weight antimicrobials produced after infection
q.e: Induced. Phytoanticipins are the pre-formed ones.

q.q: The phytoalexin of potato is
q.e: Pisatin pea, phaseollin bean, rishitin potato, camalexin Arabidopsis.

q.q: PR proteins include
q.e: They attack fungal wall polymers — and mark SAR.

q.q: When non-pathogenic micro-organisms colonise plant tissue, the plant often responds by producing
q.e: Recognition of conserved microbial patterns triggers the defence programme.

q.q: SAR is characterised by
o: Salicylic acid and PR protein accumulation
q.e: Broad-spectrum and long-lasting; mimicked chemically by BTH and INA.

q.q: ISR triggered by rhizobacteria such as Pseudomonas fluorescens depends on
q.e: It works without SA or PR protein accumulation.

q.q: Papillae deposited at the point of attempted penetration consist largely of
q.e: A rapid local wall thickening — a structural defence.

q.q: Tyloses are
o: Balloon-like outgrowths of parenchyma into xylem vessels
q.e: They block the vessel — defensive against wilt pathogens, but they also cause wilting.

q.q: In dust formulations the active ingredient is usually about
q.e: Dusts carry a low load of active ingredient on an inert carrier.

q.q: WP in a fungicide label stands for
q.e: A powder that forms a suspension in water.

q.q: EC stands for
q.e: An oil-based formulation that emulsifies in water.

q.q: A surfactant is added to a spray in order to
o: Reduce surface tension so the spray spreads and sticks
q.e: Wetting agent, spreader, sticker — all adjuvants.

q.q: The fungicide most specifically effective against rusts is
q.e: Oxycarboxin, from the carboxamide group.

q.q: Fungicides specific to oomycetes belong to the
q.e: They target rRNA polymerase, which is why they touch nothing else.

q.q: The most effective and oldest treatment for powdery mildew is
q.e: Sulphur, in use since antiquity; triazoles are the modern option.

q.q: Loose smut of wheat, with mycelium inside the embryo, is best controlled by
o: A systemic such as carboxin, or hot water treatment
q.e: Surface treatments cannot reach the embryo.

q.q: A protectant fungicide must be applied
q.e: It forms a barrier on the surface; it cannot cure established infection.

q.q: An eradicant fungicide acts
q.e: Curative or therapeutic action.

q.q: Methyl bromide and chloropicrin are
q.e: Broad-spectrum soil sterilants; methyl bromide is now largely phased out.

q.q: Single-site systemic fungicides carry a high resistance risk because
o: One mutation at the single target site defeats them
q.e: Multisite compounds such as mancozeb and copper require many simultaneous mutations, so resistance is rare.

q.q: Plant quarantine falls under the principle of
q.e: Keeping the pathogen out of an area where it does not occur.

q.q: Rogueing and crop rotation fall under
q.e: Reducing or removing inoculum already present.

q.q: Growing a resistant variety falls under
q.e: Whetzel's fourth principle.

q.q: Adjusting the sowing date so the crop escapes the pathogen is
q.e: Escape in time — a later addition to Whetzel's four.

q.q: Soil solarisation works by
o: Raising soil temperature under transparent polythene
q.e: Needs moist soil, clear polythene and hot weather.

q.q: Trichoderma antagonises pathogens mainly through
q.e: It coils around hyphae and secretes wall-degrading enzymes.

q.q: Agrobacterium radiobacter strain K84 controls
q.e: It produces agrocin 84, which kills the pathogenic strain.

q.q: Hypovirulence as a biocontrol strategy was discovered in
q.e: A dsRNA element weakens chestnut blight and spreads through hyphal anastomosis.

q.q: Cross protection means
o: A mild strain protecting the plant against a severe strain
q.e: Used against citrus tristeza and papaya ring spot.

q.q: Virus-free planting material is best obtained by
q.e: The meristem tip usually outruns the virus; Morel and Martin, 1952.

q.q: The principal nutrient supplied to the host by mycorrhizal fungi is
q.e: Phosphorus is immobile in soil; the hyphae extend the depletion zone.

q.q: Arbuscular mycorrhiza is characterised by
o: A fungal mantle around the root
Arbuscules and vesicles inside root cortical cells
q.e: Endomycorrhiza — Glomeromycota.

q.q: Ectomycorrhiza is characterised by
o: A mantle and Hartig net without entering cells
q.e: Common on forest trees — pines, oaks.

q.q: The root parasite of bajra and sorghum is
q.e: Striga (witchweed) — a partial root parasite, it has chlorophyll.

q.q: Black tip of mango is caused by
q.e: Sulphur dioxide and other emissions — orchards near brick kilns suffer.

q.q: The micro-organism used in the brewing industry is
q.e: Brewer's and baker's yeast.

q.q: Beauveria and Metarhizium are examples of
q.e: Used as biopesticides — white and green muscardine.

q.q: The term rhizosphere was coined by
q.e: Hiltner, 1904 — the zone of soil influenced by root exudates.

q.q: Agaricus bisporus is
q.e: The most widely cultivated edible mushroom.

q.q: Damping-off of seedlings is favoured by
o: High soil moisture, high humidity and dense sowing
q.e: Pythium thrives in wet soil; thin sowing and good drainage reduce it.

q.q: A scab is best described as
o: A roughened, crust-like lesion on fruit, tuber or leaf
A sunken corky lesion on bark
q.e: Apple scab, potato scab, citrus scab.

q.q: A large, irregular, diffuse discoloured area on a leaf is a
q.e: Blotch — bigger and less defined than a spot.

q.q: Fasciation refers to
q.e: A hyperplastic malformation.

q.q: Witches' broom is
o: Abnormal proliferation of shoots from one point
q.e: Typical of phytoplasma infection and some rusts.

q.q: Phyllody means
o: Floral parts transformed into leaf-like structures
q.e: Classic phytoplasma symptom — sesame phyllody.

q.q: Virescence is
o: Greening of normally coloured floral parts
q.e: Another phytoplasma symptom, often with phyllody.

q.q: Vein clearing is an early symptom of
q.e: Veins become translucent before mosaic develops.

q.q: Vein banding refers to
o: Retention of dark green colour along veins
q.e: A viral symptom — tissue along veins stays green while the rest yellows.

q.q: The difference between mosaic and mottle is that mosaic shows
o: Sharply defined patches of contrasting colour
q.e: Mottle is the diffuse, ill-defined version.

q.q: Shot hole results when
o: Necrotic spot tissue drops out leaving holes
q.e: An abscission layer forms around the lesion and the dead tissue falls away.

q.q: Gummosis is
o: Exudation of gum from bark or fruit
q.e: Citrus gummosis caused by Phytophthora.

q.q: Enations are
o: Outgrowths from leaf veins or surface
q.e: Warty proliferations seen in some virus diseases.

q.q: Epinasty is
q.e: Caused by ethylene, common in vascular wilts.

q.q: Streak and stripe differ in that a stripe is
q.e: Stripes run between veins; streaks are irregular.

q.q: Russeting describes
o: Brown corky roughening of fruit skin
q.e: Often abiotic or caused by mites and some pathogens.

q.q: Scald refers to
o: Bleached, papery lesions as if scalded by hot water
q.e: Barley leaf scald; also post-harvest superficial scald of apple.

q.q: Silvering or silver leaf is
o: A grey metallic sheen from air pockets under the epidermis
q.e: Silver leaf of stone fruit, caused by Chondrostereum purpureum.

q.q: Damping-off occurring before seedlings emerge is termed
q.e: Seed or germinating seedling rots before reaching the surface — appears as poor germination.

q.q: Wilt as a symptom indicates disruption of
q.e: Vascular occlusion or root destruction.

q.q: Rosetting describes
o: Shortened internodes giving a bunched appearance
q.e: A hypoplastic symptom — groundnut rosette, little leaf.

q.q: The complete set of symptoms characterising a disease is called a

They are more susceptible to viral diseases

q.q: The term “phytosanitary” refers to:

The measures taken to protect plants from pests and diseases during trade

q.q: What is the concept of "frequency- dependent selection" in plant pathology?

It refers to how pathogens evolve resistance based on the frequency of their presence
It deals with the genetic variation of crops
It is related to the changing planting season of crops

q.q: In plant disease management, the concept of QTL mapping is used for:

Assessing the environmental impact of diseases

q.q: Which of the following is a key element in the process of breeding for disease resistance?

Planting crops with varying maturity dates

q.q: Which of the following is true about disease-free seed production?
o: It helps in preventing the spread of seed- borne pathogens
It has no impact on disease management

It leads to an increase in disease control
It is not a concern in integrated pest management

q.e: Answer: All of the above. From the ASRB NET 2025 Plant Pathology objective question set, arranged by syllabus unit. Answer key as supplied; no explanation accompanies it.

q.e: Answer: Irrigation systems. From the ASRB NET 2025 Plant Pathology objective question set, arranged by syllabus unit. Answer key as supplied; no explanation accompanies it.

q.q: What is the primary purpose of solarization in disease management?

The ability of soil to inhibit fungal growth
The natural resistance of plants to fungal pathogens
The interaction between pathogens and beneficial microbes

q.q: Plant growth-promoting rhizobacteria (PGPR) are beneficial because they:

q.q: Which of the following statements is correct regarding integrated disease management (IDM)?

IDM combines multiple methods for disease control
IDM excludes the use of resistant cultivars
IDM is only effective for bacterial diseases

To ensure the importation of disease-free plants and seeds

Breeding crops with resistance to multiple pathogens
Ignoring environmental factors affecting disease spread

q.q: Which of the following methods is used to manage bacterial diseases in crops?

They inhibit the pathogen's ability to infect plant cells
They form a protective barrier on the surface of the plant
They enhance the plant's immune system

To reduce soil-borne pathogens and pests

q.q: Which of the following is true about the genetic basis of disease resistance in plants?
o: It is controlled by a single gene only
It involves a complex interaction of multiple genes
It does not vary among different plant species
It is unrelated to the plant’s immune system
q.e: Answer: It involves a complex interaction of multiple genes. From the ASRB NET 2025 Plant Pathology objective question set, arranged by syllabus unit. Answer key as supplied; no explanation accompanies it.

q.q: Which of the following is an example of a biocontrol agent for plant diseases?
q.e: Answer: All of the above. From the ASRB NET 2025 Plant Pathology objective question set, arranged by syllabus unit. Answer key as supplied; no explanation accompanies it.

q.q: The concept of 'parasite-mediated frequency-dependent selection' explains:

How environmental factors influence disease resistance

To prevent the spread of exotic diseases and pests

They only work for specific pathogens and are highly effective
They can replace the use of all chemical pesticides

q.q: What is the primary objective of solarization as a disease control method?

To enhance microbial activity in the soil
To improve plant resistance to diseases

q.q: Which of the following is a method of controlling fungal diseases in plants?

q.q: Which of the following is a major limitation of using genetic resistance in disease management?

q.q: What is the role of seed treatment in plant disease management?
o: To protect seeds from soil-borne diseases
To promote plant growth during early stages

q.q: Which of the following is a common symptom of bacterial blight in rice?

q.q: The use of resistant cultivars is most effective for managing:

q.q: Which of the following practices is most effective in controlling rust diseases in crops?
q.e: Answer: All of the above. From the ASRB NET 2025 Plant Pathology objective question set, arranged by syllabus unit. Answer key as supplied; no explanation accompanies it.

o: They provide long-term immunity to plants against diseases
They can lead to resistance if used continuously on the same crop

q.q: Which of the following is a key consideration when applying fungicides to manage plant diseases?
o: The weather conditions at the time of application
The compatibility of fungicides with other chemicals

o: To reduce the reliance on chemical pesticides
To improve crop yield and quality
To use a single control method for all diseases
To control disease through multiple strategies

q.q: Which of the following is an example of a pathogen that is managed through seed treatment?

q.q: What is the purpose of the TRIPS agreement in the context of plant diseases?
o: To regulate the trade of plant pathogens
To promote the use of genetically modified organisms
To establish international standards for the protection of plant varieties
To limit the import of agricultural chemicals
q.e: Answer: To establish international standards for the protection of plant varieties. From the ASRB NET 2025 Plant Pathology objective question set, arranged by syllabus unit. Answer key as supplied; no explanation accompanies it.

q.q: Which of the following pathogens is primarily transmitted through infected seed?
q.e: Answer: Tomato mosaic virus. From the ASRB NET 2025 Plant Pathology objective question set, arranged by syllabus unit. Answer key as supplied; no explanation accompanies it.

q.q: Which of the following describes a key characteristic of effective plant quarantine measures?
o: They prevent the introduction of new plant diseases into a country
They allow for the free movement of agricultural products
They ensure that all crops are genetically modified
They focus only on the control of insect pests
q.e: Answer: They prevent the introduction of new plant diseases into a country. From the ASRB NET 2025 Plant Pathology objective question set, arranged by syllabus unit. Answer key as supplied; no explanation accompanies it.

q.q: Which of the following best describes the use of transgenic plants for disease resistance?
o: It involves genetic modification to confer resistance to specific pathogens
It is only effective for viral diseases
It relies on the overuse of chemical pesticides
It has no impact on the spread of plant diseases
q.e: Answer: It involves genetic modification to confer resistance to specific pathogens. From the ASRB NET 2025 Plant Pathology objective question set, arranged by syllabus unit. Answer key as supplied; no explanation accompanies it.

q.q: Which of the following is an example of a fastidious plant pathogen?
q.e: Answer: Mycoplasma. From the ASRB NET 2025 Plant Pathology objective question set, arranged by syllabus unit. Answer key as supplied; no explanation accompanies it.

q.q: Which of the following is NOT a method of reducing pesticide resistance in plant pathogens?
o: Rotate fungicides with different modes of action
Apply pesticides at the recommended dosages
Use the same fungicide repeatedly on the same crops
Incorporate non-chemical methods into disease management
q.e: Answer: Use the same fungicide repeatedly on the same crops. From the ASRB NET 2025 Plant Pathology objective question set, arranged by syllabus unit. Answer key as supplied; no explanation accompanies it.

q.q: Which of the following practices is most effective in preventing viral diseases in crops?
q.e: Answer: All of the above. From the ASRB NET 2025 Plant Pathology objective question set, arranged by syllabus unit. Answer key as supplied; no explanation accompanies it.

q.q: Which of the following is the most significant factor in preventing the introduction of exotic plant pathogens?
o: Reducing the use of chemical fungicides
q.e: Answer: Strengthening national quarantine regulations. From the ASRB NET 2025 Plant Pathology objective question set, arranged by syllabus unit. Answer key as supplied; no explanation accompanies it.

q.q: Which of the following is the key factor that contributes to the success of cultural control methods in disease management?
o: Manipulation of environmental conditions to reduce pathogen survival
q.e: Answer: Manipulation of environmental conditions to reduce pathogen survival. From the ASRB NET 2025 Plant Pathology objective question set, arranged by syllabus unit. Answer key as supplied; no explanation accompanies it.

q.q: Which of the following is an example of a viral disease that affects cereal crops?
q.e: Answer: Wheat streak mosaic. From the ASRB NET 2025 Plant Pathology objective question set, arranged by syllabus unit. Answer key as supplied; no explanation accompanies it.

q.q: Which of the following is the most effective method for controlling root rot caused by Phytophthora species?
q.e: Answer: All of the above. From the ASRB NET 2025 Plant Pathology objective question set, arranged by syllabus unit. Answer key as supplied; no explanation accompanies it.

q.q: Which of the following is a common method for managing nematode- induced diseases in the soil?
q.e: Answer: All of the above. From the ASRB NET 2025 Plant Pathology objective question set, arranged by syllabus unit. Answer key as supplied; no explanation accompanies it.

q.q: Which of the following is a method of reducing the spread of bacterial diseases in plant nurseries?
q.e: Answer: All of the above. From the ASRB NET 2025 Plant Pathology objective question set, arranged by syllabus unit. Answer key as supplied; no explanation accompanies it.

q.q: Which of the following is a commonly used method to monitor the efficacy of disease management strategies?
o: Visual inspection of plants for symptoms
q.e: Answer: All of the above. From the ASRB NET 2025 Plant Pathology objective question set, arranged by syllabus unit. Answer key as supplied; no explanation accompanies it.

q.q: Which of the following is an example of a biological control agent used against fungal pathogens?
q.e: Answer: Both A and C. From the ASRB NET 2025 Plant Pathology objective question set, arranged by syllabus unit. Answer key as supplied; no explanation accompanies it.

q.q: Which of the following is a disadvantage of using chemical fungicides in disease management?
o: They can lead to resistance development in pathogens
They are costly and require frequent applications
They may harm beneficial organisms in the soil
q.e: Answer: All of the above. From the ASRB NET 2025 Plant Pathology objective question set, arranged by syllabus unit. Answer key as supplied; no explanation accompanies it.

q.q: Which of the following is a characteristic of systemic fungicides?
o: They are applied only to the surface of the plant
They are absorbed by the plant and transported through tissues
They are less effective than contact fungicides
They are not absorbed by plant tissues
q.e: Answer: They are absorbed by the plant and transported through tissues. From the ASRB NET 2025 Plant Pathology objective question set, arranged by syllabus unit. Answer key as supplied; no explanation accompanies it.

q.q: Which of the following is the key benefit of using resistant plant varieties in disease management?
o: It prevents the pathogen from infecting the plant
It eliminates the need for chemical pesticides
It ensures long-term immunity against diseases
q.e: Answer: It prevents the pathogen from infecting the plant. From the ASRB NET 2025 Plant Pathology objective question set, arranged by syllabus unit. Answer key as supplied; no explanation accompanies it.

q.q: Which of the following is a cultural practice used to control fungal diseases in crops?
q.e: Answer: Crop rotation. From the ASRB NET 2025 Plant Pathology objective question set, arranged by syllabus unit. Answer key as supplied; no explanation accompanies it.

q.q: Which of the following is the most effective way to manage rust diseases in plants?
q.e: Answer: All of the above. From the ASRB NET 2025 Plant Pathology objective question set, arranged by syllabus unit. Answer key as supplied; no explanation accompanies it.

q.q: Which of the following is NOT an example of a physical method for disease control?
o: Application of heat treatments to seeds
Use of physical barriers such as nets
q.e: Answer: Use of plant resistance. From the ASRB NET 2025 Plant Pathology objective question set, arranged by syllabus unit. Answer key as supplied; no explanation accompanies it.

q.q: Which of the following is a characteristic of the gene-for-gene hypothesis in plant disease resistance?
o: A single plant gene controls resistance to multiple pathogens
Resistance is conferred by the plant in response to specific pathogen genes
Pathogen resistance is achieved through genetic modification
The hypothesis is only applicable to viral diseases
q.e: Answer: Resistance is conferred by the plant in response to specific pathogen genes. From the ASRB NET 2025 Plant Pathology objective question set, arranged by syllabus unit. Answer key as supplied; no explanation accompanies it.

q.q: Which of the following is a key element of an effective disease management strategy for high-value crops?
o: Regular monitoring and early detection of diseases
Application of fungicides only after disease symptoms appear
q.e: Answer: Regular monitoring and early detection of diseases. From the ASRB NET 2025 Plant Pathology objective question set, arranged by syllabus unit. Answer key as supplied; no explanation accompanies it.

q.q: Which of the following is a benefit of using integrated pest management (IPM) alongside disease management?
o: Reduces the overall use of chemical pesticides
q.e: Answer: All of the above. From the ASRB NET 2025 Plant Pathology objective question set, arranged by syllabus unit. Answer key as supplied; no explanation accompanies it.

q.q: Which of the following pathogens can be controlled through the use of biocontrol agents such as Bacillus subtilis?
q.e: Answer: Fungal pathogens. From the ASRB NET 2025 Plant Pathology objective question set, arranged by syllabus unit. Answer key as supplied; no explanation accompanies it.

q.q: Which of the following methods can be used to manage bacterial wilt in solanaceous crops?
q.e: Answer: All of the above. From the ASRB NET 2025 Plant Pathology objective question set, arranged by syllabus unit. Answer key as supplied; no explanation accompanies it.

q.q: Which of the following is the most common mode of transmission for viral diseases in plants?
q.e: Answer: Insect vectors. From the ASRB NET 2025 Plant Pathology objective question set, arranged by syllabus unit. Answer key as supplied; no explanation accompanies it.

q.q: Which of the following is a key factor in the successful application of fungicides?
o: Application at the proper timing during the disease cycle
Regular monitoring of disease levels to determine the need for treatment
q.e: Answer: All of the above. From the ASRB NET 2025 Plant Pathology objective question set, arranged by syllabus unit. Answer key as supplied; no explanation accompanies it.

q.q: Which of the following is a key characteristic of phytoplasma diseases in plants?

They are transmitted by insect vectors

q.q: Which of the following pathogens causes a major disease in grapes known as "Pierce’s disease"?

q.q: Which of the following is a disadvantage of using chemical control methods in plant disease management?

They are always more expensive than other control methods
They are less effective against viral diseases
q.e: Answer: They can cause resistance in pathogens over time. From the ASRB NET 2025 Plant Pathology objective question set, arranged by syllabus unit. Answer key as supplied; no explanation accompanies it.

q.q: Which of the following is the most suitable cultural practice for managing soil-borne diseases in vegetables?

q.q: Which of the following is an example of a disease-resistant mechanism in plants?
q.e: Answer: Hypersensitive response. From the ASRB NET 2025 Plant Pathology objective question set, arranged by syllabus unit. Answer key as supplied; no explanation accompanies it.

q.q: Which of the following diseases is caused by Ralstonia solanacearum?

q.q: Which of the following is the main environmental factor that promotes the development of fungal diseases in crops?

q.q: Which of the following is NOT an important aspect of integrated disease management (IDM)?

q.q: Which of the following is the primary advantage of seed treatment in disease management?

It enhances the genetic potential of seeds

q.q: Which of the following is a characteristic of an effective fungicide?

It should be highly selective for the target pathogen
It has a broad-spectrum action against various pathogens
It should only act after the pathogen has infected the plant
q.e: Answer: It should be highly selective for the target pathogen. From the ASRB NET 2025 Plant Pathology objective question set, arranged by syllabus unit. Answer key as supplied; no explanation accompanies it.

q.q: Which of the following practices is most effective for managing downy mildew in grapes?

q.e: Answer: Both B and C. From the ASRB NET 2025 Plant Pathology objective question set, arranged by syllabus unit. Answer key as supplied; no explanation accompanies it.

q.q: What is the role of a plant growth- promoting rhizobacteria (PGPR) in disease management?

It directly kills pathogenic fungi in the soil
It acts as a biological pesticide
It increases the absorption of nutrients from the soil

q.q: Which of the following is NOT a benefit of using solarization for soil-borne disease control?

It is a chemical-free method of disease control
q.e: Answer: It increases the soil's moisture content. From the ASRB NET 2025 Plant Pathology objective question set, arranged by syllabus unit. Answer key as supplied; no explanation accompanies it.

q.q: Which of the following methods is used for controlling late blight in potatoes and tomatoes?
q.e: Answer: All of the above. From the ASRB NET 2025 Plant Pathology objective question set, arranged by syllabus unit. Answer key as supplied; no explanation accompanies it.

q.q: What is the primary objective of plant quarantine in relation to plant diseases?
o: To prevent the introduction and spread of exotic pathogens
To ensure the free trade of all plant species
To encourage the use of genetically modified crops
To reduce the cost of pesticides
q.e: Answer: To prevent the introduction and spread of exotic pathogens. From the ASRB NET 2025 Plant Pathology objective question set, arranged by syllabus unit. Answer key as supplied; no explanation accompanies it.

q.q: Which of the following is a physical control method used to manage fungal diseases in crops?
q.e: Answer: Both A and C. From the ASRB NET 2025 Plant Pathology objective question set, arranged by syllabus unit. Answer key as supplied; no explanation accompanies it.

q.q: Which of the following pathogens causes bacterial canker in tomatoes?
q.e: Answer: Pseudomonas syringae. From the ASRB NET 2025 Plant Pathology objective question set, arranged by syllabus unit. Answer key as supplied; no explanation accompanies it.

q.q: Which of the following is an essential aspect of seed certification in disease management?
o: Ensuring seeds are free of diseases and pathogens
Using chemical treatments on all seeds
q.e: Answer: Ensuring seeds are free of diseases and pathogens. From the ASRB NET 2025 Plant Pathology objective question set, arranged by syllabus unit. Answer key as supplied; no explanation accompanies it.

q.q: Which of the following pathogens is transmitted through insect vectors, such as aphids, in plant diseases?
q.e: Answer: Potato virus X. From the ASRB NET 2025 Plant Pathology objective question set, arranged by syllabus unit. Answer key as supplied; no explanation accompanies it.

q.q: Which of the following fungal diseases of wheat can be controlled through crop rotation and resistant varieties?

q.q: Which of the following statements is true regarding fungicide resistance in plant pathogens?

Fungicide resistance can only occur in bacteria
Resistance to fungicides is not a significant problem
Fungicide resistance can be prevented through crop rotation

q.q: Which of the following is a key factor in preventing the introduction of new pathogens into a region?

q.e: Answer: Effective plant quarantine measures. From the ASRB NET 2025 Plant Pathology objective question set, arranged by syllabus unit. Answer key as supplied; no explanation accompanies it.

q.q: Which of the following is an example of a viral disease controlled by vector management?

q.q: Which of the following is a commonly used fungicide in the management of apple scab?
q.e: Answer: Both A and B. From the ASRB NET 2025 Plant Pathology objective question set, arranged by syllabus unit. Answer key as supplied; no explanation accompanies it.

q.q: Which of the following is NOT an advantage of using resistant plant varieties in disease management?
o: It reduces the need for chemical treatments
It provides long-term protection against specific pathogens
It leads to reduced biodiversity in crops
It decreases crop loss due to diseases
q.e: Answer: It leads to reduced biodiversity in crops. From the ASRB NET 2025 Plant Pathology objective question set, arranged by syllabus unit. Answer key as supplied; no explanation accompanies it.

q.q: Which of the following is a typical symptom of root-knot nematode infection in plants?

q.e: Answer: Galls or swelling on the roots. From the ASRB NET 2025 Plant Pathology objective question set, arranged by syllabus unit. Answer key as supplied; no explanation accompanies it.

q.q: Which of the following is a common method for managing postharvest diseases in fruits and vegetables?

q.e: Answer: All of the above. From the ASRB NET 2025 Plant Pathology objective question set, arranged by syllabus unit. Answer key as supplied; no explanation accompanies it.

q.q: Which of the following is a benefit of using cultural practices in disease management?
o: They reduce the spread of diseases through the environment
They help in controlling soil-borne pathogens
They are environmentally friendly and sustainable
q.e: Answer: All of the above. From the ASRB NET 2025 Plant Pathology objective question set, arranged by syllabus unit. Answer key as supplied; no explanation accompanies it.

sheets.glossary:
97 terms across ten groups.

In this sheet

Necrotic symptoms (cell death)15

Necrosis
Death of cells or tissue, seen as browning or blackening.
Chlorosis
Yellowing due to failure or loss of chlorophyll.
Leaf spot
A limited, defined necrotic lesion on the leaf.
Blight
Rapid, extensive death of leaves, flowers or shoots.
Blotch
Large, irregular necrotic areas on leaves or fruit.
Streak / stripe
Elongated necrotic lesions running along the veins.
Canker
A localised, often sunken, necrotic lesion on stem or bark.
Anthracnose
Sunken necrotic lesion bearing acervuli (dark fruiting bodies).
Scab
Roughened, corky, crust-like lesions on fruit, tuber or leaf.
Die-back
Progressive death of shoots from the tip downward.
Damping-off
Collapse of seedlings from rot at the soil line.
Rot (soft / dry)
Disintegration and maceration of tissue, wet or dry.
Blast
Sudden death of florets, panicle or young tissue.
Scald
Bleaching or whitening of tissue as if scalded.
Shot-hole
Necrotic spots that drop out, leaving holes in the leaf.

Viral / mosaic-type symptoms6

Mosaic
Irregular light- and dark-green patches on the leaf.
Mottle
Diffuse, blurred light and dark areas (less sharp than mosaic).
Vein clearing
Veins become translucent or pale — an early viral sign.
Vein banding
Retention of green colour along the veins.
Ring spot
Chlorotic or necrotic concentric rings (typical of viruses).
Streak (viral)
Necrotic or chlorotic streaks along the leaf.

Overgrowth (hyperplasia / hypertrophy)8

Hypertrophy
Abnormal enlargement of cells.
Hyperplasia
Abnormal increase in cell number (excess division).
Gall / tumour
A localised swelling or overgrowth of tissue.
Witches' broom
Dense proliferation of shoots giving a broom-like cluster.
Leaf curl / crinkle
Distortion of the leaf from uneven growth of tissue.
Fasciation
Flattening and fusion of stems or shoots.
Enation
An outgrowth from the leaf blade or vein (often viral).
Fruit / stem galls
Swellings induced by pathogens such as Agrobacterium.

Phytoplasma / hormonal disorders5

Phyllody
Floral parts transformed into leaf-like structures.
Virescence
Greening of normally coloured floral parts.
Little leaf
Marked reduction in leaf size (e.g. brinjal little leaf).
Big bud
Abnormal enlargement of buds (phytoplasma).
Bunchy top / bushy
Shortened internodes giving a crowded, bunched habit.

Underdevelopment (hypoplasia)4

Stunting
General reduction in size and vigour of the plant.
Rosetting
Shortened internodes with leaves clustered in a rosette.
Chlorosis (hypoplastic)
Failure of chlorophyll development, giving pale tissue.
Suppression
Reduced or arrested development of an organ.

Surface / mildew growths6

Powdery mildew
White powdery fungal growth on the plant surface.
Downy mildew
Fungal growth (often greyish) on the lower leaf surface.
Rust
Pustules releasing rusty-coloured urediniospores.
Smut
Sooty black masses of spores replacing plant organs.
Sooty mould
Superficial black fungal growth on honeydew.
Gummosis
Exudation of gum from bark or fruit.

Fungal structures & spores20

Appressorium
Swollen hyphal tip that attaches and aids penetration.
Haustorium
Feeding structure of a biotroph inside the host cell.
Hypha / mycelium
A fungal filament / a mass of hyphae.
Sclerotium
A compact, melanised resting mass of hyphae.
Rhizomorph
A root-like strand of aggregated hyphae (e.g. Armillaria).
Stroma
A compact vegetative mass on which fructifications form.
Chlamydospore
A thick-walled asexual resting spore.
Conidium
An asexual spore borne on a conidiophore.
Sporangium
A sac producing (often motile) spores.
Zoospore
A motile, flagellate asexual spore.
Oospore
The thick-walled sexual spore of Oomycetes.
Zygospore
The sexual resting spore of Zygomycetes.
Ascospore / ascus
Sexual spore of Ascomycetes, borne in a sac (ascus).
Basidiospore / basidium
Sexual spore of Basidiomycetes, borne on a basidium.
Acervulus
A flat, cushion-like asexual fruiting body (Colletotrichum).
Pycnidium
A flask-shaped asexual fruiting body bearing conidia.
Perithecium
A flask-shaped ascocarp with a pore (ostiole).
Cleistothecium
A closed, spherical ascocarp with no pore.
Apothecium
An open, cup-shaped ascocarp.
Sorus
A mass or cluster of spores (as in rusts and smuts).

Nematode & feeding structures4

Stylet
Hollow spear used by nematodes to pierce and feed on cells.
Giant cell
Enlarged multinucleate feeding cell induced by Meloidogyne.
Syncytium
Fused multinucleate feeding cell induced by cyst nematodes.
Cyst
The tanned, egg-filled dead body of a cyst-nematode female.

Parasitism & infection concepts15

Pathogenicity
The ability of an organism to cause disease.
Virulence
The degree or intensity of pathogenicity of a race.
Aggressiveness
Quantity of disease a virulent isolate causes.
Biotroph
Pathogen that feeds only on living tissue.
Necrotroph
Pathogen that kills tissue and feeds on the dead cells.
Hemibiotroph
Biotrophic first, then switching to a necrotrophic phase.
Obligate parasite
Grows only on a living host, not in pure culture.
Facultative parasite
Usually saprophytic but can parasitise a host.
Inoculum
The pathogen units that initiate infection.
Inoculum potential
Energy of growth of a pathogen available for infection.
Incubation period
Time from infection to first visible symptoms.
Latent period
Time from infection to the onset of sporulation.
Predisposition
Effect of environment making a host more susceptible.
Primary inoculum
Inoculum that starts the first infections of a season.
Secondary inoculum
Inoculum produced by primary infections, spreading disease.

Resistance & epidemiology terms14

Hypersensitive response
Rapid localised cell death that confines a pathogen.
Phytoalexin
Antimicrobial synthesised by the host after infection.
Phytoanticipin
Antimicrobial present in the host before infection.
Elicitor
A molecule that triggers host defence responses.
Vertical resistance
Race-specific, major-gene resistance (reduces x0).
Horizontal resistance
Polygenic, race-non-specific resistance (reduces r).
Tolerance
Host suffers little yield loss despite being infected.
Escape
Host avoids infection by chance, not by resistance.
Immunity
Complete non-infection of a host by a pathogen.
Epiphytotic
An epidemic — sudden widespread outbreak of plant disease.
Endemic
A disease constantly present at low level in an area.
Pandemic
An epidemic spread over a very wide geographic area.
Etiology
The study of the cause of a disease.
Koch's postulates
The rules used to prove an organism causes a disease.

sheets.bact100:
100 bacteria grouped by genus and Gram reaction.

Flagella — what to remember for the exam

The types: atrichous (none) · monotrichous (one polar) · amphitrichous (one at each pole) · lophotrichous (a polar tuft) · peritrichous (all over).

Arrangement is a taxonomic key: it historically split the two big Gram-negative groups — polar flagella = Pseudomonas / Xanthomonas / Ralstonia line, versus peritrichous = Erwinia / Pectobacterium / Dickeya (Enterobacteriaceae) line.

Highest-yield facts: Xanthomonas is always monotrichous (single polar). Xylella, Liberibacter and phytoplasmas are non-motile / have no flagella. Most Gram-positive pathogens (Clavibacter, Streptomyces, Leifsonia, Rathayibacter) are non-motile — Curtobacterium is the motile exception. Spiroplasma has no flagella but is motile by helical rotation.

Also worth knowing: the flagellum's protein is flagellin = the H antigen (serotyping); flg22, a flagellin epitope, is the PAMP recognised by the FLS2 receptor in plant immunity.

sheets.mode:
A listening script — roughly twelve minutes read aloud.

In this sheet
Have your phone read this page aloud. iOS: Settings → Accessibility → Spoken Content → Speak Screen, then swipe down with two fingers. Android: Select-to-Speak, or any read-aloud app.

Five groups of fungicide are learnt together, sound alike, and blur together. So instead of a table, each group gets a story: what the fungicide does, why that kills the fungus, and one hook that holds it in place.

The five, in one breath5

  • Benzimidazoles hit beta-tubulin.
  • Triazoles hit ergosterol.
  • Carboxin hits succinate dehydrogenase.
  • Strobilurins hit cytochrome b c one.
  • Metalaxyl hits RNA polymerase, and only in oomycetes.

1Benzimidazoles and beta-tubulin

Carbendazim. Benomyl. Thiophanate-methyl. All three are the same weapon.

Tubulin is the protein that builds the spindle. The spindle is what pulls chromosomes apart when a cell divides. Break the tubulin, and the fungus cannot divide. It is not poisoned, exactly. It is sterilised. It stops multiplying.

The hook is the sound. Benzimidazole. Beta-tubulin. Both start with the same letter. Ben, beta. Nothing else in the list starts with B.

One extra fact that gets asked. Benomyl is not really the active molecule. Once inside the plant it breaks down into carbendazim, and carbendazim does the work. So if a question offers you both, and asks what benomyl converts to, the answer is carbendazim. Thiophanate-methyl does the same thing. Three names, one target.

Ben, beta.

2Triazoles and ergosterol

Propiconazole. Tebuconazole. Hexaconazole. Triadimefon. Anything ending in conazole or azole, put it here.

Every cell needs a membrane. Animal membranes are held together by cholesterol. Fungal membranes use a different sterol, called ergosterol. That difference is the whole reason this group works. Block ergosterol, and the fungus cannot build a membrane. We are unharmed, because we do not use ergosterol.

The specific enzyme blocked is C-fourteen demethylase. That is why the group is called DMI, standing for demethylation inhibitor. You may also see SBI, sterol biosynthesis inhibitor — same idea, wider family.

The hook is that fungi are not animals. When you hear azole, think membrane. Think the sterol that is theirs and not ours.

Azole, ergosterol.

3Carboxin and succinate dehydrogenase

Carboxin. Oxycarboxin. And the modern ones, boscalid and fluxapyroxad.

This group attacks breathing. Specifically it jams complex two of the respiratory chain, the enzyme called succinate dehydrogenase. The fungus cannot make energy, so it dies.

The group name is SDHI — succinate dehydrogenase inhibitor. The name tells you the target, which is a gift. If you can remember the abbreviation, you already have the answer.

Two more facts, both frequently asked. Carboxin was the first true systemic fungicide, in nineteen sixty-six, by von Schmeling and Kulka. Before it, fungicides sat on the surface; carboxin moved inside the plant. And carboxin is used against smuts and rusts — loose smut of wheat in particular, because the fungus is dormant inside the embryo where a contact fungicide can never reach.

SDHI. The name is the answer.

4Strobilurins and cytochrome bc1

Azoxystrobin. Kresoxim-methyl. Anything with strobin in it.

This group also attacks breathing, which is exactly why it gets confused with carboxin. But it hits a different point in the chain. Not complex two. Complex three — the cytochrome b c one complex, at a site called the Q-o site, the quinone outside site. Hence the group name, QoI.

Here is how to keep it apart from carboxin. Both stop respiration. But carboxin is old and hits complex two; strobilurins are newer and hit complex three. Two before three, old before new.

And a hook for the name itself. Strobilurins were originally derived from a woodland mushroom, Strobilurus — a fungus that produced a compound to kill other fungi. We copied it.

Strobin, Q-o, complex three.

5Metalaxyl and RNA polymerase

Metalaxyl. The phenylamide group, also called acylalanines.

Metalaxyl blocks RNA polymerase. Stop RNA polymerase and you stop transcription, and nothing gets built. But the crucial point, the one that gets examined, is not the enzyme. It is the specificity.

Metalaxyl works only on oomycetes. Only the water moulds. Pythium. Phytophthora. Plasmopara. Peronospora. Downy mildews, late blight, damping-off. It does nothing to a rust, nothing to a powdery mildew, nothing to Fusarium.

Why? Because oomycetes are not really fungi. Different lineage, cellulose walls instead of chitin, closer to algae than to mushrooms. Their biochemistry is different enough that a compound can target them alone. So if a question says a fungicide is specific to oomycetes, you barely need to think.

Metalaxyl, oomycetes, RNA polymerase.

The pairs that blur

Look at what these five have in common, and you can see why they blur.

Carboxin and strobilurins both stop respiration. That is one pair to keep apart, and complex two versus complex three does it.

Benzimidazoles and triazoles are both systemics, usually learnt in the same sentence. Beta-tubulin versus ergosterol. Ben and beta; azole and ergosterol.

When an MCQ offers two mechanisms that both sound plausible, that is the moment to slow down. Half a beat. Ask which letter the group starts with, or which complex number it is. The hook will surface.

Multisite versus single-site

Every fungicide above hits exactly one target. One enzyme, one site. That makes them powerful and specific. It also makes them fragile. A single mutation at that one site, and the fungicide is worthless — often against the whole group at once.

Contrast mancozeb. Or copper. Or chlorothalonil. Or sulphur. These are multisite: they interfere with many enzymes at once, non-specifically. Copper simply denatures proteins wherever it finds them. To become resistant to that, a fungus would need many simultaneous mutations, which effectively does not happen.

So the rule. Single-site means high resistance risk. Multisite means low resistance risk. Strobilurins and benzimidazoles are famous for resistance failures in the field; mancozeb has been used for decades and still works. That is not a coincidence — it is the direct consequence of how they act.

This is also why fungicides are sold in mixtures, and why rotation between groups is recommended. You are trying to avoid handing the fungus a single target to adapt to.

The rest of the cast5

Tricyclazole
Rice blast. Blocks melanin. Sounds harmless, but melanin is what makes the appressorium wall strong enough to hold pressure. Without it the appressorium cannot generate turgor and cannot punch through the cuticle. The fungus is alive and completely unable to enter.
Dicarboximides
Iprodione and vinclozolin, for Botrytis and Sclerotinia — grey mould and white mould.
Organophosphates
Edifenphos and kitazin, for rice blast.
Streptomycin
For bacteria, acting on the thirty S ribosomal subunit, stopping protein synthesis.
Phytoplasmas
From a different chapter, but related: phytoplasmas have no cell wall, so penicillin does nothing and tetracycline works. Penicillin no, tetracycline yes.

The last minute7

Benzimidazoles
Beta-tubulin. Mitosis.
Triazoles
Ergosterol. C-fourteen demethylase. DMI.
Carboxin
Succinate dehydrogenase. Complex two. SDHI. First systemic, 1966. Smuts and rusts.
Strobilurins
Cytochrome bc1. Complex three. QoI.
Metalaxyl
RNA polymerase. Oomycetes only.
Multisite
Mancozeb, copper, chlorothalonil, sulphur. Low resistance risk.
Single-site
Everything else. High resistance risk.

How disease develops, and how an epidemic builds.

Two diagrams that the epidemiology questions keep returning to.

Disease needs a susceptible host, a virulent pathogen and a favourable environment, together and for long enough. The cycle describes how the pathogen gets from one host to the next, and how many times it can do so in a season.

Tobacco mosaic virus (TMV)p74

TMV belongs to the genus Tobamovirus, which is a sub microscopic, rigid, rod-shaped particle which produces mosaic like symptoms in plants.
In recent ICTV classification Tobamovirus comes under the family of Virgaviridae
TMV is a single stranded RNA (+ss RNA) made up of 5 % NA (RNA) and 95 % protein coat.
TMV consists of 158 - Amino acids (Anderer and Tsugita, 1960) 2130 - Capsomere subunits (coat protein, CP) 6400 - Nucleotides (6.4 kb)
TMV consists 130 helix turns of protein subunits, each helix containing 16 1/3 (49) sub units per turn, and the pitch of the helix is 2.3 nm.
TMV amino acid molecular weight 17,600 daltons (17.6 kDa/ 17.6 kd/ 17.06 K) determined by Knight.

Terms and quick factsp75–76

•Genome size of TMV is 6.4 kb
•Refraction index of TMV is 1.57
•TMV genome can be altered by using ADP (Adenosine di phosphate)
•TMV molecular weight 39 million dalton
•Nucleic acid molecular weight of TMV – 2 × 106 dalton
•TMV is a rigid, helical rod-shaped virus particles and measure about 300 × 18 nm
•TIP (Thermal inactivation point) of TMV is 93 °C
•Dilution end point 10-6
•TMV producing inclusion bodies are called X bodies (crystalline and amorphous inclusion
bodies)
•TMV Resistant gene is N1
Cell to cell movement of TMV is mediated through plasmodesmata with the help of movement protein. TMV produces a 30 kDa movement protein called P30 which enlarges the plasmodesmata and facilitates the movement.
TMV is not transmitted by insects, nematodes or other vectors, but mechanical transmission/ sap transmission.
TMV containing 4 ORF rings (ORF
Open reading frame)
Surprisingly, TMV can also mediate the movement of unrelated viruses, such as potato leaf roll luteovirus (PLRV), which are normally limited to the host phloem.
It has been reported that, purified TMV is still infectious even after 50 years of storage in the laboratory conditions (4°C/ 40°F). Note – TMV produce movement protein size of 30 kDa Coat protein size of 17.5 kDa Replicase enzyme size of 126 kDa & 183 kDa

1st discoveries associated with TMVp77

•1st recognised plant virus in the world.
•1st inclusion bodies produced plant virus to be noticed (Ivanovsky).
•1st cross protection technique developed (McKinney, 1929).
•1st identifiable phenotypic mutant of plant virus is reported (McKinney).
•1st virus to be chemically purified/ crystallised (Stanley, 1935; Bawden, 1936).
•1st coat protein to be sequenced (Anderer and Tsugita, 1960).
•1st antigen.
•1st sap transmission.
•1st coat protein mediated gene resistance (Powell-Abel and Beachy, 1986)
•1st virus shown to encode a cell to cell movement protein (Deom, 1987).
•1st to prove that specific antigen infecting plants (Beale).
•1st serological studies of plant virus are to be reported (Beale).

Agrobacterium radiobacter strain K1026, is the result of a simple genetic alteration of a naturally occurring bacterium Agrobacterium radiobacter strain K84.
Except for the deletion of a small portion of DNA removed in K84, the two strains are essentially identical and have the same characteristics.
Removal of this genetic material prevents the transfer of resistance from strain K1026 to other strains.

Autoclavep146

The autoclave was invented by Charles Chamberland in 1884
The name originated from Greek auto - self (ultimate meaning) Latin clavis - meaning key, “So autoclave is a self-locking device”
The mechanism involved is saturated steam under pressure
It is used for sterilizing solid media, liquid media, glassware, equipment’s, rubber products and supplies by subjecting them to high-pressure saturated steam at 121 °C (249 °F) for around 15-20 minutes depending on the size of the load and the contents
(The exact temperature and pressure are 121.6° C for 15 lbs for 15 – 20 min)

Polymerase chain reaction (PCR)/ Thermocyclerp154

PCR is laboratory (in vitro) technique used to amplify target nucleic acid (DNA) sequence into many copies (millions or billions) in the presence of primers (oligonucleotide primers).

By using thermo stable enzyme Taq polymerase (isolated from Thermus aquaticus, Chien et al., 1976) that can amplify target nucleic acids

LAMP works under the principle of autocatalytic strand displacement reaction where nucleic acid amplifies using BST (Bacillus Stereo thermophillus) DNA polymerase at constant temperature to produce millions of copies of DNA

Paul D.N. Hebert et al (2003) was first to propose DNA barcoding system, a standardized method of identifying species and allocating unknown sequences to higher taxa such as orders and phyla.

One gene one enzyme hypothesisp163

G.W. Beadle and E.L. Tatum (1941) evolved the concept of one gene-one enzyme hypothesis with their studies conducted in red bread mould (Neurospora crassa).
Hypothesis
Each gene responsible for producing a single enzyme that in turn affects a single step in a metabolic pathway. The concept which united the fields of genetics and biochemistry.
The concept was a major breakthrough that recognises the role of genes in specifying protein structures.
Norman Horowitz named the concept as “one gene
one enzyme hypothesis” in 1948, before it was called ‘genes produce enzymes that control a single metabolic step’.

Hypersensitivity and mechanism of hypersensitivityp164

Hypersensitivity/ Hypersensitive response (HR) is a cell defense mechanism or type or programmed cell death that can be used by host plants which prevents the spread of disease caused by pathogen.
Synonyms
Suprasensitivity, hypersuceptability, hyperergy
E.C. Stakman (1915) introduced the term and concept of hypersensitivity in physiological plant pathology.
The HR occurs only in specific host-pathogen combination in which the host and pathogen are incompatible.

Phenolic theoryp166

J.C. Walker (1940) was first to propose and demonstrate the chemical nature of disease resistance in plants.
The phenolic substances which plays a major role in plant protection and defense activation in onion.
Eg
Coloured varieties of onion, red onions, contains phenolic substances (Catechol and Protocatechuic acid) in the dry scales of bulbs, which are strongly toxic to Colletotrichum circinans (onion smudge). Whereas these phenolic substances are absent in white onion which is highly susceptible to smudge disease.

Phytoalexinsp167

Phytoalexins are low molecular weight antimicrobial compounds produced in considerable amounts by plants in response of biotic and abiotic factors (pathogens, parasites, chemicals, enzymes and toxins etc.) and confer protection against infecting parasite.
Phyto
plant, Alexin – protecting substance (phytoalexins are plant protecting substances, in literature alexin means “to ward off”).
Muller and Borger (1940) proposed the concept while studying with the interaction between potato and Phytophthora infestans system.

Toxin, classification and role of toxins in pathogenesisp171

1. Phytotoxins
Any compound produced by the microorganism which is toxic to plants is called phytotoxin.
Produce few or no symptoms.
Phytotoxins has no role in pathogenicity.
Eg
Alternaric acid, lycomarasmin and cochliobolin. 2. Vivotoxins
Diamond and Waggoner (1953) coined the term “vivotoxin” and defined as substance produced in the infected hosts by the pathogen and/ or its host which functions in the production of disease but is not itself the initial inciting agent of the disease.
It produces majority of the symptoms which determines the virulence
Vivotoxin is usually non-specific.
Eg
Fusaric acid, pyricularin and lycomarasmin 3. Pathotoxins
This toxin may be produced by the pathogen, host or interaction between them, which plays major role in disease production and development.
Pathotoxin mainly determines the pathogenicity and produce characteristic symptoms of the disease.
Eg
Pyricularin, ten toxin, tab toxin and victorin

RNA interference (RNAi)p182

The biological process in which RNA (dsRNA) molecule inhibits the expression of gene/ regulates the gene expression by destructing mRNA molecule, in which it ultimately inhibits/ affects the production of proteins.
Other names
Co-supression, post-transcriptional gene silencing (PTGS), Quelling.
Thi smechanism was 1st described by Andrew Fire (Stanford university) and Craig C. Mello (Massachusetts Medical School) in nematode Caenorhabditis elegans (lowly worm), in 1998 and shared noble prize in 2006 for their most exciting discovery.
Hamilton and Baulcombe (1999) was first to report post transcriptional gene silencing in plants.

Meristem tip culturep183

Morel and Martin (1952) developed meristem tip culture for the production of virus free plants. The first virus free plants were developed in Dahlia to eliminate Dahlia mosaic virus.
Examples
Elimination of viruses like PVA, PVX, PVY, PVS, PLRV (potato), TMV (tobacco), CaMV (cauliflower), CMV (banana) etc. by using meristem tip culture.

Agrobacterium mediated gene transfer in plantsp184

Characteristics of Ti-plasmid
It is a circular, extra chromosomal, double stranded self-replicating, tumour inducing structure in bacteria (A. tumefaciens).
Ti plasmid has two components i. Octopine
Two T-DNA regions: TL (14 kb) and TR (7 kb) ii. Nopaline – Contains one T-DNA region (20 kb), size is about 200 kb.

Structure of Ti-plasmidp185

a. T-DNA
In nopaline-type Ti plasmids, the T-DNA is a 23,000-nucleotide-pair segment.
It carries 13 known genes including genes encoding enzymes that catalyze the synthesis of phytohormones (the auxin, indole 3-acetic acid and the cytokinin isopentenyl adenosine).
These phytohormones are responsible for the tumorous growth of cells in crown galls. b. Vir region
It contains the genes required for the T-DNA transfer process.
These genes encode the DNA processing enzymes required for excision, transfer, and integration of the T- DNA segment.
Phenolic compounds such as acetosyringone act as inducers of the vir genes.
At least nine vir gene operons have been identified. These includes vir A, vir G, vir B1, Vir C1, Vir D1, D2, vir D4 and vir E1, E2

Hybridoma technology, production of monoclonalp186

antibodies
Hybridoma technology is a method for producing large numbers of identical antibodies (also called monoclonal antibodies), Fusions of myeloma cell lines with B cells to create hybridomas that could produce antibodies.
Kohler and Milstein (1975) were 1st to develop hybridoma technology for the production of monoclonal antibodies and shared Nobel Prize in 1984 in the field of Physiology and medicine. The term hybridoma was coined by Leonard Herzenberg in 1975.

Terms and quick factsp187

Specific medium used for Hybridoma technology (production of monoclonal antibodies) is - HAT Medium (HAT- Hypoxanthine aminopterin thymidine)
Did you know
The viruses that contains reverse transcriptase enzyme are known as retroviruses. The enzyme reverse transcriptase was independently isolated by Martin Temin and David Baltimore (they received Nobel Prize in Physiology or medicine in 1975).

CRISPR/ Cas9 technologyp188

CRISPR/Cas9 is a technique that allows highly specific and rapid modification of DNA in a genome, the complete set of genetic instructions in an organism.
Full name
Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats (CRISPR).
CRISPR/ cas9, gene-editing technique was first reported in Escherichia coli by Ishino et al. 1987

parasitism & infection concepts virulence the degree or intensity of pathogenicity of a race.
parasitism & infection concepts aggressiveness quantity of disease a virulent isolate causes.
parasitism & infection concepts biotroph pathogen that feeds only on living tissue.
parasitism & infection concepts necrotroph pathogen that kills tissue and feeds on the dead cells.
parasitism & infection concepts hemibiotroph biotrophic first, then switching to a necrotrophic phase.
parasitism & infection concepts obligate parasite grows only on a living host, not in pure culture.
parasitism & infection concepts facultative parasite usually saprophytic but can parasitise a host.
parasitism & infection concepts inoculum the pathogen units that initiate infection.
parasitism & infection concepts inoculum potential energy of growth of a pathogen available for infection.
parasitism & infection concepts incubation period time from infection to first visible symptoms.
parasitism & infection concepts latent period time from infection to the onset of sporulation.
parasitism & infection concepts predisposition effect of environment making a host more susceptible.
parasitism & infection concepts primary inoculum inoculum that starts the first infections of a season.
parasitism & infection concepts secondary inoculum inoculum produced by primary infections, spreading disease.

resistance & epidemiology terms phytoalexin antimicrobial synthesised by the host after infection.
resistance & epidemiology terms phytoanticipin antimicrobial present in the host before infection.
resistance & epidemiology terms elicitor a molecule that triggers host defence responses.
resistance & epidemiology terms vertical resistance race-specific, major-gene resistance (reduces x0).
resistance & epidemiology terms horizontal resistance polygenic, race-non-specific resistance (reduces r).
resistance & epidemiology terms tolerance host suffers little yield loss despite being infected.
resistance & epidemiology terms escape host avoids infection by chance, not by resistance.
resistance & epidemiology terms immunity complete non-infection of a host by a pathogen.
resistance & epidemiology terms epiphytotic an epidemic — sudden widespread outbreak of plant disease.
resistance & epidemiology terms endemic a disease constantly present at low level in an area.
resistance & epidemiology terms pandemic an epidemic spread over a very wide geographic area.
resistance & epidemiology terms etiology the study of the cause of a disease.
resistance & epidemiology terms koch's postulates the rules used to prove an organism causes a disease.

➢ mycelium – group of hyphae collectively called as mycelium. ➢ hyphae – it is a microscopic, thread like, thin, transparent tubular filamentous structure filled with protoplasm. hyphae is divided into • septate hyphae – presence of cross walls. • aseptate hyphae/ coenocytic hyphae/ non-septate hyphae – absence of cross walls. ➢ rhizoid – it is anchoring or absorbing organ of rhizopus. ➢ sporangiophore – it is a stalk like structure that bears sporangia. ➢ sporangia – spore bearing structure, where spore are packed inside. a sporangium is a sac like structure with a membranous wall. ➢ sporangiospores – these are the spores produced from sporangium (plu: sporangia) ➢ homothallic – male and female organs are produced on the same thallus. • eg – pythium ➢ heterothallic – male and female organs are produced on different thallus. • eg – phytophthora ➢ appressorium – attachment organ of fungi

tobacco mosaic virus (tmv) • tmv belongs to the genus tobamovirus, which is a sub microscopic, rigid, rod-shaped particle which produces mosaic like symptoms in plants. • in recent ictv classification tobamovirus comes under the family of virgaviridae • tmv is a single stranded rna (+ss rna) made up of 5 % na (rna) and 95 % protein coat. • tmv consists of 158 - amino acids (anderer and tsugita, 1960) 2130 - capsomere subunits (coat protein, cp) 6400 - nucleotides (6.4 kb) • tmv consists 130 helix turns of protein subunits, each helix containing 16 1/3 (49) sub units per turn, and the pitch of the helix is 2.3 nm. • tmv amino acid molecular weight 17,600 daltons (17.6 kda/ 17.6 kd/ 17.06 k) determined by knight.
